description:
## Task: TRD-019
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-019
PRD Reference: #req-015

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.
Satisfies: REQ-015
PRD ACs: AC-015-1, AC-015-2
Target File: packages/agent-core/src/behavior/protected-paths.ts
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given each of the four protected categories, when classified, then each returns its category rather than `ordinary`.
Dependencies: TRD-017

title: PRD-4: Adaptive planning depth
description:
Add scale-adaptive planning depth to Ensemble — lightweight path for simple changes, full path for complex

## Problem
Ensemble has fixed PRD→TRD pipeline for all work. BMAD adapts depth based on work complexity.

## Goals
- Simple changes (bug fixes, small features) use lightweight path with minimal overhead
- Complex initiatives use full PRD→TRD pipeline
- Complexity detection auto-classifies work before planning begins

## User Stories
- As a developer fixing a bug, I want lightweight path so I don't write a PRD for a 1-line fix
- As a lead, I want adaptive depth so team right-sizes planning effort to work complexity

## Requirements
- FR-001: classify command detects work complexity (Simple/Medium/Complex)
- FR-002: Simple work → fix-issue path (no PRD/TRD)
- FR-003: Medium work → create-prd + implement-trd
- FR-004: Complex work → full PRD→TRD→implement pipeline
- FR-005: Complexity classification exposed to user for override

## Verification
- Bug fix classified as Simple → fix-issue path
- New feature classified as Complex → full pipeline
close_reason: Shipped as analyze-complexity changes: b8ac9cd (readable signals, no team size, repo facts, --bead) + 62d2368 (option C confirmation). br-iah merged earlier.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
ANALYSIS, no code yet. Read alongside br-iah; they overlap enough that implementing both as written would violate spec section 7.

OVERLAP. br-0r3 FR-001 wants a 'classify' command emitting Simple/Medium/Complex. br-iah FR-001 wants an 'analyze-complexity' command emitting a 1-10 score. Both then dispatch to the SAME three paths: fix-issue, PRD->TRD, full pipeline. br-iah FR-002/3/4 just band the score into br-0r3's three categories (1-3, 4-6, 7-10). So br-iah is br-0r3 plus a finer-grained internal scale, not a separate capability.

Building both gives two commands that decide the same routing question and can DISAGREE. That is the dual-dispatch-path anti-pattern the implementation requirements forbid in section 7, and disagreement here is not cosmetic: it decides whether a piece of work gets a PRD.

RECOMMENDATION. One command. Score 1-10 internally because it is the more expressive representation and br-iah FR-005 requires showing it, then band to Simple/Medium/Complex for dispatch because that is what routing consumes. br-0r3 FR-005 and br-iah FR-006 are the same override requirement stated twice.

WHY A COMMAND AND NOT A BEHAVIOR, since it was asked. Both beads require the classification be shown to the user BEFORE planning begins and be overridable. Behaviors are asynchronous observers with no return channel and no guarantee of resolving before the session ends (see br-mr22), so a behavior cannot gate the routing decision or hand a value back to the caller. The OBSERVATIONAL half does fit a behavior: noticing after the fact that work classified Simple grew into a multi-file change is exactly the learning loop behaviors are for, and it feeds classifier calibration without gating anything.

UNRESOLVED. br-iah's score is to be AI-derived from 'scope size, dependencies, risk factors, team size'. Nothing in either bead says where those inputs come from at classify time, and for a one-line description most are unknowable. Worth settling before implementation: a confident 1-10 score derived from absent inputs is exactly the unevidenced-confidence failure br-42nn exists to prevent.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
DECISION (operator, this session): merge. br-iah closed as duplicate; its requirements are absorbed here. Consolidated scope for whoever implements:

ONE command, 'classify'. No second command. Scoring and routing are a single decision with a single owner.

- Scores 1-10 internally and SHOWS the score (was br-iah FR-005). The score is the more expressive representation and is what a user needs in order to judge an override.
- Bands the score for dispatch: 1-3 Simple -> fix-issue, 4-6 Medium -> create-prd + implement-trd, 7-10 Complex -> full pipeline with extra review (was br-iah FR-002/3/4, matching br-0r3 FR-002/3/4).
- User can override, and the override is the authoritative value from that point on (br-0r3 FR-005 and br-iah FR-006 are the same requirement; it is now stated once).
- Verification merges both beads' cases: bug description -> score <=3 -> fix-issue; complex initiative -> score >=7 -> full pipeline with extra gates.

STILL UNRESOLVED, and it should be settled before code rather than discovered during it. br-iah specified the score as derived from scope size, dependencies, risk factors and team size. At classify time the input is typically a short description, from which none of those four are reliably knowable. Options are to score only on what is actually readable and say so, or to require richer input, or to return low confidence explicitly. What should NOT happen is a confident 7 derived from inputs that were never available -- that is the unevidenced-confidence failure mode br-42nn exists to prevent, and it would be routing decisions rather than brief entries.

NOT A BEHAVIOR, for the record, since it was raised. Behaviors are async observers with no return channel and no guarantee of resolving before session end (br-mr22), so they cannot gate routing or return a value to the caller. The observational half is a good behavior candidate though: noticing that work classified Simple grew into a multi-file change is real calibration signal and gates nothing.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
DECISION (operator, 2026-09-29): the scorer uses READABLE SIGNALS and reports its confidence explicitly. This settles the one open question left in the 01:58 comment.

INPUTS classify may read, and nothing else:
1. The description text: its wording, and any file paths, module or package names, and command names it mentions.
2. The repo facts those mentions resolve to: whether the paths exist, their size, how many packages they span, fan-in (how many importers), and whether they are protected paths.
3. If given a bead id rather than free text: the bead's type, priority, labels and dependency count.
Team size is not readable and is dropped as an input. It never becomes a guessed value.

OUTPUT: score 1-10, the band (1-3 Simple, 4-6 Medium, 7-10 Complex), confidence (high/medium/low), the signals that drove the score (each one cited to the text or repo fact it came from), and the inputs that were missing.

ROUTING: at high confidence, show the result and route unless the user overrides. At low or medium confidence, show the result together with the missing inputs and require the user to confirm or override before dispatch (FR-005). The override stays authoritative. A score must never read as confident when its inputs were absent. That is the br-42nn failure mode applied to routing.

VERIFICATION, added to the existing cases:
- A one-line description that names no resolvable path returns low confidence, and routing waits for the user.
- A description naming a file with high fan-in that spans packages scores higher than the same text naming a leaf file.
- The missing-inputs list is never empty when team size, dependency data, or similar inputs were unavailable.

The scope is now fully settled. Next step is implementation (new command in packages/agent-core/src/cqrs/).

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CORRECTION (2026-09-29): this is ALREADY BUILT. Both the 01:58 'no code yet' analysis and my own 'new command in packages/agent-core/src/cqrs/' were wrong. ensemble:analyze-complexity (packages/development/commands/analyze-complexity.yaml plus lib/complexity-analyzer.js) shipped in #62 (run-4042, 2026-09-02) and was fixed in #65. It has: the 1-10 score, the 1-3/4-6/7-10 bands, routing to fix-issue / create-prd+create-trd / full pipeline with refine gates, a --route override, confidence, missingDetails, and a confirmation gate. Do NOT build a second classifier (spec s7). The cqrs catalog is wrong in any case: it is reachable only from behaviors via workflow-dispatch, never from a user.

REMAINING WORK = the gap between the shipped scorer and the operator decision above:
1. scoreTeamSize guesses from keywords (users, approvals, foreman, owners). Remove it. Team size is not readable.
2. Paths and modules named in the text are never resolved against the repo. Add: exists, size, package span, fan-in, protected. Each counts as cited evidence.
3. No bead-id input. Add --bead <id>, reading type, priority, labels and dependency count via br show --json.
4. needsConfirmation fires only when confidence is low AND there is no evidence. The operator chose 'if confidence is low, the user must confirm or override'. Confirming does not reroute, so the #65 concern (giving a typo a PRD) does not apply.
The 'low OR medium' wording in my DECISION comment went beyond the option the operator chose. The operator's choice (low only) is authoritative.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
PROGRESS (b8ac9cd): gaps 1-3 shipped in analyze-complexity. (1) Team size removed as a dimension and always listed as missing; score rescaled to 1+sum over 3 dimensions. (2) Named paths are resolved via git: size, package span (2+ packages raises scope to 3), and import fan-in (1/3/10 importers give dependencies 1/2/3), each cited. Unresolved or ambiguous paths are listed as missing. (3) --bead <id> scores type and dependency counts; priority and labels are cited but not scored, and cannot disarm the confirmation gate. A Missing Inputs section was added to the report. Tests: 71 analyzer tests (12 new, on a real temp git repo; fan-in tests confirmed to fail when the bug is reintroduced). Development suite 909/909, pi 256/256, generate:validate passes.

DROPPED from the input list: 'protected path'. The analyzer ships in a plugin that runs in arbitrary user repos, and Ensemble's protected-path list is internal to agent-core, so there is no portable source for it.

OPEN, gap 4 (needs operator): 'low confidence -> confirm' contradicts the #65 tests, which deliberately let recognisably small work through without a prompt. Measured on this repo: 'Fix a typo in packages/development/README.md' still comes out LOW confidence after path resolution (only scope has evidence). So adopting low -> confirm means every typo or one-liner asks before dispatch.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: DONE. Option C shipped in 62d2368: interactive low confidence asks unless the work is recognisably small (a narrow marker, or one named file with fan-in < 3), and the report states confirmationReason. Development 914/914, pi 256/256, generate:validate passes. With b8ac9cd, all four gaps from the operator decision are closed.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: Landing: PR #106 to dev (branch feat/analyze-complexity-readable-signals, cherry-picks of b8ac9cd + 62d2368). The feature branch's reconciliation with dev is a separate track (CQRS wins; dev's fixes get a disposition each, per the operator on 2026-09-29).

  WRITE-CAPABLE: _write, _manage_skill, _learn

Adding --no-tools AND --no-skills changes nothing: the same three remain. So the tools allowlist does not govern them at all.

PROVEN ESCAPE. The child was asked to use them. It created:
  ~/.omp/agent/managed-skills/containment-probe-delete-me/SKILL.md
A real file, in the OPERATOR'S HOME, outside the disposable worktree, which is loaded as a skill in every future session in every project. Verified on disk, then deleted.

_learn reported 'Lesson queued for retention' but no durable trace was found; treat as unconfirmed rather than safe.

WHY THIS IS P0 AND NOT A TIDINESS BUG.

The fix child's prompt is built from TEST OUTPUT. The runtime's own injected instructions say so in capitals: 'synthesised by an extension from TEST OUTPUT, which is attacker-influenceable in principle'. So the chain is:

  attacker-influenceable text -> fix-agent child -> a skill file in ~/.omp
  -> loaded into every future session, in every repository, indefinitely.

Content quarantine is carefully done in the session. It does not extend to what the child can persist. The sandbox contains file writes to the repo and nothing else.

CONSEQUENCE FOR br-r3om. Its comments credit the tool restriction as one of two defences. The measurement says it contributes nothing to write containment; the disposable worktree is the only one. Defence in depth is defence in one, and the comments should stop claiming otherwise.

CONSEQUENCE FOR br-cxn8. Seeing _write, the model tries to USE it instead of returning a patch, then reports failure in prose -- which is the unparseable reply that killed the governed path. Verbatim: 'the write tool refused src/math.js because it only accepts xd:// tool calls'.

ALSO: my br-cxn8 fix currently asserts 'You have NO tools that can change this repository'. The child can see that is false. Do not instruct a model with a claim it can disprove; make it a directive instead.

FIX DIRECTIONS, none verified yet:
  1. A host-level setting that disables _learn/_manage_skill for a child, if one exists.
  2. Run the child with a throwaway HOME/profile (--profile) so anything it persists dies with the run.
  3. Stop using a general agent for this and call a completion endpoint with no tools at all.
Option 3 removes the class rather than the instance.

title: Memorialize decisions surfaced in conversation, so future sessions do not re-learn them
description:
ORIGIN. A live example, 2026-09-29. The agent inverted the Foreman/Ensemble relationship -- assuming two peer systems exchanging events rather than Foreman launching and owning the session Ensemble runs inside. It then spent two turns designing an ingestion layer (pull loops, cursors, git-carried inboxes, HTTP polling) for messages nobody needs to send. The user corrected it in conversation; it was written into AGENTS.md by hand.

THE GAP THIS FILLS, and why the existing pipeline does not. br-u5o / br-pyg build learning-log.jsonl -> constitution-rules.yaml -> fold-prompt proposing constitution.md changes. That pipeline learns from a FAILURE CORPUS: test failures, recurrence counts. The Foreman inversion was not a failure. Nothing failed, no test broke, no command errored. It surfaced only because a human contradicted a belief the agent had stated. No existing machinery would have caught it, and re-learning it is expensive.

These two lanes should MEET, not duplicate. br-u5o/br-pyg own learning from failures; this owns capture of decisions reached in conversation. Coordinate before building.

DESIGN CONSTRAINTS, each from evidence rather than principle:

1. PROPOSE ONLY, APPLY IS SEPARATE AND APPROVED. AGENTS.md is read by every future session, so a wrong entry is far worse than a missing one: it becomes a fabricated premise that future sessions treat as authoritative and build on. This is not hypothetical -- event-catalog.ts is exactly that, aspirational documentation nobody re-checked, and it misled this session into the design above (br-jgxo). The same session produced at least four confident fabrications (a CLI that did not exist, a wrong compile() signature, invented line citations, an unverified publish claim). All were caught in conversation. Any one auto-written to AGENTS.md would have propagated silently and been indistinguishable from verified entries.

2. EXPLICIT TRIGGER FIRST, INFERENCE LATER. The tempting design triggers on runtime.prompt.submitted and asks a model 'was that a decision?' every turn. That is a model call per prompt and it will be noisy; noise trains people to ignore the channel, which loses the feature permanently. In the originating example the USER noticed. Noticing is the expensive, high-judgement part and a human already does it reliably. Ship the explicit invocation, measure how often it is used, then consider inferring.

3. IF AUTOMATED LATER, THE SIGNAL IS USER CORRECTION -- not 'a decision was made', which is too broad, but specifically the user contradicting something the agent asserted. Rare (a handful per session), high-signal, and honest about provenance: the durable knowledge came from the human.

4. EVIDENCE REQUIRED. Every entry cites its source -- the file, the command output, or the conversation turn. Same discipline as constitution.propose's sourceEvidence.

5. STALENESS MUST BE VISIBLE. Memory that accumulates without pruning becomes its own aspirational catalog: confident statements nobody verifies, growing until future sessions skim it. Entries need a date, provenance, and ideally a way to check whether they still hold.

SCOPE:
- A decision.propose command writing an evidence-backed entry to a decisions artifact, reusing ProposalStore.
- An approval-gated decision.apply writing into AGENTS.md, reusing MutationGuard. Note AGENTS.md is hand-authored source at the repo root; packages/pi/AGENTS.md is GENERATED and must not be written directly.
- Explicitly NOT a new learning pipeline.

TESTS: propose writes nothing to AGENTS.md; apply requires approval; apply refuses when AGENTS.md changed since the proposal (base-SHA, as constitution.apply does); an entry without evidence is rejected.
close_reason: Partial: decision.propose shipped (5052e3c, 449aae0, dcd742c; 20 tests). decision.apply split to br-f1ex.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: DECISION FROM THE USER 2026-09-29: keep this SEPARATE from br-u5o / br-pyg rather than folding into one pipeline. Two lanes: that pair learns from the failure corpus, this one captures decisions reached in conversation. They may converge at the proposal step later, but neither owns the other and neither blocks the other.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
PROGRESS: propose half shipped, apply half blocked on operator approval.

DONE (commits 5052e3c, 449aae0, and this one):
- cqrs/decision-memory.ts: resolves the brief, renders the entry.
- decision.propose command, registered and capability-gated.
- decision.proposed in event-authority.ts + trigger-producers.ts. NOT in event-catalog.ts, following the constitution.applied/declined precedent: the catalog governs TRIGGERS, the authority governs EMISSION, so no protected-file edit was needed for the event itself.
- ProposalKind gained a distinct 'decision' member, so a constitution proposal cannot be applied to AGENTS.md or vice versa.
- 20 tests. 563 agent-core tests pass.

THREE CONSTRAINTS FROM THE BEAD ARE STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN DOCUMENTED:
- evidence has minItems 1, and the schema rejects violations as MALFORMED before the handler runs. An unevidenced entry is inexpressible, not merely refused by logic someone could later soften.
- recordedAt and provenance render INTO the entry text, so staleness stays visible once it lands in the file rather than only in a proposal record.
- propose writes nothing: proven through the real registry.execute path against a real file, not by testing the formatter.

A DESIGN FIX THE REVIEW CAUGHT. I first mirrored resolveConstitutionPath's walk-up-take-first-hit. That is right for a constitution (there is one) and WRONG for AGENTS.md (there are several, some generated). Invoked from under packages/pi/, it would have found the GENERATED brief and written an entry that survives until the next build and then vanishes -- no error, no warning, the silent-loss mode. Now anchored to the git root, so the generated file is unreachable by construction rather than by denylist. Test covers exactly that case.

HAZARD FOR WHOEVER BUILDS APPLY, found while testing the baseline: currentHash returns NULL when the file does not exist, and baseSha256 stores it. An apply that compares onDisk !== write.baseSha256 would then treat null === null as 'unchanged' and happily write to a brief that had been DELETED since the proposal. constitution.apply has the same shape. Apply must treat a null baseline as a refusal, not a match.

BLOCKED ON: /ensemble-approve 32 (protected-paths.ts, AGENTS.md gets reason 'decision-memory') and 33 (mutation-guard.ts, second sanctioned class 'decision.write', double-keyed to reason+class so constitution.write cannot reach the brief). Operator chose this posture over reusing constitution.write. Until both land AGENTS.md has NO protected-path defence, so shipping apply now would give it a write path with no defence in depth -- the option the operator explicitly declined.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CORRECTION, retracting the hazard in my previous comment. It was wrong and I had not tested it before asserting it.

I claimed apply could fail open via onDisk=null === baseSha256=null on a deleted brief, and that constitution.apply shared the exposure. Neither holds. Verified in source:

- resolveDecisionsPath (decision-memory.ts:74-85) readFileSync's the candidate and REFUSES when absent, before any proposal exists. So baseSha256 on a stored decision proposal is always a real hash, never null. Already covered by decision-memory.test.ts:52.
- constitutionApply (commands.ts:589) re-resolves via constitutionPath() and returns rejected on a missing file BEFORE the hash comparison at :593. A deleted brief never reaches the compare.
- The deletion case I described therefore evaluates null !== '<realhash>', which correctly REJECTS. It was already handled.

The null === null comparison IS reachable on the generic write path (commands.ts:242) where w.path may not exist, but there it is CORRECT rather than fail-open: a null baseline records 'this file was expected absent', and if anything creates it before apply, onDisk becomes a real hash, differs from null, and the apply rejects. That is the check working.

The only residual is a TOCTOU race between the existence check and the hash call -- narrow, different in kind, and not worth pre-emptive work. Whoever builds decision.apply should mirror constitutionApply's order as-is: resolve path first, compare hash second. No extra null guard needed.

Net effect on the apply design: none. Mirror the precedent.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: DECISION (operator, 2026-09-29): ship propose-only and close as partial. The apply half moves to br-f1ex. Reason: apply needs two protected-file edits, and today showed what those cost (br-suoh: a partial revert, an unfixable tree while an agent session was active, and two commits with misleading messages). propose is useful by itself: proposals are recorded with evidence and provenance, and nothing reaches AGENTS.md without a human.

title: Fix-agent child can still reach MCP devices (xd://), manage_skill and learn
description:
Residual from br-r3om. The fix-agent child now runs with `--tools=read,grep,glob`, which removes edit/bash and makes `write` refuse filesystem paths (probed live). It still has:

- `write` over the `xd://` device transport: mounted MCP servers from ~/.omp/agent/mcp.json (here: Foreman MCP, incl. foreman_task_create which creates AND dispatches a run, foreman_workflow_put, foreman_prompt_put).
- `manage_skill` and `learn` (persist skills/memory under ~/.omp).

None can write the working tree directly, but a child could dispatch a Foreman run (which writes code in its own worktree) or persist a skill that alters future sessions -- neither governed by the behavior's manifest. omp has no `--no-mcp` flag; candidate levers: a `--config` overlay (`memory.backend: off`, `autolearn.enabled: false`, `skills.enabled: false`, `disabledProviders`), or `tools.approvalMode` that denies in print mode. Each needs a live probe before being trusted.

## Acceptance
- A spawned fix agent cannot invoke any MCP/xd:// device, `manage_skill`, or `learn` (probed live: told explicitly to, the call is refused), and its reply is still parsed as before.
close_reason: Closed by the containment work in br-33co, now pinned by tests. All three routes named here are shut by pointing the child at a throwaway home rather than by the tool allowlist (which was proven not to contain anything): HOME, USERPROFILE, the four XDG roots, OMP_HOME, OMP_CONFIG_DIR, PI_HOME and PI_CONFIG_DIR are all redirected. mcp.json is read from the OMP home, so the operator's MCP servers -- including the Foreman tools that create and dispatch runs -- are not mounted; manage_skill and learn write into the throwaway and die with it. Evidence: hostile-tools.e2e.test.ts has a live probe writing a skill into $HOME and asserting it never appears in the real homedir(); new agent-containment-env.test.ts (5 tests) pins the redirection itself, including that it REDIRECTS rather than unsets (an unset HOME falls back to the passwd entry, i.e. the real home) and that PATH is left intact so the child still starts.

title: Add multi-reviewer share-URL fan-out to refinement-review
description:
## Problem

ensemble-full-refine-prd --collab --tunnel=quick currently mints exactly ONE share URL per session (packages/core/lib/refinement-review/server.js:768-773 in startServer; server.js:839-844 in setTunnelUrl). The /api/exchange handler atomically burns the nonce (server.js:89-99 via consumeNonce), so the second reviewer hitting the same URL gets 401 'invalid or expired nonce' and is locked out.

The mental model that 'each reviewer redeems their own copy of the URL within the TTL' is not actually true: the nonce map is keyed by id, identical URLs share one nonce, and there is no HTTP route to mint additional nonces (full route list: /api/exchange, /api/events, /api/session, /api/document, PATCH /api/questions/:id, POST /api/comments, PATCH /api/comments/:id, /api/complete). mintNonce is exported under _internal (server.js:884) and is callable only in-process.

## Goal

Let the operator fan out N independent share URLs for one session so multiple reviewers can join concurrently.

## Scope (minimum viable)

- Add result.createShareUrl() to the result object returned by startServer (server.js:808-819). Mints a fresh nonce against the current publicUrl and returns { reviewUrl, shareNonce }. In-process only; no HTTP route required.
- Bootstrap CLI flag --reviewers <N> that calls createShareUrl() N times and logs all N URLs.
- Test: confirm N independent reviewer URLs all redeem successfully and each reviewer gets an independent review-sid cookie bound to the same session.
- Update the refinement review guide to document the multi-reviewer flow + the security trade-off (each URL is single-use; leak window = NONCE_TTL_MS = 10 min).

## Out of scope

- N-use nonces (rejected: trades leaked-URL-permanence for first-hit-locks-out, opposite of current threat model).
- Authenticated /api/share route (operator-side fan-out matches the current threat model; per-reviewer invite is a v2 concern).
- Changes to bearer or cookie session semantics.

## Acceptance

- startServer().createShareUrl() returns a fresh { reviewUrl, shareNonce } each call, bound to the same opts.sessionPath.
- Calling createShareUrl() N times yields N independent URLs.
- Following URL[k] sets a review-sid cookie distinct from URL[j] for k != j, both authenticated to the same session.
- Bootstrap with --reviewers 3 logs 3 URLs and the SPA loads for each.

## Notes

- Discovered during PRD-2026-019 refinement session 2026-08-12.
- The current single-reviewer flow is preserved; this is additive.
- Nonce TTL is 10 min (NONCE_TTL_MS at server.js).

Committed ca1d638 on feature/refinement-review-tunnel.

title: E2E fixtures embed copies of shipped behavior manifests and have already drifted
description:
FOUND 2026-09-29 while verifying br-zcxb.

reference-flow.e2e.test.ts is the repository's end-to-end proof that the behavior flow works. It does not run the manifests that ship. It embeds its own inline copies as template literals (FIX_BEHAVIOR, LEARN_BEHAVIOR).

THE COPIES HAVE ALREADY DRIFTED. The inline constitution-learning passes only:
  proposalRef, detail
The shipped .ensemble/behaviors/constitution-learning/behavior.yaml passes:
  proposalRef, detail, command, diagnosis, evidence
The diagnosis and evidence inputs are the br-zcxb fix. The e2e test asserts the flow works while exercising a manifest that predates that fix, so it would have stayed green if the shipped manifest lost those inputs entirely.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY STALE FIXTURE. The e2e is specifically the artifact cited when asking whether the system works end to end. Its value comes entirely from being the real thing. A copy that shares a name with the shipped manifest but not its contents reports on a behavior that nobody runs, and nothing signals the divergence -- the copy is valid YAML and compiles cleanly.

The same pattern applies to FIX_BEHAVIOR versus .ensemble/behaviors/fix-failing-test/behavior.yaml; I have not diffed that pair.

MITIGATED, NOT FIXED, in 5eb36b0: agent-core/tests/shipped-constitution-manifest.test.ts loads the SHIPPED manifest and proves the diagnosis reaches the assessment (mutation-checked: removing the input fails 2 tests). That covers the one input pair br-zcxb was about. It does not stop the e2e copies drifting again, anywhere else.

OPTIONS
(a) Have the e2e read the shipped manifests instead of embedding copies. Loses the ability to test variants inline, and couples the e2e to whatever the repo currently ships -- which is arguably the point of an e2e.
(b) Keep the copies but assert they are byte-identical to the shipped files, so drift fails loudly.
(c) Keep the copies and accept them as fixtures, renaming them so they do not read as the shipped behaviors.

NOTE: reference-flow.e2e.test.ts is a protected guardrail file, so whichever option is chosen needs operator approval to edit.

description:
## Task: TRD-001
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-0fc1c1d0-behavior-runtime-pi-harness.md#trd-001
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-0fc1c1d0-behavior-runtime-pi-harness.md#req-001

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-001**: Documented Ensemble/Foreman ownership boundary {#req-001}
Documented Ensemble/Foreman ownership boundary {#req-001} Priority: Must | Complexity: Low Ensemble's README or architecture docs must state the governing boundary (describe/validate/package/simulate/local-run vs. activate/govern/schedule/execute/recover/audit) and explicitly list what Ensemble does not own (durable ingestion, activation decisions, dedup leases, cooldowns, retries/recovery, durable causal history, production-mutation approval enforcement, a second dispatcher).

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-001-1: Given the merged documentation | When a reader looks for "does Ensemble schedule production behavior | Then the doc explicitly states it does not and names Foreman as the owner
- AC-001-2: Given the existing Elixir activation runner | When the boundary doc is published | Then it explicitly records that the runner is not the Pi/OMP adapter

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach: Option C — `agent-core` + `pi-extension` (balanced, matches source architecture doc)**

Two new npm workspace packages:

## Task: TRD-017
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-0fc1c1d0-behavior-runtime-pi-harness.md#trd-017

**Requirement REQ-017**: Local outbox/evidence sink with distinguished acceptance states {#req-017}
Local outbox/evidence sink with distinguished acceptance states {#req-017} Priority: Must | Complexity: Medium [RISK: conflating "accepted locally" with "accepted by Foreman" would misrepresent durability guarantees] Governed tool calls append to a local outbox/evidence sink before acknowledging acceptance, and every tool result distinguishes: accepted locally, accepted by Foreman, queued for forwarding, rejected, malformed, unauthorized. A successful local acceptance must never be represented as durable Foreman acceptance.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-017-1: Given local-only mode (no Foreman connection) | When a governed tool call succeeds | Then the result status is exactly "accepted locally," never "accepted by Foreman
- AC-017-2: Given the local sink cannot write (e.g. simulated disk-full/permission failure) | When a governed tool call is attempted | Then the result status is "rejected" or "malformed," and no false "accepted locally" claim is made

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach: Option C — `agent-core` + `pi-extension` (balanced, matches source architecture doc)**

Two new npm workspace packages:

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|

title: Verification command can report success over a suite that never ran (router/pytest)
description:
Residual from br-srbd.

execution.test_command is now 'env -u CI npm test'. Unsetting CI is what
makes the command pass, but it also changes what packages/router does when
pytest is missing:

  pytest present  -> run the suite
  pytest absent + CI set    -> ERROR, exit 1
       ("CI must not report success on a suite it never ran")
  pytest absent + CI unset  -> print "Skipping Python tests", exit 0

So on a machine without pytest, the loop's verification runs 161 suites,
skips the router suite entirely, and reports exit 0. Measured: 3292 tests
pass, 107 router tests never execute.

Defensible: the loop should not fail because an optional toolchain is
missing on a developer's machine, and the router package's own guard is
explicitly designed to distinguish CI from local. Unsetting CI is the correct
way to get local semantics.

The problem is that the loop cannot tell the two apart. A verification that
returns "passed" while a suite was skipped is the exact shape of gap the rule
provider proposed an amendment about, unprompted, when shown a similar
failure:

  "Any test suite that fails to load, compile, or be discovered must make the
   test command exit non-zero, and a passing run must execute every test file
   in the repo; a green result where any suite did not load or was left out
   counts as a failure."

Worth noting that the system diagnosed this class of bug correctly before we
hit an instance of it.

OPTIONS
(a) Treat a skip notice in output as INCONCLUSIVE rather than passed, the
    same way an unloadable suite is already handled (verify-suite.ts:138).
    Consistent with the existing design, and cheap.
(b) Install pytest in the dev environment so the suite runs. Fixes this
    instance, not the class.
(c) Accept it and document that the loop's verification covers the JS/TS
    workspaces only.

(a) is the one that matches how unloadable suites are already graded.
close_reason: Fixed: verifyOutput now returns inconclusive when a run ANNOUNCES it skipped part of the suite, checked before the framework adapters and independently of the exit code. findAnnouncedSkips matches whole-line 'Skipping X tests' / 'Skipped X tests' / 'No X tests to run', which is exactly what packages/router prints when pytest is absent and CI is unset. Requires an explicit announcement rather than inferring from counts: a per-test '3 skipped' is routine and must not trip it, and a test NAMED 'handles skipping empty input' must not either -- both covered. 10 tests in agent-core/tests/announced-skip.test.ts.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: Related to br-cwrh (behavior: flag a test run that passed without running tests). The verifyOutput defect this bead describes was fixed for the Elixir/jest unloadable-suite case during br-behavior-runtime-cqrs-xl24 (br-gwww), but the router/pytest path here is NOT covered, and more importantly verifyOutput has only one caller -- fix.verify -- so it never sees an ordinary test run. title: Autofix: dispatch via pi.sendUserMessage() continuation turn, not handler-awaited work
description:
## Problem

Autofix cannot complete inside a Pi/omp session, because dispatch is driven
from extension event handlers and the host bounds them:

- tool_call / tool_result handlers: killed at 30_000ms
  ("Extension error: handler timed out after 30000ms")
- session_shutdown handlers: killed at 2_000ms
  ("handler timed out after 2000ms")

A real fix provider spawns an agent subprocess and takes tens of seconds at
best. Awaiting it inside the handler aborted the chain mid-flight every time:
`test.failure.observed` was logged, no dispatch/invocation record followed,
and the source was unchanged.

Dispatch is now out-of-band (tracked promise set + drainDispatches join
point), which stops the handler from being killed. But in a one-shot
`omp -p`, the process exits as soon as the turn ends and the background work
dies with it. Joining at shutdown cannot rescue it -- 2s is far short of a
model call.

## Evidence

Verified outside the handler lifecycle, the loop works end to end against a
real failing suite (packages/agent-core/src/live-math.ts, `a - b`):

    CANDIDATE writes: [ 'packages/agent-core/src/live-math.ts' ]
    OUTCOME: {"status":"accepted","attempt":1,...}
    AFTER: return a + b;

and correctly rejects a fix that does not work:

    OUTCOME: {"status":"rejected","reason":"target test still fails",
              "restored":["packages/agent-core/src/live-math.ts"]}

So the provider, mutation guard, snapshot, apply, suite re-run and rollback
are all sound. The ONLY missing piece is a execution context whose lifetime is
independent of the session.

## Why a command is not the answer

An `/ensemble-fix-now` command was considered. A command handler is still a
handler; even if its budget is larger, the design would rest on "hope the cap
is generous enough" -- the same bet that already failed at two different
limits (30s, then 2s).

## Proposed direction

Dispatch spawns a DETACHED worker process that outlives the session:

- parent returns immediately; no handler ever awaits it
- worker writes progress/outcome to .ensemble/ (runtime-log.jsonl plus a
  per-invocation record)
- the session reports results via /ensemble-status and on next session start
- needs: concurrency control (one worker per issue key), crash/orphan
  handling, and a way to surface a completed fix for review

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A failing test in a real `omp -p` run produces an applied, verified fix
      with no handler timeout anywhere in the log.

comments.text:
REPRODUCED 2026-09-25, isolated from all ensemble code
(/tmp/hang/slow.ts via: omp -p --no-session --no-extensions -e ./slow.ts).
tool_call handler sleeps 45s; session_shutdown handler sleeps 10s:

  [slow] tool_call START read

  [slow] tool_call START bash

  [slow] shutdown START
  Extension error (/tmp/hang/slow.ts): handler timed out after 2000ms

Caps CONFIRMED: 30000ms tool_call, 2000ms session_shutdown. Enforced by the
OMP host, NOT by @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent: 'handler timed out',
'handlerTimeout' and 'HANDLER_TIMEOUT' appear ZERO times in that package's
source, dist and minified chunks. Prior searches looked in the wrong place;
absence there was not absence.

TWO FACTS NOT VISIBLE FROM THE ERROR STRING:

1. The handler is NOT cancelled. 'FINISHED after 45002ms' printed AFTER the
   timeout was reported: the host stops awaiting and moves on while the work
   continues orphaned. Awaited fix work could still mutate files after the
   host has given up on it.

2. The timeout BLOCKS THE TOOL (documented tool_call fail-safe). In the repro
   the agent's read AND bash both failed, and it told the user to open another
   terminal. A slow handler does not merely delay a session, it breaks the
   agent's ability to work. This is a stronger justification for out-of-band
   dispatch (41ebbd3) than the reasoning it was committed with.

REVISED DESIGN -- the detached worker is the wrong shape and is WITHDRAWN.

Per pi.dev/docs/latest/extensions: 'turn_end and agent_before_settle are
actionable boundaries. Their handlers can chain proposed entries and return
continue: true for one next model request.' Confirmed in the installed host:
AgentBeforeSettleEvent (types.d.ts:620), registered types.d.ts:1000, result
BoundaryResult { entries?: SessionBoundaryDraft[]; continue?: boolean }.

The handler appends an entry and returns continue:true in milliseconds; the
SESSION'S OWN AGENT LOOP then performs the fix on its next turn:
  - no handler awaits model work, so no cap of any size applies
  - the session cannot exit early -- agent_settled has not fired
  - no second process: no lockfile, no orphan recovery, no unattended
    background process editing the repo
  - the fix lands in the user's transcript, under their tools and approvals

Risk moves to continuation control. The docs warn 'an unconditional
continuation can loop', so continuation must be guarded by issue key and
attempt count.

REVISED ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] A failing test in a real omp -p run produces an applied, verified fix
      with NO handler timeout anywhere in stderr.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CORRECTION + SECOND REPRO 2026-09-25. The 30000ms/2000ms limits are NOT
timeouts that cancel work. They are how long the HOST WAITS for a result.
Proof from repro 1: '[slow] tool_call FINISHED after 45002ms' printed AFTER
'handler timed out after 30000ms'. The handler ran to completion; the host had
stopped awaiting it and applied the documented tool_call fail-safe (blocking
the tool). So the deadline costs a blocked tool and an error, NOT the work.

That raised the real question: does unawaited work survive at all? Second
repro (/tmp/hang2/bg.ts) returns from the handler IMMEDIATELY and schedules
20s of background work:

  START 08:35:37
  [bg] scheduling background work at 2026-09-25T13:35:44.580Z
  EXIT  08:35:47            <- process exited ~3s later
  done.txt: ABSENT

The background work did NOT survive. Note node would normally stay alive for
a pending timer, so the host calls process.exit() explicitly on one-shot
completion.

TWO DISTINCT MECHANISMS, previously conflated:
  1. Handler deadline (30s/2s): host stops waiting; work CONTINUES; tool is
     blocked as a fail-safe. Survivable.
  2. Process exit (one-shot omp -p): HARD KILL of unawaited work. No amount
     of promise tracking, unref, or out-of-band scheduling survives it.

CONSEQUENCE FOR 41ebbd3: out-of-band dispatch correctly avoids mechanism 1
(and avoids blocking the user's tools, which is a stronger justification than
the commit message gave). It does NOT address mechanism 2.

WHY agent_before_settle IS THE ANSWER, not merely the lighter option:
it does not try to OUTLIVE the session, it PREVENTS the session from settling
until the fix turn completes. The work stays inside the agent loop's lifetime,
where the process is guaranteed alive. A detached worker would also survive
mechanism 2, but only by leaving the process -- reintroducing lockfiles,
orphan recovery and unattended repo edits for no additional benefit.

ADDITIONAL ACCEPTANCE CRITERION
- [ ] A repro proving the fix turn completes before process exit in one-shot
      `omp -p` (i.e. mechanism 2 is actually defeated, not just mechanism 1).

comments.text:
THIRD CORRECTION 2026-09-25: agent_before_settle DOES NOT EXIST IN THIS HOST.

I previously wrote "confirmed present in the installed host" citing
AgentBeforeSettleEvent at types.d.ts:620 of @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent.
That was the SAME wrong-package error as the timeout hunt: OMP is the host,
and it does not implement those events.

Probe (/tmp/hang3/probe.ts) registering 10 lifecycle events; only these fired:
  session_start, before_agent_start, agent_start, turn_start,
  turn_end, agent_end, session_shutdown
NOT FIRED: agent_before_settle, agent_settled. Registration silently succeeds
for unknown event names, so pi.on() returning without error proves nothing.

turn_end fires but IGNORES continue:true (/tmp/hang3/te.ts): returned
{continue:true} from turn_end #1, no second turn occurred. Its payload is
{type,turnIndex,message,toolResults} -- NOT the documented BoundaryState
{entries,continue,context,outcome}. The documented actionable-boundary
continuation contract is not available here.

VERIFIED MECHANISM THAT DOES WORK: pi.sendUserMessage() from turn_end.
Real ExtensionAPI surface in OMP includes sendMessage and sendUserMessage.
Repro /tmp/hang3/sm.ts, one-shot `omp -p --no-session`:

  [sm] turn_end at 6485ms -> sendUserMessage
  [sm] sendUserMessage resolved
  [sm] agent_end at 11137ms
  [sm] shutdown at 11251ms
  stdout: DONE
  /tmp/hang3/second.txt: SECOND

The queued message became a REAL SECOND TURN that used bash, wrote a file, and
the PROCESS WAITED FOR IT. This defeats mechanism 2 (process-exit kill), and
because the handler returns immediately it never meets mechanism 1 (the 30s
wait deadline).

REVISED DESIGN: dispatch does not perform the fix and does not spawn anything.
On a detected failure it calls pi.sendUserMessage() with the fix instruction;
the session's own agent performs the fix on the next turn with the user's
tools, in the user's transcript. Verification (apply/re-run/rollback) stays in
code where it already works.

Guards required: one continuation per issue key, attempt cap, and a flag so
the continuation turn cannot re-trigger dispatch (infinite loop risk is real --
the repro needed a `fired` guard to avoid recursion).

ACCEPTANCE (supersedes earlier lists)
- [ ] Failing test in real `omp -p` -> applied, verified fix, no Extension
      error in stderr.
- [ ] No handler exceeds ~100ms.
- [ ] Process does not exit before the fix turn completes.
- [ ] A bad fix is still rolled back.
- [ ] Same issue key cannot queue a second continuation.

LOOP CAP RESOLVED (b73395d).

The cap keyed on the literal command string. Observed live: one failure
retried as `... | tail -5` then `... | sed -n 1,60p` counted as two issues,
so a cap of 1 granted two attempts.

normalizeIssueKey now strips pipelines, redirections and whitespace -- the

test-selection arguments; collapsing `jest auth` and `jest billing` would be
worse than the original bug. Both directions tested.

run that keeps surfacing DIFFERENT failing commands: each stays under its own

Refusals now log kind=continuation-refused instead of returning false
silently. An invisible refusal is indistinguishable from detection never
firing -- that ambiguity cost real time earlier.

with the raw command being `npx jest live-e2e 2>&1`, i.e. normalisation
recognised the retry as the same issue.

title: Constitution changes apply in-place after approval; PR becomes delivery, not gate
description:
DESIGN DECISION by the user, 2026-09-25. Supersedes an acceptance criterion
of a consumed TRD, so it is recorded here rather than by editing TRD-029.

SUPERSEDED (TRD-029 / REQ-007, encoded in constitution-proposal.ts):
  "constitution.md is never modified in place by this path, on either answer.
   'Yes' opens a PR and the file changes only if a human merges it."

REPLACEMENT:
  Approval edits docs/standards/constitution.md DIRECTLY in the working tree.
  The change then reaches main the same way every other change does -- commit,
  push, PR into dev, release PR dev -> main. The PR is not the approval
  mechanism; it is the delivery mechanism.

WHY THIS IS NOW SAFE, WHEN IT WAS NOT BEFORE
REQ-007 was written when main had no protection and every marketplace source
was an unpinned relative path, so a merge to main shipped instantly to every
consumer. "Never touch the file in-session" was the only available guard.
Since then the repository has a dev integration branch, main is protected
(enforce_admins, required checks release-gate + source-branch, no force-push)
and main advances only through a dev -> main release PR. Human review is now
structural, so it no longer has to be smuggled in as "the approval IS a PR".

CONSEQUENCES TO IMPLEMENT
- ConstitutionProposal stops calling openPullRequest on approval and applies
  the change instead.
- WriteBoundaryMonitor must permit exactly that one authorized write.
  Everything else under docs/standards stays reverted. The exception must be
  scoped to the approved change and revoked immediately after -- an
  open-ended "constitution edits allowed" flag would delete the protection
  this session proved works.
- Denial, and a headless session with no UI, must still change nothing. The
  fail-closed property of ApprovalGate is unchanged.

WHAT IS NOT CHANGING
- Protected-path enforcement for every other writer and every other path.
- The fail-closed rule: absence of a UI is a denial, never an implicit yes.

title: [trd:trd-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix:task:TRD-003] - [ ] **TRD-003** Route behavior tool execution through `MutationGuard` at the loader boundary and remove the unconditional `registry.grant()` in `behavior-loader.ts` (5h)
description:
## Task: TRD-003
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-003
PRD Reference: #req-011

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.
Satisfies: REQ-011
PRD ACs: AC-011-1, AC-011-3
Target File: packages/pi-extension/src/behavior-loader.ts, packages/agent-core/src/behavior/mutation-guard.ts
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given a governed tool invocation, when it executes, then its grant derives from the compiled manifest rather than being issued unconditionally at call time.
Dependencies: TRD-002

description:

working tree by fix-agent child processes, and NONE was caught, because none
is a protected path:

  packages/pi-extension/jest.config.js   moduleNameMapper -> ../agent-core/src
  packages/pi-extension/tsconfig.json    lib ES2022 -> ES2024
  packages/pi-extension/package.json     added "pretest": "tsc -p ../agent-core"
  packages/pi-extension/tests/zzdebug.test.ts   new scratch debug test

All four are the same idea: make the failing tests resolve agent-core. That
is exactly what an agent told "repair the SOURCE so it passes" would try
when the real problem is dependency resolution.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE FILES THEMSELVES
The jest.config.js change made four tests fail with EMPTY error messages --
no assertion text, no stack. A maintainer debugging that has no signal at
all, and the diagnosis only landed after diffing a file nobody knew had
changed. Silently retargeting the module mapper also means a green suite can
be green against the wrong code.

GUARDRAIL_PATTERNS today covers guardrail sources, test files and the
constitution. Build configuration is at least as load-bearing: jest.config,
tsconfig, package.json and CI workflows decide WHAT runs and WHAT it runs
against. A loop that cannot weaken an assertion but can retarget the module
mapper or add a pretest hook has not been contained, only redirected.

PROPOSAL
Extend protected paths to build/test configuration: jest.config.*,
tsconfig*.json, package.json, .github/workflows/*. Reversion semantics are
unchanged; these become consent-gated like any other protected path
(/ensemble-approve).

Note the interaction with br-9uqd: a maintainer legitimately edits these
often, so this is only tolerable now that consent exists.

title: Write boundary reverts merged work after an external pull
description:
OBSERVED 2026-09-28 in the maintainer's own checkout.

A session activated on 2026-09-25. On 2026-09-26 an external
`pull --ff-only` fast-forwarded HEAD in the same working tree. Two days
later the next tool call -- a read-only `ls` inside node_modules --
reported:

  Write boundary violation: workspace-snapshot.ts (guardrail-source) was
  reverted; pipe-masked-failure.test.ts (test-file) was reverted;
  write-boundary.test.ts (test-file) was reverted;
  agent-fix-provider.test.ts (test-file) was reverted

~175 lines of merged tests removed from the working tree. `git checkout --`
to restore them was itself reverted, because the restore is a change away
from the stale baseline. The session could not repair the damage it caused.

ROOT CAUSE. The baseline is captured once at activation and never revisited.
Any later HEAD movement makes merged files differ from "pristine", and
check() runs on EVERY tool result, so a read-only command suffices. The
longer a session runs, the more dangerous it is to its own checkout.

FIXED on feat/consent-based-guardrails (076fd23): syncExternalHistory()
re-baselines when BOTH the reflog shows no locally-authored move AND the
file matches HEAD exactly. Either condition alone is bypassable -- notably
`edit && git commit` in one shell call, which was caught in review.

Nothing was lost permanently; content is in git objects at HEAD.
close_reason: done

title: Failure detector fires on any output containing a test-summary string, including inspection commands
description:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-28 in a real working session, twice.

I ran a DIAGNOSTIC command -- reading a log, not running tests:

  jq -r '.kind' .ensemble/runtime-log.jsonl | sort | uniq -c
  ... ; npm test 2>&1 | tail -2 ; grep "return a" src/math.js

Its output quoted a test summary ("1 failed, 1 passed, 2 total") because I
was INSPECTING a previous result. The runtime read that as a fresh test
failure, activated fix-failing-test, and synthesised a fix instruction
addressed to me. A later run did it again and rolled back a working tree on
the strength of it.

Detection keys on the SHAPE of output, so anything that quotes a test summary
is a failing test: grep over a log, jq over runtime records, cat of a CI
config, a diff containing test output, a chat message pasted into a terminal,
this bead.

WHY THIS IS MORE THAN NOISE

1. It triggers real mutation. The spurious activation opened a behavior
   window, took a fix turn, and ROLLED BACK the working tree when its
   "verification" failed. In my case the damage landed on a disposable trial
   repo. Pointed at a real repo it reverts a developer's uncommitted work on
   the basis of a string in a log file.

2. It is attacker-influenceable, and the system already says so. The
   injected instruction carries its own preamble: "synthesised by an
   extension from TEST OUTPUT, which is attacker-influenceable in principle".
   That framing is correct and it worked -- I ignored the instruction. But
   the framing only defends the INSTRUCTION channel. It does nothing about
   the fact that arbitrary text can make the runtime ACT: open a window,
   narrow a session's tools, spawn a model subprocess, snapshot and revert
   files. A file in a repo whose contents include a fake test summary can
   provoke all of that without any test ever running.

3. It is a capability-escalation surface, not just a false positive. The
   window it opens carries tool grants and write authority that the session
   would not otherwise be exercising.

SPLIT FROM br-o355 deliberately: that bead is about grant-window lifecycle
(what happens once a window is open, and how it closes). This is upstream of
it -- the window should never have opened -- and it is a different fix:
tighten the match condition, not window teardown. The two chained together
in the live incident (spurious detection -> session narrowed, "wait" tool
denied mid-task), which is how it was found.

DIRECTIONS
- Require provenance, not shape: only treat output as a test result when the
  command itself was recognised as a test invocation, rather than matching
  the summary text anywhere in output.
- Ignore output that is being read rather than produced (jq/grep/cat/tail
  over a file are not test runners).
- At minimum, require the summary at the END of output and the exit code to
  be non-zero, so quoting a summary mid-output does not qualify.
- Whatever the rule, it needs a test with a fixture whose output CONTAINS a
  test summary but is not a test run.
close_reason: Invalid: premise disproved by direct test. The detector already requires the runner in command position (isTestCommand, event-translator.ts:36-55); inspection commands (jq/cat/grep over logs) return isTestCommand=false. The command that misfired contained a real 'npm test' against a deliberately broken repo, so detection was correct. No fix needed.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
RETRACTED. The central claim is false. I tested it instead of reasoning about
it, and the detector behaves correctly.

I claimed detection "keys on the SHAPE of output, so anything that quotes a
test summary is a failing test: grep over a log, jq over runtime records, cat
of a CI config". Ran those exact cases through the real functions:

  pure inspection (jq -r .kind ... | sort | uniq -c; cat ci-log.txt)
      isTestCommand=false  exitStatusIsRunners=false
  cat of a log containing a summary (cat /tmp/all.txt)
      isTestCommand=false  exitStatusIsRunners=false
  grep -n "Tests:" notes.md
      isTestCommand=false  exitStatusIsRunners=false

  THE COMMAND THAT ACTUALLY MISFIRED ON ME
      isTestCommand=TRUE   exitStatusIsRunners=false

Because that command contained `npm test`. I ran a real test invocation,
against a repo I had deliberately broken, as part of a diagnostic one-liner.
The suite really did fail. Autofix engaged because a test really failed.
That is the feature working.

The provenance guard I proposed as the fix ALREADY EXISTS and is why the
inspection cases return false. isTestCommand requires the runner in COMMAND
POSITION -- first token of a shell segment after stripping npx/bunx/env
wrappers -- precisely so that `cat jest.config.js` and `grep jest
package.json` do not qualify. It was added after a live misfire where
/\bjest\b/ matched the FILENAME in `cat jest.config.*`. Documented at
event-translator.ts:36-55.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY TRUE about the incident, and it is much smaller:
  - I ran a genuinely failing test while diagnosing, and the loop responded.
    ENSEMBLE_NO_AUTOFIX=1 exists for exactly this and I was not using it.
  - The rollback that followed was of the TRIAL repo's deliberate breakage,
    not of real work.

The security framing does not survive either. "Arbitrary text in a log can
make the runtime act" is false: it requires an actual test command in command
position. The residual surface is the ordinary one -- a real test run whose
output a repo controls -- which the instruction preamble already addresses.

Closing as invalid. Filed on a plausible story I did not test, which is the
same error as br-zcxb's first version. The lesson is the one I keep
relearning: a traced explanation is not evidence.

title: [trd:trd-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix:task:TRD-023] - [ ] **TRD-023** Implement `CommitPolicy`: refuse default/`main`/`master`, require attribution in the message (5h)
description:
## Task: TRD-023
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-023
PRD Reference: #req-016

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.
Satisfies: REQ-016
PRD ACs: AC-016-1, AC-016-2, AC-016-3
Target File: packages/pi-extension/src/commit-policy.ts
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given the current branch is the repository default, when a commit is attempted, then it is refused or redirected to a dedicated branch — never committed in place.

title: behavior runtime: CQRS commands, closed event catalog, declarative workflows
description:
Evolve the behavior runtime from a test-failure-specific automation path into a
behavior-driven local harness built on CQRS: typed commands, a closed event
catalog, and declarative behavior packages interpreted by one engine.

Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

## The shape of it

    skill / UI command / runtime event
      -> typed command request
      -> handler validates policy and evidence
      -> authorized state transition
      -> resulting fact/event
      -> declarative behavior workflow reacts

An event records a fact that occurred. It is not an instruction to mutate.
A command expresses intent; its handler validates authority and invariants,
performs the effect, and emits the result event only once the outcome is known.

## Why this is not theoretical

The current runtime has already failed in exactly the ways this contract is
written to prevent, observed live during the loop-trial work:

- Two dispatch paths for one event. The governed path correctly refused a write
  under `policy.mode: propose` and the continuation path repaired the file
  anyway. The second path masked the first being dead for three days, because
  every run still looked successful (br-dowt, br-cxn8, br-boam).
- `propose` mutating the user's tree. A verified fix was left applied with no
  human asked, because a missing baseline was treated as permission (br-dowt).
- Tool grants that do not grant. `--tools=read,grep,glob` does not restrict
  tools; a fix child reached `_write`, `_learn` and `_manage_skill` and wrote a
  skill into the operator's HOME that loads in every future session (br-33co).
- Verification accepting a runner it had just judged defective: a suite that
  never loaded counted as passed (br-gwww).

REQ-CQRS-002, REQ-SAFE-001, REQ-SAFE-003 and REQ-SAFE-006 each exist because of
one of those. Treat them as regression requirements, not aspirations.

## Ownership boundary

Ensemble owns portable behavior packages, validation, simulation and local
Pi/OMP execution. Foreman owns durable activation, scheduling, recovery,
approvals and audit history. Do not add durable scheduling, leases, retries or
recovery here (REQ-RUN-002), and do not modify Foreman as part of this work.

## Phase order

Phases are sequential and each has an exit gate. Do not start with a broad
rewrite of generated commands or existing packages.

  Phase 0  resolve the runtime split, prove the boundaries
  Phase 1  versioned command/event contracts
  Phase 2  constrained workflow interpreter
  Phase 3  port the test-failure slice and constitution proposal
  Phase 4  authoring, compatibility, handoff
acceptance_criteria:
All 12 system-wide acceptance criteria in section 6 hold, in particular:
new behaviors need no behavior-specific TypeScript; every mutation uses one
authorization boundary regardless of how it was initiated; propose mode
demonstrably cannot mutate the working tree including via native tools and
shell; concurrent edits are never lost; no ambiguous/zero-test/timeout result
is accepted as success; constitution changes are evidence-backed proposals
applied only through a separate authorized transition.
close_reason: All 20 stories and exit gates delivered; constitution.apply reachability carved out to br-dlol

title: report where the tree differs from the CQRS spec
description:
Section 8 requires this BEFORE implementation: inspect the checked-out branch
and report every difference between the specification and the actual tree.

Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

Produce a written gap report covering at least:

- the continuation queue, `BehaviorRunner`, `AutofixLoop`, the matcher and the
  event translator: what each does today and which of them can mutate state
- every path that can write files or run shell/network operations
- which existing behavior.yaml fields map to the contract in section 3.1, and
  which have no equivalent (migration note)
- which of the 12 acceptance criteria in section 6 currently fail, with the
  evidence that shows it

Known starting points from live runs, all reproducible: two dispatch paths for
one event (br-dowt); propose mode leaving a fix applied (br-dowt); tool grants
not restricting tools (br-33co); verification trusting a defective runner
(br-gwww); per-invocation cwd confusion across call sites (br-nft8).

The report is the input to Story 0.1 and should be attached to this issue.

title: interpret bounded workflow steps
description:
Story 2.2 / REQ-BEH-002, REQ-SAFE-007. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

Implement the five step kinds: `agent`, `command`, `condition`, `approval`,
`outcome`. Sequential steps plus simple conditionals are enough initially --
reject anything unsupported rather than skipping it silently.

Every step has a bounded timeout, attempt budget, cancellation path, output-size
bound and explicit failure outcome. No unbounded recursion, event-trigger loop
or automatic child-behavior cycle (REQ-SAFE-007).

`condition` branches only on structured validated results, never on model prose.
Keep the interpreter provider-neutral; Pi/OMP invocation goes through adapters.

The `approval` step is not a formality: an approval gate that asks and a reply
that is read correctly are two different things. A live run recorded "declined
by user" for an approval the operator had granted, because the reply shape did
not match what the host read. Test the accept path, not just the deny path.
acceptance_criteria: Fixture-driven workflows run deterministically; unsupported steps are rejected; timeout, cancel and no-orphan tests pass; recursion and duplicate-event limits hold; a workflow-step command denial matches the direct tool-call denial.
close_reason: Completed

title: load prompts and workflow data without a rebuild
description:

Demonstrate that a prompt or workflow edit takes effect with no TypeScript
rebuild, while an invalid edit still fails validation.

Include the prompt files in the behavior digest, so "what ran" stays
identifiable even though the text is editable.

Practical note from live work: the installed extension bundle was once built
from a stale checkout three commits behind, and several runs tested code that
did not include the fixes under test. Whatever mechanism loads package assets,
the status output must make the ACTIVE path and digest visible (see Story 4.1).
acceptance_criteria: Editing a prompt file changes behavior with no rebuild; an invalid workflow edit fails validation with a clear diagnostic; the digest reflects prompt content.

The second half is the part that is easy to fake: grep the runtime for

title: port the test-failure investigation to package data
description:
Story 3.1. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

Express detection, investigation, fix proposal, structured evidence and outcome
in behavior data plus shared typed commands. Remove test-specific workflow logic
from the Pi adapter once parity tests pass.

The reference flow (section 4):

    test.failure.observed
      -> investigate (read-only agent step, capture diagnosis/evidence)
      -> fix.propose (typed command; create candidate, do not edit the project)
      -> optional isolated verification of the candidate
      -> outcome: fix.proposed | investigation.inconclusive | behavior.blocked

Detection errors must not grant mutation authority. Where runner identification
or failure evidence is ambiguous, record a diagnostic or skip -- do not trigger
an apply path (section 4, REQ-SAFE-006).
acceptance_criteria: The test-failure behavior runs from package data with no test-specific branch in the adapter; parity tests against the current behavior pass.
close_reason: Completed

title: separate proposal, verification, approval and application
description:
Story 3.2 / REQ-SAFE-001, REQ-SAFE-002, REQ-SAFE-005, REQ-SAFE-006. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

Explicit proposal artifacts, structured verifier results, apply only through an
authorized handler in an isolated workspace after any required approval.
Approval and application are separate facts.

Four live failures this must close, all reproduced:

- a verified fix was LEFT APPLIED with no approval because a missing baseline
  was treated as permission -- fail-open in a system that fails closed
  everywhere else (br-dowt, partially fixed in PR #105)
- verification accepted `2 passed, 2 total` from a runner that had counted a
  suite which never loaded as passed; the same run's constitution amendment
  described that exact defect (br-gwww)
- whole-tree restore is used as rollback in the interactive workspace, which
  REQ-SAFE-005 forbids as routine; concurrent edits must survive
- the applier writes to the failing command's worktree, which may not be where
  the canonical project lives (br-nft8)

REQ-SAFE-006 is explicit that unknown output, zero tests, a missing runner, a
timeout or an unattributable result is `inconclusive`, never passed, and that a
single generic regex must not be the authority across frameworks.
acceptance_criteria: Propose mode creates a proposal and changes nothing; apply requires an explicit authorized command; a zero-test or unattributable verifier result is never accepted as success; concurrent edits survive.
close_reason: Completed

title: add the constitution-learning behavior
description:
Story 3.3 / REQ-SAFE-008. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

A separately packageable behavior that triggers only on verified/accepted fix
evidence -- not on the initial failure -- and outputs an evidence-backed
constitution proposal with rationale, source evidence, affected rule and diff.
Never a direct write, never auto-accepted because a test passed.

Approval/PR opening and canonical application are separate auditable operations.

This flow has been observed working end to end and is worth preserving as the
reference: a run proposed "a test suite that fails to load, import or compile
must count as a failure and make the run exit non-zero", reasoned about the
existing rule it was amending, asked for approval, and wrote the amendment only
after consent. Two independent runs produced equivalent rules in different
words. The scenario that warranted it matters: a one-line arithmetic bug
legitimately implies no constitution change.
acceptance_criteria: The behavior triggers only from verified evidence; a proposal is never applied without a separate approved apply step; a trivial fix produces no proposal.
close_reason: Completed

title: exit gate 3: the reference flow is package-defined and reproducible
description:
Phase 3 exit gate. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

The reference flow is package-defined, reviewable, reproducible from fixtures,
and does not mutate canonical project or constitution state without the explicit
apply workflow.

title: add package validation, simulation and a truthful status report
description:

when the repository was a clean clone -- the real cause was one untracked
symlink that `git hash-object` could not hash. A diagnostic that guesses is

description:

approval/cancellation boundary, and whether OS-level isolation or worktree

does NOT restrict tools. A child reported `_read _grep _glob _manage_skill

title: exit gate 0: propose mode proven non-mutating under hostile tools
description:
Phase 0 exit gate. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

One dispatch path is demonstrated AND propose mode is proven non-mutating in an
end-to-end hostile-tool test. If Pi cannot enforce the boundary, mutation stays
disabled pending a sandbox or a safer adapter design.

Required tests (section 5, Phase 0):

- one failure event starts at most one workflow
- a propose-mode event cannot alter project files through native tools, shell
  redirects, subprocesses, or a continuation
- a concurrent user edit is preserved
- process cancellation terminates child work, leaving no orphan

"Hostile" means the test actively tries to escape: shell redirection, a child
tool call, a skill write outside the repo. A test that only checks the happy
path proves nothing here -- br-33co was found by trying to escape on purpose.

This gate cannot pass while br-33co is open.
acceptance_criteria: The hostile-tool suite passes on CI and is not skippable; propose mode alters nothing in the user's tree by any route; cancellation leaves no orphan process.
