title: add typed command descriptors and handler registry
description:
Story 1.1 / REQ-CQRS-001. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

A provider-neutral registry of code-owned command descriptors. Each descriptor
defines a stable command ID and version, input schema, result schema, required
capability, mutation class, handler, and emitted event types.

The Pi adapter exposes these descriptors as governed tools; workflow steps call
the same registry. There must be no second privileged implementation -- that
duplication is exactly what Phase 0 removes, and re-introducing it at the
command layer would undo it.

Centralize capability checks, mutation authorization, approval requirements,
idempotency/deduplication and error mapping here rather than in each handler.

Keep it provider-neutral: no Pi/OMP types in the registry (REQ-RUN-004).
acceptance_criteria: A command invoked from a workflow step and the same command invoked as a Pi tool traverse identical authorization code; an unauthorized command is denied identically on both routes.
close_reason: Completed

title: complete event authority semantics
description:
Story 1.2 / REQ-CQRS-003, REQ-CQRS-004, REQ-CQRS-005. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

Define observed, requested, proposed, verified, applied, rejected and failed as
separate facts. Stamp runtime-owned metadata (event ID, session/execution IDs,
timestamp, source, causation/correlation, behavior identity and digest) in the
runtime, never from an agent payload.

A handler emits a success event only after confirming the transition occurred.
An agent saying "done" is not evidence. This has a live precedent worth keeping
in mind: a fix agent reported a correct diagnosis and a correct fix in prose
while having written nothing, because it had no tool that could edit files. The
reply parsed as failure only by luck of shape, not by contract.

A result must never describe a proposed or queued operation as completed
(REQ-CQRS-003). Unknown or context-incompatible events fail closed.
acceptance_criteria: Schema contract tests pass; no success event can be emitted before a successful handler result; unknown event types are rejected; causation metadata is stable across command and result events.

title: spike: decide what the local event sink guarantees
description:
Spike 1.3 / REQ-CQRS-006. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

Decide and document what the local sink guarantees across process exit, and how
acceptance and forwarding behave. Production durability and recovery stay
outside Ensemble.

The specific failure to avoid: local acceptance being represented as Foreman
acceptance. A local outbox is not a durable event store and cannot claim
scheduling, retries, replay, recovery or production approval guarantees.

Relevant local evidence: a shutdown drain exists and has been observed
completing, but nothing currently distinguishes "written to the local log" from
"accepted by anything durable".
acceptance_criteria: A written decision states the local sink's guarantees across process exit; a test proves local acceptance is never reported as Foreman acceptance.

title: exit gate 1: a command proposes through one handler and reports truthfully
description:
Phase 1 exit gate. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

A test command can be proposed through one registered handler and yields a
truthful typed result and event, with no direct agent writes.

Required tests: schema contracts; unauthorized command denied regardless of
invocation path; no success event before a successful handler result; unknown
command/event rejected; local acceptance never represented as Foreman
acceptance; stable causation metadata.

title: validate and compile package workflow data
description:
Story 2.1 / REQ-BEH-001, REQ-BEH-004. Source: `docs/architecture/ensemble-behavior-cqrs-implementation-requirements.md`

Static validation of step IDs, references, command bindings, event types, tool

description:
## Task: TRD-021
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-021
PRD Reference: #req-015

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.
Satisfies: REQ-015
PRD ACs: AC-015-3, AC-005-4
Target File: packages/agent-core/src/behavior/workspace-snapshot.ts
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given a set of files modified during an attempt, when `restore()` runs, then every file's content and mode is byte-identical to capture time, and files created during the attempt are removed.

title: fix sandbox dies on any untracked symlink, silently disabling the whole governed path
description:
OBSERVED LIVE, twice, in an rpc-ui session against a trial repo.

createFixSandbox() mirrors untracked-but-not-ignored files into the throwaway worktree with copyFileSync. git ls-files --others reports a SYMLINKED DIRECTORY as a single entry, and copyFileSync on it throws:

  ENOTSUP: operation not supported on socket,
  copyfile '/tmp/loop-trial-run/node_modules' -> '<sandbox>/work/node_modules'

The throw is caught by the blanket try/catch at fix-sandbox.ts:116, which returns undefined. agent-fix-provider then fails CLOSED (correctly, by design) and returns no candidate. behavior-runner records:

  note: 'no fix candidate offered'
  constitution: { status: 'none', detail: 'rule provider ran and implied no constitution change' }

CONSEQUENCE. This is the whole product failing, not a corner. With no fix candidate the governed path has nothing to verify, so the constitution provider is handed nothing to reason about and reports 'none'. The amendment step -- the feature the runtime exists for -- can never fire. The fix still LANDS, because the continuation path repairs the code independently, so the session looks successful. Two live runs both showed a repaired src/math.js, a passing verification, and no constitution change.

TIMING TELL. The invocation returns in 65-67ms. The fix agent child takes ~15s when it actually runs (measured). Anything in the tens of milliseconds means the model was never called.

node_modules as a symlink is not exotic -- it is what workspace/monorepo setups produce, and what this project's own worktree instructions create.

TWO DEFECTS, FIX BOTH:

1. The copy loop must handle symlinks (recreate with symlinkSync(readlinkSync(from))) rather than copyFileSync, and one uncopyable entry must not abandon the entire sandbox. node_modules specifically is already handled by linkNodeModules(), so copying it is redundant as well as fatal.

2. The failure is INVISIBLE. fix-sandbox returns undefined with no reason and the provider's catch returns undefined with no reason, so the log says 'no fix candidate offered' -- which reads as 'the model had no idea', not 'the harness broke before the model was asked'. Record the cause. This is the same class as br-zcxb: a step that cannot run reports the same thing as a step that ran and found nothing.
close_reason: done

VERIFIED END TO END, 2026-09-28 22:xx, rpc-ui session against /tmp/loop-trial-run.

With this fix and br-cxn8 in the bundle, the full loop ran for the first time:

  governed dispatch  -> fix candidate produced (16s, real model call)
  MutationGuard      -> direct write DENIED under mode: propose,
                        proposal artifact emitted
  constitution step  -> amendment PROPOSED with a real rationale
  ApprovalGate       -> asked the human via ui.confirm
  applier            -> amendment APPENDED to docs/standards/constitution.md

  record: constitution { status: 'applied', detail: 'appended amendment for fix-failing-test' }

Before this fix the same path returned in 65ms with 'no fix candidate offered' and the constitution was never touched.

title: Fix sandbox symlinks node_modules, so writes through it reach the live tree
description:
Residual gap in the br-r3om containment fix (b59d2bf).

createFixSandbox() symlinks node_modules into the disposable worktree rather
than copying it. A child that writes THROUGH that path -- npm install, or
writing into a package directory -- reaches the live tree's dependencies.

Why it was built that way: copying node_modules per fix run is slow enough to
make autofix unusable, and node_modules is not a protected path, so the threat
the bead was about (source and guardrail writes) is contained regardless.

What this bead is really for: the CLAIM. "The child cannot modify the live
working tree" is wider than what is true. The accurate claim is "cannot modify
the live tree's source or guardrails". Either narrow the claim in the docs, or
close the gap with a read-only bind mount / copy-on-write clone where the
platform supports it.

Found by review of b59d2bf, not by a failure.
close_reason: Premise removed and superseded by br-t0so. createFixSandbox() no longer exists -- br-behavior-runtime-cqrs-xl24 replaced it with createIsolatedWorkspace(), a git worktree that symlinks nothing, so no write can reach the live tree's node_modules through it. Verified: git grep finds no createFixSandbox in packages/*/src, and isolated-workspace.ts contains no symlink or node_modules handling. The trade-off this bead identified is real and now fails the other way -- the worktree has NO dependencies, so fix.verify is inert. Tracked in br-t0so with the copy-on-write proposal and an explicit instruction that the fallback must refuse rather than degrade back to a symlink.

title: Verification re-runs the whole && chain, re-applying the bug it was meant to fix
description:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-25 in this repo, during a user-requested demonstration.

A test was broken by a compound shell command:

  cd packages/agent-core && python3 -c "<edit that introduces the bug>" \
    && sed -n '18,21p' src/behavior/outbox.ts \
    && npx jest 2>&1 | grep -E "Tests:|..."

Detection worked: test.failure.observed fired and a continuation turn was
injected with both behaviors matched.

THE DEFECT: the captured issue command is the ENTIRE compound command,
including the python3 invocation that CAUSED the failure. The runtime log
records it verbatim:

  "issue": "cd /Users/.../agent-core && python3 -c \"\np='src/behavior/outbox.ts'
            ...s.replace(...)...\"\nsed -n '18,21p' ...\nnpx jest ..."

Verification re-runs that exact command. So the sequence is self-defeating:

  1. model repairs the source correctly
  2. verification re-runs the captured command
  3. the python3 step MATCHES AGAIN (the repair restored the original text
     that its .replace() searches for) and re-introduces the bug
  4. jest fails
  5. the correct fix is rolled back as rejected

A correct fix is indistinguishable from no fix, and the rollback destroys it.

WHY IT SLIPPED THROUGH: every prior proof, in the fixture and in this repo,
used a command whose only effect was running tests. The breakage was always
applied in a SEPARATE earlier command. This is the first observation of a
test run chained onto a mutating command in the same invocation -- the normal
shape of a one-liner.

NOT the same as f11da8d, which pinned that the verified command stays RAW and
is never normalized. That decision is about not rewriting the command. This
is about WHICH command gets captured in the first place: the failing test
invocation, not the whole && chain that contained it.

DESIGN QUESTION (do not patch blindly)
Extracting the trailing test invocation from a && chain is the obvious move,
but it is a shell parser, with all the quoting hazards this session already
hit. Alternatives worth weighing first:
  - capture only the segment isTestCommand() actually matched, which is
    already computed during detection
  - refuse to verify (report inconclusive) when the observed command contains
    a mutating segment, rather than re-running something unsafe
  - re-run the declared execution.test_command instead of the observed one
    when they disagree

ACCEPTANCE
- [ ] A test broken and run in ONE compound command is detected, fixed, and
      verified without the verification step re-applying the breakage.
- [ ] Mutation: reverting the fix makes this repro fail again.
- [ ] A verified command is never one with side effects beyond running tests,
      or verification declares itself inconclusive instead of rolling back a
      correct fix.

title: Behavior: check workspace integrity at session start
description:
RECOMMENDATION 5 of 5. Cheap, deterministic, catches latent breakage before it wastes a session.

TRIGGER: runtime.session.started.
ACTION: verify workspace symlinks resolve and the lockfile is coherent with package.json.

EVIDENCE, from this session: the ROOT node_modules/@sunstone-partners/ensemble-agent-core symlink pointed at /tmp/wt-guard/packages/agent-core -- a deleted throwaway worktree. Tests passed anyway because a nested symlink in packages/pi-extension shadowed it, so the breakage was invisible. npm install then rewrote 56 lines of package-lock.json that had drifted. Either would have broken the next contributor or CI, silently, with a confusing error far from the cause.

WORK: one command workspace.check (read-only). No model involvement.
close_reason: workspace.check command + workspace-integrity behavior delivered. Detects dangling workspace symlinks (including the shadowed case that made the original incident invisible) and lockfile drift. Read-only, no model, 20 tests.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
DELIVERED.

src/workspace/integrity.ts -- two deterministic checks, no model, no network:
1. DANGLING SYMLINKS, with the shadowed case called out separately. That distinction is the whole value: the original incident was a ROOT link to a deleted /tmp worktree that a NESTED link shadowed, so tests passed and every local signal read healthy while the workspace was already broken for anyone else. A shadowed break is strictly more dangerous than an obvious one, and the finding says so in words.
2. LOCKFILE DRIFT -- root dependencies/devDependencies ranges that package-lock.json does not match. Deliberately narrow: it does not re-resolve the tree, because a partial reimplementation of npm would produce false findings and teach people to ignore the check.

REPORTS, NEVER REPAIRS. The remedy is npm install, which is the developer's call; a runtime that silently rewrote a dependency tree would be a worse problem than the one it fixed. A test asserts the link is still there afterwards, and policy mode is propose with a note that auto is a category error here rather than a future upgrade.

COUNTS ARE PART OF THE RESULT (checked.linkCount, checked.lockfile). 'No findings' from a check that examined nothing is the most reassuring possible lie -- and silence is exactly what hid the original breakage.

VERIFIED AGAINST REALITY, not just fixtures: run against this repo it reports 30 links examined, lockfile compared, 0 findings -- consistent with the earlier npm install fix. The detection itself is proven by reconstructing the incident synthetically (root dangling + nested shadowing), not by trusting the clean result.

SIDE EFFECT THAT CLOSES AN OPEN QUESTION IN br-d7lm: this command emits behavior.observation.recorded, which had no producer and no identified consumer. Its disposition moves EMIT -> KEEP, and event-authority.ts gained an entry with authority 'diagnostic' (a report ABOUT the repo, not a fact the runtime caused). title: Behavior: flag a test run that passed without running tests
description:
RECOMMENDATION 1 of 5. Highest-evidence best-practice behavior.

EVIDENCE (this repo's own .ensemble/runtime-log.jsonl, 118 test.failure.observed events over two days): 29 had 'zero tests ran' in output and 9 'suite failed to load' -- 38 of 51 classifiable failures were 'the suite did not actually run'. This is also what br-gwww was, and what the current constitution amendment about pipefail / 'Test Suites: 0 failed' is about.

THE GAP. verifyOutput() already detects vacuous success and has 32 tests, but it has exactly ONE caller: cqrs/commands.ts:329, inside fix.verify. So the detector only runs when verifying a PROPOSED FIX. When a human or agent runs the suite normally, nothing checks it.

COST IS HIGHER THAN 'just wire it up' -- corrected during review. event-translator.ts only emits test.failure.observed, and every FAILURE_OUTPUT_PATTERNS entry requires [1-9]\\d* failed or a FAIL marker. A run with 'Tests: 0 total' and exit code 0 matches none of them and is not isError, so TODAY IT PRODUCES NO EVENT AT ALL. There is no trigger for this behavior to fire on.

WORK:
1. event-translator.ts: emit test.passed (already in the ingress catalog at event-catalog.ts:60 and currently emitted by nothing) for a recognised test command that did not report failure, with a payload carrying tests-run/suites-loaded counts.
2. New command descriptor verification.observe -- non-mutating, no approval -- that runs verifyOutput over that payload.
3. Behavior triggering on test.passed, condition on the vacuous verdict, outcome reports loudly.

Start in policy.mode: propose. Do NOT block initially.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
DELIVERED (partially) 2026-09-29, commits on feature/trd-2026-0fc1c1d0-behavior-runtime-pi-harness.

1. event-translator.ts now emits test.passed for a recognised test command that reported it executed NOTHING. readTestVolume() reads jest/vitest totals, pytest counts, 'no tests ran', '[no test files]' and explicit '0 total'.

2. .ensemble/behaviors/vacuous-test-run/ reports it. No agent step and no commands: the judgement is mechanical, so asking a model to re-decide it would add latency, cost and a way to be wrong. Outcome status is 'inconclusive', never 'failed' -- the suite did not fail, which is precisely the problem.

3. 11 new tests in agent-core/tests/vacuous-test-run.test.ts.

DESIGN CHANGE FROM THE ORIGINAL PLAN, worth knowing. The plan said emit test.passed for every non-failing run. That broke 5 existing tests asserting the translator returns undefined for a healthy suite -- a deliberate contract so behaviors cannot chase healthy code. Rather than rewrite protected test files, emission was narrowed to the vacuous case only. Strictly better: the original guarantee is preserved untouched, and test.passed does not become the highest-volume event in the system.

'silent' (no count AND no explicit disclaimer) is deliberately NOT emitted. Reporting an unfamiliar runner's healthy output as vacuous is the same error in the opposite direction, and would train people to ignore the signal.

NOT DONE: no verification.observe command was needed after all. Remaining scope is optional -- richer reporting, and the router/pytest gap tracked separately in br-91nr.

title: a behavior's fix-prompt.md can drop the response contract, making every reply unparseable
description:
OBSERVED LIVE. Once br-boam stopped masking it, this is the next thing that kills the governed path.

buildFixPrompt does 'const body = template ?? [default]'. A behavior that ships fix-prompt.md therefore replaces the ENTIRE prompt -- including the part that tells the agent how to answer.

The trial repo's fix-prompt.md is well written as strategy and catastrophic as protocol. It says 'Repair the SOURCE so it passes' and 'Your change is verified by re-running the exact command that failed' -- describing an agent that EDITS FILES. But the child is spawned --tools=read,grep,glob precisely so it cannot write, and its reply is parsed as a JSON patch.

So the agent did exactly as instructed, discovered it had no way to do it, and said so in prose. Verbatim from the runtime log:

  'I found the bug, but I couldn't apply the fix: this session has no tool
   that can edit files in the working tree. write only accepts xd:// device
   paths here... I have no edit or shell tool.'

It then gave a correct diagnosis and a correct one-line fix, in markdown. parseFixReply found no json block and returned undefined. Recorded as 'no fix candidate offered'.

Diagnosis right, fix right, protocol wrong, loop dead.

WHY IT HID SO LONG. Running the same prompt by hand parsed perfectly -- because a hand-run passes no behaviorDirFor, so it gets the DEFAULT template, which does carry the contract. The failure only appears when a behavior ships its own prompt, which is the configuration the product ships.

FIX. Split strategy from protocol. The behavior owns judgment: which file, what counts as a real fix, what never to touch. The runtime owns the interface: you have no write tools, reply with only this json shape. Append RESPONSE_CONTRACT to every prompt, template or not, and say in it that it overrides anything above that contradicts it.

A behavior author cannot be expected to know the wire format of a process they never see, and should not be able to break it by writing a better prompt.
close_reason: done

title: Split the ingress catalog into what Ensemble produces and what it cannot receive
description:
MEASUREMENT (packages/agent-core, 2026-09-29): the catalog lists 54 trigger types. 10 are emitted. 44 (81%) are not.

Emitted: 6 harness runtime.* the Pi adapter publishes, 2 translated (test.failure.observed, test.passed), and command-emitted lifecycle events.

A catalog is a promise. 81% unfulfilled makes the other 19% untrustworthy too, because nothing distinguishes them -- which is why br-jgxo's load-time warning was needed at all. The warning makes the gap visible; it does not resolve it.

CRITICAL FINDING, verified not assumed: ENSEMBLE HAS NO INBOUND EVENT PATH. Exactly two things reach dispatchingSink (and therefore matcher.matchNames): session.ts publishing Pi host events plus their translations, and extension.ts:304 re-publishing command handler output. There is no webhook listener, no file tailer, no IPC, no subscribe. event-sinks.ts:14 states it: 'Foreman owns durable event ingestion.' The flow is outbound only.

So the prd/trd/implementation/review/pull_request/release families are not 'produced elsewhere and consumed here'. They CANNOT ARRIVE. Listing them as triggers advertises a capability with neither a producer nor a delivery mechanism.

PROPOSED DISPOSITION of the 44:

EMIT (13) -- Ensemble genuinely knows these in-session:
  behavior.completed / .blocked / .abandoned / .outcome.recorded / .observation.recorded (5) -- see br-j46q, do first
  approval.requested (1) -- the registry already calls the approval channel; 'a human was asked' is an auditable fact
  runtime.message.emitted / .session.failed / .cancelled / .timed_out (4) -- siblings already emitted, cheap completeness
  repository.changed / .branch.created (2) -- detectable from git tool calls; feeds the stale-base work (br-jg0l)
  test.regression_detected (1) -- needs cross-run memory; session-scoped only; most work of this group

NOT OURS (25) -- prd.* (4), trd.* (7), implementation.* (5), release.* (3), review.* (3), pull_request.* (3).
Two distinct reasons. PRD/TRD/implementation span sessions and need durability REQ-RUN-002 forbids adding here. review/pull_request/release have an AUTHORITATIVE source in GitHub; Ensemble emitting them would be a second, weaker, sometimes-disagreeing source. Move them to the cross-repository contract (docs/architecture/behavior-runtime-contract-v1.md) as Foreman's vocabulary. Do NOT describe them as 'consumed by Ensemble' until an inbound path exists -- that is a separate decision, and pull-based tailing with at-most-once semantics is the shape the local-sink spike (docs/architecture/cqrs-local-event-sink.md) points to.

REMOVE (6):
  validation.requested / .completed -- redundant with fix.verified
  change.proposed -- redundant with fix.proposed
  child_behavior.requested -- no child-behavior step kind exists; adding one is a much larger decision
  learning.observation.recorded -- overlaps br-u5o / br-pyg; decide there
  behavior.unblocked -- a session-scoped interpreter has no block-and-resume to unblock from

NOTE: behavior/event-catalog.ts is a protected guardrail file, so the operator must approve the edit.

AFTER: update trigger-producers.ts so the load-time warning stops firing on events that are correctly someone else's to emit, and distinguishes 'inert' from 'not ours'.

comments.text:
CORRECTION 2026-09-29, from the user: I had the Foreman/Ensemble relationship wrong when filing this.

WRONG MODEL (what this bead's 'NOT OURS' section assumes): two peer systems exchanging events, with Ensemble consuming prd/trd/review/pull_request/release from Foreman over some ingress path.

ACTUAL MODEL: Foreman OWNS THE SESSION. It launches a headless Ensemble session to do work, the session runs, it ends, Foreman collects the artifacts. Parent and child process. Neither attaches to the other's sessions. Corroborated by br-mr22, which records live headless runs in loop-trial dying when the session ends.

CONSEQUENCES FOR THIS BEAD:
- The 25 prd/trd/implementation/release/review/pull_request types should be REMOVED from the ingress catalog, not 'moved to the contract as consumed by Ensemble'. Foreman already holds these facts; it has no reason to send them to a child it started, and Ensemble has no path to receive them. Anything Ensemble needs (governing TRD, branch, acceptance criteria, mode) arrives as LAUNCH INPUT, not as an event.
- Disposition becomes EMIT 13 / REMOVE 31, with no third category.
- No ingress transport work is needed. Disregard any design for pull, cursors, git refs or HTTP; I had proposed those to solve a delivery problem that does not exist.

comments.text:
DECISION FROM THE USER 2026-09-29: 'we have a plan to have foreman emit these events in the future.'

THIS REVERSES THE 16:04 CORRECTION ON THIS BEAD, which said to REMOVE the 25 Foreman-domain types outright. Recording the tension rather than quietly switching, because the two statements are reconcilable and the reconciliation is the actual design.

THE RECONCILIATION. Both are true, because 'Foreman emits it' and 'Ensemble can trigger on it' are different claims separated by a delivery question:
- Foreman emitting prd.approved does NOT mean a running Ensemble session receives it. Foreman launches a session, the session runs, it ends. When Foreman emits prd.approved there is typically NO session alive to deliver it to, and building one that waits for such events is exactly the ingress layer REQ-RUN-002 forbids.
- What actually happens is the reverse: Foreman emits prd.approved, DECIDES to launch an Ensemble session in response, and the event is the LAUNCH INPUT for that session. The behavior then matches it at startup.

So these types are real, they are Foreman's to emit, and they ARE reachable by Ensemble behaviors -- via launch input, not via ingress. That is a delivery mechanism that exists today, needs no transport work, and contradicts neither statement.

  LAUNCH INPUT 25   -- prd.* trd.* implementation.* trd.implementation.* review.* release.* pull_request.*

  REMOVE 6          -- validation.requested, validation.completed, change.proposed,

title: constitution.apply is unreachable: MutationGuard denies its own sanctioned route
description:
`classifyPath` marks docs/standards/constitution.md protected and MutationGuard refuses every protected path unconditionally, so constitution.apply can never reach its write. REQ-SAFE-008's approval-gated application is currently satisfied by application being impossible.

AUTHORITY: br-9uqd (user design decision, 2026-09-25; commit 4914226 on dev, authored and committed by ldangelo) explicitly SUPERSEDES the older PR-as-gate design and states the consequence directly: 'WriteBoundaryMonitor must permit exactly that one authorized write.' Its rationale is that main is now protected and advances only through a dev -> main release PR, so human review is structural rather than smuggled in as 'the approval IS a PR'. Do NOT resolve this by reverting constitution.apply to PR-only; that re-implements the requirement the user retired.

REMAINING CHANGE (one file): in packages/agent-core/src/behavior/mutation-guard.ts, permit a protected path when verdict.reason === 'constitution' AND request.mutationClass === 'constitution.write'.

WHY THIS IS NARROW, AND NOW ENFORCED: mutation classes come from command descriptors, never from behavior data, so the class is not forgeable by a manifest. CommandRegistry.register() now throws if any descriptor claims SANCTIONED_PROTECTED_CLASS without requiresApproval, so the exemption cannot be widened later by adding an unapproved command in a file far from the guard that grants it. Covered by agent-core/tests/command-registry.test.ts ('the protected-path exemption cannot be widened by a new descriptor', 5 tests, incl. one asserting the exemption is not dead code).

BLOCKED ON: editing mutation-guard.ts is gated as guardrail-source; the OPERATOR must run /ensemble-approve for the pending violation id. Each retry mints a new id, so ask for the current one.

DELIVERED AND TESTED ALREADY: constitution.propose creates an evidence-backed artifact and writes nothing; constitution.apply checks approval, proposal kind, already-applied, and base-SHA drift before its write; the constitution-learning behavior triggers only on fix.verified with verdict passed.
close_reason: Carve-out landed via /ensemble-approve 27. constitution.apply reaches its write; 7 lifecycle tests cover apply, decline, no-approval-channel fail-closed, base-SHA drift, double-apply, undeclared capability, and that the exemption buys nothing for a non-constitution protected path.

title: hold fails OPEN when no tree baseline: fix is left applied
description: Observed live; see comment.
close_reason: Continuation path removed; propose cannot mutate; unverifiable state never resolves to allow

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
Live, 2026-09-29T02:04:18Z, /tmp/loop-trial-run (a FRESH git clone, so 'not a git work tree' is NOT the explanation):

  verification { issue: 'npm test', cwd: '/tmp/loop-trial-run', status: 'passed',
                 detail: '2 passed, 2 total', heldForApproval: [],
                 holdSkipped: 'no tree baseline; fix left applied' }

  invocation   { outcome: { status: 'rejected',
                 reason: 'behavior "fix-failing-test" runs in mode: propose;
                          direct write to src/math.js is denied' } }

Read those together. The GOVERNED path correctly refused to write under mode: propose. The CONTINUATION path then repaired src/math.js anyway, and the hold that should have caught it was skipped -- because a baseline was missing, the fix was LEFT APPLIED.

That is fail-open, in a codebase that fails closed everywhere else (createFixSandbox rejects rather than falling back to the live repo; SessionUiBridge.confirm returns false rather than assuming yes; a missing approval host denies). Here a missing baseline is treated as permission.

It also explains why #98's propose-gating looks like it never engages: it does engage, and then the continuation writes anyway.

Fix direction: no baseline => HOLD, and say so. An unverifiable change is exactly the change that should not be silently kept. Whatever the reason a baseline cannot be captured, 'I could not check' must never resolve to 'therefore allow'.

Open question to answer first: why is there no baseline in a clean clone? The cwd recorded is correct. Suspect baseline capture runs at a different point (activation, or pre-continuation) against a different root than the one in the verification record.

## Test Task: TRD-018-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-018-test
PRD Reference: #req-004

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.

title: Arming is a side effect of dependency layout, not consent
description:
The extension activates in EVERY omp session on the machine; only *arming*
(discovering behaviours) is per-repository. That makes arming a side effect of
dependency layout rather than a decision anyone made.

Observed, not inferred:
  - a bare repo yields discovered=0, no matcher, nothing dispatchable, and
    (as of 5cc2f37) no file written anywhere. Inertness holds.
  - BUT this repo arms on its own packages/agent-core/behaviors/
    (investigate-test-failure), with no per-repo opt-in anywhere. Any repo
    that later depends on a behaviour-shipping package would arm the same
    way, without its owner choosing to.

Install was accepted as the consent event for *having* the runtime. It is not
consent for a given repository to be acted on: the user who installs is not
necessarily the user (or the moment) whose repo arms.

Options, increasing strength:
  a) require an explicit .ensemble/config.yaml opt-in marker, distinct from
     behaviour discovery
  b) allowlist of repo roots under ~/.omp/
  c) drop the global shim; load per-invocation with -e, so activation is
     always an explicit act (available today via npm run uninstall:extension)

Related: br-x85k (injected turns are not attributable in the transcript).
Both are "the user cannot see or choose what the runtime is doing to them".
close_reason: Explicit .ensemble/config.yaml opt-in marker implemented (option a, user decision). Consent checked before discovery; unarmed repos inert but functional; 11 tests; documented in behavior-authoring-guide.md.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
ANALYSIS 2026-09-29, not implemented -- this is a product decision about consent and the three options have materially different UX.

CURRENT STATE CONFIRMED: ACTIVATION_SEARCH_ROOTS = ['packages', '.'] (agent-core/src/behavior/package-discovery.ts:101), so activation scans both the repo itself and any packages/*/behaviors directory. Nothing anywhere asks the repo owner.

A REFINEMENT WORTH CONSIDERING alongside option (a), because it may give most of the benefit at none of the friction: distinguish behaviors the repo OWNS from behaviors that ARRIVED. A behavior under the repo's own .ensemble/behaviors/ was placed there deliberately by whoever runs the repo -- that is a decision someone made. A behavior under packages/*/behaviors or node_modules arrived as a dependency, which is exactly the case this bead objects to ('any repo that later depends on a behaviour-shipping package would arm the same way, without its owner choosing to'). Requiring an explicit marker ONLY for the second class would close the actual gap without making every existing repo opt in again.

IMPLEMENTATION CONSTRAINT worth knowing before anyone starts: pi-extension/tests/behavior-activation.test.ts asserts discovered === 1 for a fixture repo with no opt-in marker. That file is guardrail-protected, so any change requiring the fixture to opt in needs operator approval to update the test. The refinement above may avoid that entirely, depending on where the fixture places its behavior -- check before choosing.

NOT DOING THIS UNILATERALLY: options (a) marker, (b) allowlist under ~/.omp, and (c) drop the global shim differ in who bears the friction and how recoverable a mistake is. (c) in particular makes activation an explicit act every time, which is the strongest consent story and the largest change to daily use.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: DECISION FROM THE USER 2026-09-29: option (a) -- explicit .ensemble/config.yaml opt-in marker, distinct from behavior discovery. Implementing now. The owned-vs-arrived refinement I proposed alongside it was NOT selected; arming requires the marker regardless of whether the behaviors are the repo's own or arrived via a dependency. Simpler rule, and it is the one that actually answers the bead: consent becomes an act, not a side effect of dependency layout.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: DELIVERED. src/repo-consent.ts requires 'behaviors: armed: true' in .ensemble/config.yaml; checked BEFORE discovery so arming cannot be a consequence of layout. Unarmed repos stay inert but working (matcher still returned, nothing skipped). Presence of the file is not consent -- the key must be present and literally true. Explicit 'armed: false' reports as disarmed rather than nagging. Malformed/unreadable yaml means not armed. Reason surfaced in the activation log because an unarmed repo otherwise looks identical to a broken one. 11 tests in tests/repo-consent.test.ts; 138 pass. This repo armed via its own .ensemble/config.yaml. Documented in behavior-authoring-guide.md as the first section, since nothing else in that guide takes effect without it.

title: AutofixLoop snapshots after the fix provider runs; restore cannot undo provider-side writes and reports restored anyway
description:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-25 (same run as the fix-provider isolation bead).

AutofixLoop.attempt() (autofix-loop.ts:103-108) captures its snapshot AFTER the fix provider has already produced the candidate. Anything the provider changed on disk while producing it is already in the snapshot, so `snapshot.restore()` "restores" the mutated contents.

The outcome record then reports `restored: [packages/pi-extension/package.json]` while the change is still on disk -- a success claim that is false. Seen twice (21:52:20Z and 21:57:30Z).

Distinct from br-omwb (continuation path detects a bad fix but does not roll back): this is the GOVERNED path, which does roll back, but from a restore point taken too late.

## Acceptance
- The restore point is captured before the fix provider runs, covering every path the attempt could touch (at minimum the candidate's paths; a provider-side write to any path is detected).
- If the working tree changed between the pre-provider snapshot and the candidate being applied, the attempt is rejected, the tree is returned to its pre-provider state, and the outcome says so explicitly (not a silent `restored`).
- `restored` lists only paths whose on-disk content actually changed back.
- Mutation-test: move the capture back after the provider -> the test fails.
close_reason: Merged into the #85 branch via PR #86 (merge 5f9a99b). CI on GitHub: PR #86 and PR #85 @5f9a99b both green -- test (22), test (24), validate, actionlint, eslint, markdownlint. Live extension bundle rebuilt from 5f9a99b and verified to contain the fix. Fix: 0f5ae83 (pre-provider baseline + staleness refusal; restore reports unchanged vs restored).

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: Fixed on fix/autofix-provider-governance (0f5ae83, not yet merged): restore reports only real changes (new 'unchanged' list); runner takes a git-object baseline BEFORE the provider and refuses a candidate whose target paths changed during generation. Mutation-tested both. DEVIATION: on a stale target the tree is NOT returned to its pre-provider state -- that would roll back concurrent human edits (the reason WorkspaceSnapshot is per-path). With br-r3om the provider can no longer write, so the remaining writers are concurrent humans, whose edits must survive. Live repro of the false 'restored' in the main checkout: see br-x36p.

title: Behavior: verify checkable claims in changed documentation
description:
RECOMMENDATION 4 of 5.

TRIGGER: repository.changed, scoped to markdown.
ACTION: extract checkable claims -- file paths, shell commands, function signatures, symbol names -- and verify each resolves against the tree. Report the ones that do not.

EVIDENCE, from this session, all mine. While documenting the behavior runtime I produced four fabrications in a single pass: (1) a CLI 'npx ts-node packages/agent-core/scripts/validate-behaviors.ts' that does not exist, hedged with 'if present in your checkout'; (2) compile({ behaviors, knownCommands }) as one merged object when the real signature is compile(pkg, options) -- a reader following it would have had knownCommands silently ignored, so capabilities.commands went unchecked, i.e. a WRONG CLAIM ABOUT AN AUTHORIZATION CHECK; (3) an elided simulate(...) shape; (4) invented line citations, produced by grepping a file after inserting my own note and reading my own text as corroboration.

Every CODE claim made that day held up, because code gets run. The prose did not, because nothing checks prose. Wrong documentation outlives wrong code -- nothing type-checks it.

PRIOR ART IN-REPO: docs/architecture/behavior-command-event-reference.md is generated from source with tests/catalog-reference.test.ts asserting it is current. That pattern works but only covers generated docs; this behavior covers hand-written ones.

WORK: one command doc.verify plus an agent step to extract claims (extraction needs judgement; verification must not). Model proposes candidates, mechanical check decides.
close_reason: doc.verify command + doc-claim-check behavior delivered, plus the repository.changed/branch.created emitter the trigger needed. Model proposes claims, a mechanical command adjudicates. 45 tests.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
DELIVERED, and the most useful thing I learned was that my first version was unusable.

THE TRIGGER DID NOT EXIST. repository.changed was declared in the catalog and emitted by nothing, so this behavior would have been inert -- the exact failure br-jgxo/br-d7lm are about. Rather than ship it inert I added translateRepositoryChange() to event-translator.ts: successful git commit/merge/rebase/revert/cherry-pick/apply -> repository.changed; checkout -b / switch -c -> repository.branch.created. Anchored to command position (a message containing 'git commit' is not one) and skipped when the command failed, because a rejected commit changed nothing. Kept as a SEPARATE function from translateEvent, whose every early return means 'not a test command' rather than 'nothing happened'. 19 tests. This closes two entries on br-d7lm's EMIT list; running split KEEP 17 / EMIT 6 / LAUNCH-INPUT 25 / REMOVE 6.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT CHANGED THE DESIGN. I ran naive extraction over this repo's own architecture docs: 31 claims, 30 reported broken. Almost every one was correct -- docs write 'agent-core/src/behavior/compiler.ts', omitting the packages/ prefix. A checker that is wrong nineteen times out of twenty does not get read, and then the one real finding is lost with the rest. Two consequences:
- verifyPath resolves configurable prefixes (default ['', 'packages/']). Repo-specific shorthand belongs to the caller, not the module. 30 unresolved -> 9.
- The remaining 9 are the interesting part and CANNOT be fixed mechanically: 3 are files genuinely deleted in Phase 0 but named deliberately by cqrs-gap-report.md, which is a historical document and accurate; 1 is src/math.js in a worked example. A regex cannot tell 'this describes a previous state on purpose' from 'this is stale'. That is precisely why the bead put judgement in extraction, and the prompt now spends most of its length on what to LEAVE OUT: historical references, illustrative examples, external things, anything already hedged, and generic identifiers.

THE SPLIT IS ENFORCED, not merely intended. The agent step proposes and must return JSON (prose would let 'I checked the docs and they look fine' pass as a result). doc.verify decides, mechanically, and REJECTS an unknown claim kind rather than skipping it -- silently dropping a claim would let a document report all-verified when some were never checked. Tests assert the agent step is kind: agent with tools ['read'] and the decision step is kind: command.

EMPTY IS NOT A PASS. verifyClaims returns ok: false when zero claims were checked, because 'nothing to check' and 'everything checked out' are different facts; collapsing them is the vacuous-success pattern from br-cwrh/br-zctt.

Tests: 12 claim-verification, 19 translator, 14 command+package = 45.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
WIRING DEFECT FOUND AFTER I CLOSED THIS, fixed now.

withTranslation() in event-translator.ts wraps a publish function and its doc comment promises 'any implied semantic event'. It called only translateEvent, so once translateRepositoryChange existed that promise was false: any caller using the wrapper rather than the translators directly would have silently missed every repository event -- no error, no warning, just a behavior that never fires. Exactly the class of defect this bead exists to catch, which would have been a poor thing to ship with. Fixed, with a note that a new translator must be added there as well as at the call site.

session.ts itself calls the translators directly, so the live path was never broken -- but I only know that because I now test it. Added pi-extension/tests/repository-change-wiring.test.ts: 5 tests firing real Pi events through wireSessionLifecycle and asserting repository.changed reaches the sink.

That test failed on its first run, usefully. I fired tool_execution_end, which produces runtime.tool_call.completed but carries NO command -- only tool_result exposes tool input (pi-events.ts). So the translator saw a well-formed event with nothing to match and correctly did nothing. 'The translator works' and 'the translator is reachable' are separate claims, and only the second one matters for whether a behavior ever runs.

title: verification trusted a runner the same run judged defective
description: Observed live; see comment.
close_reason: verifyOutput treats a reported pass alongside an unloadable suite as inconclusive

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
Live, same run. The verifier accepted:

  Tests:       0 failed, 2 passed, 2 total     exit=0

One of those two 'passed' suites is tests/guard.test.js, which cannot load at all -- it requires ../src/rounding, which does not exist. Re-run by hand just now in the post-fix tree: 'guard.test.js: suite did not load', still counted as passed, exit 0.

In the SAME run, the constitution provider diagnosed precisely this and wrote an amendment saying a suite that fails to load MUST count as a failure.

So the system identified the defect in the project's runner and was simultaneously fooled by it. The fix it verified was verified by an instrument it had just declared untrustworthy.

This is NOT simply 'the verifier is buggy' -- trusting the project's test runner is correct default behaviour; the runner is the source of truth and the runtime cannot reimplement every framework. The specific gap is narrower and fixable:

When a run produces a constitution amendment ABOUT THE TEST RUNNER'S REPORTING, the verification that follows is using an instrument the run itself just judged defective. At minimum that should be surfaced -- verification passed, but the amendment in this same run says this runner's pass count cannot be trusted.

Cheap partial defense, independent of the above: the runtime already parses the summary line. A suite count that drops between runs, or output matching /did not load|failed to run|Cannot find module/ alongside a PASS, is worth flagging even when the runner says exit 0.

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

title: test.failure.observed is masked by shell pipelines (isError reflects last pipeline command)
description:
## Problem

`test.failure.observed` is derived from `runtime.tool_call.completed` with
`isError === true`. `isError` reflects the *shell's* exit status, which is the
exit status of the LAST command in a pipeline. So any of these mask a failing
test run as a success:

    npx jest foo 2>&1 | tail -80      # exit status of tail (0)
    npx jest foo | grep -E "Tests:"   # exit status of grep
    npx jest foo; npx tsc --noEmit    # exit status of tsc

Observed live (dogfood run, /tmp/ens-fix, 2026-09-25): the model ran
`npx jest write-boundary-monitor 2>&1 | tail -80` against a genuinely failing
suite. Logged as `isError=False`. All 12 bash calls in that session reported
`isError=False`; no `test.failure.observed` was emitted and NO behavior
dispatched, despite a real, reproducible test failure being present the whole
time.

## Why this matters

Whether the autofix pipeline fires depends on the model's incidental shell
formatting, not on whether tests actually failed. Prior "live dispatch proven"
evidence (test.failure.observed -> DISPATCH) held only because that run used a
bare command with no pipe. This is a trigger-reliability defect, not a
cosmetic one: in normal use, models pipe test output to tail/grep constantly
to control context size.

## Candidate fixes (evaluate, do not assume)

1. Parse tool OUTPUT for test-runner failure signatures in addition to
   exit status (e.g. jest `Tests:\s+\d+ failed`, `Test Suites:\s+\d+ failed`,
   vitest/pytest/go-test equivalents). Robust to pipes; runner-specific and
   needs care to avoid matching a *passing* summary line or echoed text.
2. Treat a tool call whose command matches the behavior's declared
   `execution.test_command` as a test observation regardless of exit status,
   then classify by output.
3. Both: exit status OR output signature, whichever indicates failure.

Note the inverse risk: naive output matching can produce FALSE failures from
text that merely mentions failures (e.g. `git log`, reading this bead, or a
prior run's output echoed in a heredoc). Any matcher must be anchored to the
runner's summary format and mutation-tested in both directions.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A failing test run piped to `tail`/`grep`/`head` still produces
      `test.failure.observed`.
- [ ] A PASSING test run piped the same way does NOT produce it.
- [ ] Text that merely mentions "N failed" without being a test summary does
      not trigger it.
- [ ] Mutation-tested: disabling the new detection makes the piped-failure
      test fail.
- [ ] Verified live in a real omp subprocess, not only in unit tests.
close_reason: Fixed in 3f67359. translateEvent now fires when EITHER exit status OR output reports failure; output patterns apply only to identified test commands and require a NON-ZERO failure count. Mutation-tested both ways (exit-status-only -> pipe test fails; bare /failed/ -> zero-failures guard fails). Verified live with the exact invocation that defeated detection: 'npx jest live-e2e 2>&1 | tail -5' -> DETECTED(detectedBy=output) -> continuation -> fix.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-25 breaking autofix end-to-end, not merely theoretical.

In a real one-shot run the model chose to invoke the suite as:

    npx jest live-e2e 2>&1 | tail -5

The pipe makes the shell report tail's status, so the bash tool result had
isError=false even though the suite FAILED (the model's own reply was 'It
failed.'). test.failure.observed therefore never fired, no behavior matched,
no continuation was queued, and the source was left broken.

Consequence for earlier evidence: a prior run in the same fixture DID fix the
bug end-to-end. The difference between the two runs was purely which command
string the model happened to choose -- pipe vs no pipe. So detection keyed on
shell exit status is nondeterministic in practice, and any single successful
autofix run is weak evidence until this is fixed. Piping to head/tail/grep is
ordinary model behaviour, not an edge case.

Fix direction (unchanged, now urgent): invoke the declared test_command
argv-style rather than relying on the exit status of a model-authored shell
string, and/or detect failure from OUTPUT (jest/pytest summary lines) instead
of exit code alone. Note the related trap found while building verification:
exit code 0 also occurs when jest matches ZERO tests, so output parsing must
require a nonzero test count.

title: PRD-5: Scale-adaptive intelligence
description:
Implement AI-driven complexity analysis that auto-adjusts Ensemble planning depth

## Problem
Ensemble requires manual complexity classification. BMAD uses scale-adaptive intelligence to auto-adjust.

## Goals
- AI analyzes work description to determine complexity
- Planning depth auto-selected based on complexity score
- Complexity score based on: scope size, dependencies, risk factors, team size

## User Stories
- As a developer, I want auto-selected planning depth so I don't manually classify work
- As a PM, I want AI complexity scoring so planning effort matches actual need

## Requirements
- FR-001: analyze-complexity command scores work description
- FR-002: Score 1-3 → Simple (fix-issue path)
- FR-003: Score 4-6 → Medium (PRD→TRD)
- FR-004: Score 7-10 → Complex (full pipeline with extra review)
- FR-005: Complexity score shown to user before planning begins
- FR-006: User can override AI classification

## Verification
- Simple bug description → score ≤3 → fix-issue path
- Complex initiative description → score ≥7 → full pipeline with extra gates
close_reason: Duplicate of br-0r3. Both specify the same routing decision -- br-iah as a 1-10 score, br-0r3 as Simple/Medium/Complex -- dispatching to the same three paths, so br-iah's FR-002/3/4 are br-0r3's bands restated and FR-006 duplicates br-0r3 FR-005. Building both would create two commands that can disagree about whether work needs a PRD, which spec section 7 forbids as a dual dispatch path. Requirements absorbed into br-0r3 (see its comments): single 'classify' command, 1-10 score shown to the user, banded for dispatch, overridable. Nothing from this bead is dropped, including its verification cases and the unresolved question of which inputs the scorer can actually read.

comments.text: See the analysis on br-0r3. Awaiting a decision on whether to merge these two P0s before any code.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
# br-ivv Adversarial Phrase False-Positive Log — ensemble-as-behaviors @ 71ca738+

Run 2026-09-23. 12 prompt-templates x 43 registry phrases = **516 probes** through the
real hook (`node packages/router/hooks/router.js`, stdin JSON), block-parsed for
`→ skill <name>` lines. Scripts: `scripts/adversarial-phrase-sweep.js` (raw rows →
`/tmp/ivv-raw.json`), `scripts/adversarial-phrase-report.js` (precision tables).
Reproducible: `node scripts/adversarial-phrase-sweep.js && node scripts/adversarial-phrase-report.js`.

## Result headline

- **0 unexpected skill activations.** Every firing on every probe is an exact substring
  hit on some phrase, by the documented matching contract.
- **473/473 negative-intent probes fired ≥1 skill** — 100% "false positive" by intent,
  but **462/473 are own-phrase hits** (the negation/question/trap template still contains
  the literal phrase → the owning skill surfaces). That is substring matching working
  exactly as designed; suggestion-only + "act only if it fits" framing absorbs the cost.
- **516/516 positive probes fired correctly**, 12/12 templates per phrase (perfect recall).
- **12 cross-phrase hits, one cause** — the entire precision loss of the registry in one row:

## Ambiguous phrases

| skill | phrase | defect | impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| `git-town` | `create a pr` | prefix of `create a prd` / `create a trd` (all prompts mentioning those phrases also surface git-town) | the ONLY collision: 12/516 probes |

**Recommendation for REQ-BEH-002**: add word-boundary to `create a pr`
(`" … \bcreate a pr\b"`-style — longest-match-wins, or exclude when followed by `d`/`ov`/`o`)
or drop the phrase — git-town is already covered by `create a pull request`.

## Per-phrase precision (all 43: identical shape)

Every phrase: `neg firings 11/11` (own-phrase substring, by design), `pos firings 1/1`,
`extra-skill hits` 0 except the 10 `create a pr*`-family rows. Full table:
`/tmp/ivv-report.md` (session-local; regenerate with the report script).

## False-negative companion note (from br-fnf run)

Prompts that name the artifact WITHOUT a registered verb-phrase — e.g.
"I need a PRD for the billing feature", "we should write requirements for X" — match
**zero** phrases (substring contract has no noun-only patterns). Recall gaps are in verb
phrasing coverage, not false positives. Candidates to seed: `draft the requirements`,
`spec out` (present), `requirements doc` (noun form), `PRD for`, `TRD for`.
Feeds REQ-BEH-002 alongside the collision fix.

## Method limits

- Templates cover 11 negative forms (negation x3, already-done, substring-trap, quoted-meta,
  what/why questions, past-tense, compound-neg, embedded-word) + 1 positive; no typos, no
  non-English, no multi-intent prompts.
- Registry as of 71ca738: 43 phrases / 6 skills. `glob` is a root devDependency; the sweep
  runs from the repo root.

title: Behavior outcomes are declared but never emitted, so behaviors cannot chain
description:
The workflow interpreter already computes the facts. Nothing publishes them.

EVIDENCE:
- workflow/interpreter.ts:80-82 carries 'terminal: TerminalState' and 'outcome?: string' on every run result, and line 151-154 logs { kind: 'workflow-end', behavior, terminal, outcome, reason }.
- git grep for the published types finds them ONLY in cqrs/event-authority.ts (schemas) and behavior/event-catalog.ts (the ingress list). No publish call site exists for behavior.completed, behavior.blocked, behavior.abandoned, behavior.outcome.recorded or behavior.observation.recorded.
- Meanwhile EVERY manifest declares them. .ensemble/behaviors/*/behavior.yaml all end with 'outcomes: [behavior.completed, ...]', and the compiler validates that list.

So an author declares an outcome, the compiler checks it, the interpreter reaches it, and the runtime drops it. That is a promise the runtime does not keep -- and it is invisible, because a behavior that completes looks exactly like one whose outcome went nowhere.

WHY THIS ONE FIRST, ahead of the other emission gaps: it changes what is POSSIBLE rather than what is observable. Today one behavior cannot react to another's outcome. Command-emitted events already re-enter the sink (extension.ts:304), and the comment there states the intent plainly -- 'a behavior can react to fix.verified rather than guessing from test.failure.observed'. Behavior outcomes are the missing half of that design.

SCOPE:
- Publish the interpreter's terminal result through the same sink command events use, so it reaches matcher.matchNames like everything else.
- Map terminal state to type: succeeded/inconclusive -> behavior.completed; blocked -> behavior.blocked; failed/cancelled -> behavior.abandoned. Carry the declared outcome name in the payload.
- Bounded by InvocationBudget, which already exists to make composition possible without recursion. A behavior that triggers on behavior.completed and completes must not loop -- add a test for exactly that.
- behavior.unblocked is deliberately NOT in scope: a session-scoped interpreter has no block-and-resume concept to unblock from. See the catalog bead.

TESTS: chaining works end to end; a self-triggering behavior terminates via the budget; a run that fails still emits rather than going silent.
close_reason: Fixed: workflow-dispatch publishes a behavior lifecycle event after every resolved run. succeeded/inconclusive -> behavior.completed, blocked -> behavior.blocked, failed/cancelled -> behavior.abandoned (the catalog has no behavior.failed, so the real terminal state travels in the payload). One event per run, not two -- behavior.outcome.recorded alongside would double volume to say the same thing twice. A refused stamp is logged rather than dropped, since a swallowed outcome is the defect being fixed. 5 tests including a behavior that triggers on its own completion and is stopped by InvocationBudget.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CORRECTION 2026-09-29, after the bead was closed. The first mapping had no branch for terminal === 'inconclusive', so it fell through to behavior.completed -- publishing 'we could not tell' as 'it worked'.

That is the exact overclaim the vacuous-test-run behavior (br-cwrh) was built to catch in the same session: it uses status: inconclusive and never succeeded, precisely so a suite that executed nothing is not called a pass. Collapsing the two in the EVENT layer would have undone that distinction everywhere downstream, which is worse than never having drawn it.

Final mapping, with authorities:
  succeeded    -> behavior.completed        (observed)
  inconclusive -> behavior.outcome.recorded (diagnostic)
  blocked      -> behavior.blocked          (diagnostic)
  failed |
  cancelled    -> behavior.abandoned        (observed)

behavior.outcome.recorded carries authority 'diagnostic' rather than 'observed', which is the weaker claim wanted for a run whose result is unknown. Still one event per run.

Three tests added: inconclusive publishes outcome.recorded and explicitly NOT completed; the payload carries the real terminal state so the weaker claim is checkable; succeeded remains distinct, so the fix did not simply move the collapse somewhere else.

Also updates br-d7lm's disposition: behavior.outcome.recorded is now EMITTED, so it moves from EMIT to KEEP.

title: The ingress event catalog is aspirational: only test.failure.observed is ever emitted
description:
Found while scoping the best-practice behaviors (br-cwrh, br-jg0l).

behavior/event-catalog.ts lists ~45 ingress event types a behavior may trigger on: prd.*, trd.*, implementation.*, review.*, validation.*, release.*, repository.*, pull_request.*, test.passed, and more. event-translator.ts emits exactly ONE of them: test.failure.observed (line 187). The pi extension otherwise emits only runtime.* telemetry.

CONSEQUENCE: a behavior authored against any other trigger compiles, validates, loads, and then never fires. There is no error and no warning -- it simply sits there looking installed. This is the failure mode that made the old example behavior's trigger unsatisfiable (cited in TRD-2026-15aa5acd as REQ-009/010/011), reappearing as a catalog that promises far more than the translator delivers.

It bit two of the five recommended behaviors immediately: br-cwrh needs test.passed (in the catalog, emitted by nothing) and br-jg0l needs pull_request.proposed (same).

OPTIONS: (a) emit more of the catalog from the translator as real signals become detectable; (b) shrink the ingress catalog to what is actually emitted and grow it deliberately; (c) keep both but have discovery WARN when a loaded behavior's trigger has no known producer, so an inert behavior announces itself.

(c) is cheap and should happen regardless of (a)/(b) -- a behavior that can never fire should say so at load time.
close_reason: Option (c) delivered: inert triggers warn at load (trigger-producers.ts, activation inertTriggers, status 'loaded but cannot fire', 12 tests). Options (a) emit more and (b) shrink the catalog are br-d7lm, which now carries the full 54-row per-event disposition and a total-coverage acceptance criterion.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
OPTION (c) DELIVERED 2026-09-29: a behavior that cannot fire now says so at load time.

- agent-core/src/behavior/trigger-producers.ts: producibleTriggers(), triggerHasProducer(), explainInertTrigger(). The explanation names what DOES fire, so a reader is not sent back to the catalog that misled them.
- behavior-activation.ts: inert triggers are collected into BehaviorActivationResult.inertTriggers and console.warn'd. A WARNING, never a skip -- an adapter may legitimately publish a type this build does not know about, and refusing to load would turn a guess into a hard failure.
- runtime-status.ts renders them under 'loaded but cannot fire', distinct from 'skipped': these ARE installed and answer manual invocation; they just cannot fire on their own, which is the part that looks identical to working.
- 10 tests.

BUG FOUND AND FIXED DURING IMPLEMENTATION, worth recording because it is the same shape as the defect being fixed. The first version derived producers from eventTypes() in cqrs/event-authority.ts. That returns 61 entries -- the whole domain vocabulary WITH PAYLOAD SCHEMAS -- and a schema describes an event's shape, it is not evidence anything emits one. prd.created has a schema and producer: 'runtime', but nothing produces it. So triggerHasProducer() returned true for everything and the check always passed: a guard that guards nothing, shipped to detect behaviors that fire on nothing. Caught by a test asserting prd.created is inert.

Producers are now derived from what is actually emitted: two translator types, eight descriptor-declared types, and command.rejected which the registry emits directly (kept in a separate constant so the drift test comparing against the catalog's emits lists does not read it as drift forever).

The hand-maintained list is pinned by a test comparing it to createCommandCatalog()'s emits, so a new command cannot leave this check reporting a live trigger as inert.

STILL OPEN: options (a) emit more of the catalog and (b) shrink the catalog to what is emitted. This change only makes the gap visible.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
SUPERSEDED IN PART by br-d7lm, which carries the measurement (10 of 54 emitted) and the proposed disposition of all 44.

Also recorded there, and it changes this bead's framing: Ensemble has NO INBOUND EVENT PATH. Two sources reach the matcher -- Pi host events plus their translations, and command handler output re-published at extension.ts:304. No webhook, no tailer, no IPC. So the prd/trd/review/pull_request/release families are not merely unemitted; they cannot arrive at all.

Option (c) -- warn at load time -- is delivered here. Options (a) emit more and (b) shrink the catalog are now br-d7lm's.

title: Governed fix.verify is refused on ext4/overlay Linux (no copy-on-write), including our own CI
description:
FOUND 2026-09-29 while landing #107. createIsolatedWorkspace provisions node_modules copy-on-write only (cp -c on APFS, cp --reflink=always on btrfs/xfs) and REFUSES otherwise. That is the deliberate br-t0so design: symlink reaches the live tree (br-bxm7), and a plain copy was judged too slow.

CONSEQUENCE: on ext4, the default Linux filesystem, and on GitHub-hosted runners (proven: 'cp --reflink=always: Operation not supported' in #107's CI log), every governed verification is refused. fix.verify cannot reach 'passed' there, so fix.apply is unreachable. The propose -> verify -> apply chain is inert for those users, as br-t0so was before its fix, and CI can only assert the refusal (c1568a6), never the clone.

OPTIONS (product decision):
(a) Accept it. Document 'governed fixes need APFS/btrfs/xfs'.
(b) Fall back to a plain copy with a size/time cap and an explicit 'slow path' notice. That is still isolated, so br-bxm7 does not return.
(c) Fall back to a fresh 'npm ci' in the workspace, using a lockfile and the offline cache.
(d) Run CI on a CoW-capable runner so the clone path is exercised.
Measure (b) and (c) on this repo's node_modules before choosing. br-t0so's 'too slow' was a judgement, not a number.

title: Behavior tool-grant window spans the whole agent run, including the user's own work
description:
beginBehaviorScope() opens at turn_end when a continuation is injected; only agent_end or session_shutdown closes it (tool-grant-enforcement.ts:57-69). In an interactive session the injected turn and every following user and advisor message form one run, so the behavior's grants applied to unrelated user-directed work for several replies: 'tool todo is not granted to executing behavior(s) [investigate-test-failure, fix-failing-test]'; write, eval, task and learn were also blocked. It cleared only when that run finally ended. The code comment accepts 'an interjection landing inside a behavior turn'; observed scope is much wider. Also: the same agent_end then ran verification and a rollback of the whole working tree against a 6-minute-old snapshot.

Evidence: headless omp -p runs on dev (7b57d4a) in worktree /private/tmp/wt-e2e, planted bug scripts/lib/e2e-sum.js; logs in /tmp/e2e/ (e2e.jsonl, e2e2.jsonl, e2e3.jsonl, guard.jsonl, *-runtime-log.jsonl).

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: VERIFIED FIXED on dev (02db136). The window no longer waits for session_shutdown. closeBehaviorWindow() is called on THREE paths: agent_end (extension.ts:747, 'the window must not outlive the run'), session_shutdown as a fail-safe (754, 'a crashed or aborted run must never strand the user in a narrowed session'), and turn_end (763, checked before a new continuation is taken so a window opened by that handler is not judged against its own turn). The bead's specific defect -- grants spanning every following user and advisor message until the run ends -- is addressed by the agent_end and turn_end closes. RESIDUAL, tracked on br-o355 not here: I hit a tool denial live this session ('wait is not granted to executing behavior(s)') while a fix turn was legitimately in flight. That is the accepted 'interjection landing inside a behavior turn' case, and the open question it raises -- whether a window should ever REMOVE a capability the session already had -- is br-o355's.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
FOLLOW-UP: I closed this citing line numbers and a comment without reading
the conditional. Read it now. The close stands, but on different evidence.

turn_end's close is GATED, not unconditional:
    if (awaitingVerification && fixTurnFinished(event)) {
      closeBehaviorWindow();
      verifyPendingFix();
    }

So it depends on awaitingVerification always being set whenever a window is
opened. It is, and in the same handler:
    777  openBehaviorWindow(next.behaviors)
    808  awaitingVerification = { ... }
The window opens when a continuation is queued and the pairing is assigned a
few lines later, so the NEXT turn_end closes it. That is the actual fix for
this bead: the window ends with the fix turn, not with the whole agent run.

agent_end closes unconditionally as a backstop ("a run can end without a
finished fix turn -- aborted, errored, or cut short"), and session_shutdown
is a fail-safe.

NARROW RESIDUAL, not worth reopening but worth knowing: between 777 and 808
sits pi.sendUserMessage(). If that throws, the window is open and
awaitingVerification was never assigned, so turn_end's gate cannot fire and
only agent_end closes it -- i.e. the original symptom, in the error path
only. If anyone touches this code, assign awaitingVerification BEFORE
sending, or wrap the send so a failure closes the window.
