ldangelo
comments.text:
LIVE REPRODUCTION, on the maintainer's own session, 2026-09-28.

An autofix continuation fired off a broken test file of mine. Some time later -- across several unrelated turns of my own work (editing source, running jest, rebuilding a bundle, launching a live trial run) -- a tool call was refused:

  tool 'wait' is not granted to executing behavior(s)
  [investigate-test-failure, fix-failing-test]
  (granted tools: [bash, edit, ensemble.bash, glob, grep, read])

This is the bead's original complaint, observed rather than argued: the behavior window was still open over work that had nothing to do with the fix turn, and it narrowed the operator's own toolset.

Mechanism, confirmed: the window closes at the first turn_end where fixTurnFinished(event) is true, and that predicate is 'the turn ended with NO tool calls'. Every turn I took used tools, so none of them qualified, and the window persisted across all of them.

I downgraded this to non-blocking earlier today on the grounds that it does not stop an approval from resolving. That was right about approvals and wrong about impact: it degrades every session it spans, and it took a refused tool call rather than a code reading to see it.

The close condition should be tied to the FIX TURN's identity -- the turn opened by sendUserMessage -- not to a heuristic about whether some turn happened to call tools.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
REASSESSED 2026-09-29 on feature/trd-2026-0fc1c1d0-behavior-runtime-pi-harness. Substantially narrowed, NOT closed.

PREMISE CHANGED. This bead describes a scope opened at turn_end when a CONTINUATION is injected, closed only at agent_end or session_shutdown. The continuation path was deleted by br-behavior-runtime-cqrs-xl24 (section 7 forbids two dispatch paths), so that mechanism no longer exists. beginBehaviorScope now opens immediately before matcher.onEvent and is released in a finally around it (extension.ts:162-177); agent_end and session_shutdown remain only as fail-safes against a crashed run stranding the user.

Window therefore went from 'the injected turn plus every following user and advisor message' to 'the duration of one dispatch'.

RESIDUAL RISK, still real. The dispatch is deliberately NOT awaited (extension.ts comment: the host stops waiting on a handler after 30s and blocks the tool as a fail-safe). So a behavior dispatch runs CONCURRENTLY with the user's own work, and the tool_call hook plus the scope are both process-global. A user tool call issued while a dispatch is in flight is still evaluated against the behavior's grants. The window is much smaller, but it is not zero, and the reported symptom -- 'tool todo is not granted to executing behavior(s)' hitting user-directed work -- remains reachable.

A real fix needs per-caller attribution at the tool_call hook so the scope applies only to calls originating from the behavior's own agent invocation. Whether Pi's tool_call event carries anything usable for that is unverified and should be checked before anyone designs around it.

CORRECTION to an earlier note of mine: I had recorded that tool-grant-enforcement.ts:104-107 'intersects rather than unions' scoped grants. That is wrong. Line 100-102 allows the call if ANY scoped behavior grants the tool, and 104-107 builds a union purely for the denial message. No intersection bug exists.

PR #94 (fix/behavior-scoped-write-boundary) is NOT on this branch -- git merge-base confirms c6b93dd 'merge: integrate #94, #95 and #96' is not an ancestor of HEAD. The narrowing described above came from the CQRS port, independently. At merge, check which implementation survives rather than assuming they compose.

title: Autofix hijacked a main-session test run: narrowed tools, failed rollback, WIP commit swept uncommitted work
description:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-29, main checkout, branch feature/trd-2026-0fc1c1d0-behavior-runtime-pi-harness, during br-0r3 work.

SEQUENCE.
1. The main agent ran 'npx jest tests/complexity-analyzer.test.js' on its own uncommitted change. One NEW test failed because of a bad fixture that the agent had just written.
2. investigate-test-failure + fix-failing-test fired on that output. The instruction arrived as a user-role turn. It was labelled 'MACHINE-GENERATED ... NOT FROM THE USER', but the channel is still a user turn. That contradicts br-x85k's close reason ('no longer injects turns').
3. For the rest of that turn, the MAIN agent's tools were narrowed to [ensemble.bash, glob, grep, read]. edit and bash were refused ('not granted to executing behavior(s)'). The main agent could not apply a one-line fix to its own test. See br-kluf.
4. The autofix reported: verification FAILED, and rollback FAILED ('pre-existing changes could not be re-applied: patch failed: complexity-analyzer.js:468 ... complexity-analyzer.test.js:217').
5. HEAD gained 1dfa6f5 '[pi] Work in progress' (author ldangelo). It contained the main session's uncommitted option-C work, swept in automatically. [INFERENCE] this came from the pi host's auto-commit on session exit for the autofix child running in the main checkout, not in an isolated worktree. The message is not in this repo.

NOTHING LOST. The content survived in 1dfa6f5. It was amended to 62d2368 with an honest message.

WHY IT MATTERS. It is the br-x13x pattern (autofix fires on a deliberate or in-progress failure) plus two new harms: a rollback that cannot restore pre-existing work, and an auto-commit that writes the user's uncommitted work to HEAD under a meaningless message. The last is the same class as br-suoh's mislabeled f2198b1.

EXPECTED. (a) Don't fire on a failure in a file the main session modified in the current turn, or at minimum don't narrow the main session's tools. (b) Never commit in the main checkout. (c) If rollback cannot restore pre-existing changes, leave the tree untouched, not half-restored.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: SECOND INSTANCE 2026-09-29, now CROSS-WORKTREE. During the CQRS/dev reconciliation, a subagent ran 'npx jest' in its own isolated worktree /tmp/ensemble-reconcile, and the test was red on purpose mid-merge. The host session's ensemble extension turned that output into an injected '[ensemble:autofix]' instruction. It narrowed the SUBAGENT's tools until a toolless turn, then re-ran root 'npx jest' INSIDE /tmp/ensemble-reconcile. No damage. But it shows the trigger is not scoped to the host's repo or to the session that owns it: any bash output in any cwd, from a child agent, qualifies. Same root as br-x36p (the governed path runs against the wrong repo). Source: local://reconcile-disposition.md, 'Other open items'.

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.

title: Behavior-scoped tool grants (per-invocation enforcement) instead of session-wide union
description:
## Problem

Tool grants are declared per-behavior (`capabilities.tools` in behavior.yaml)
but enforced session-wide. Enforcement is now the UNION of all loaded
behaviors' grants (see "Current state"), which composes correctly but is
coarser than the manifest implies: a behavior that declares
`tools: [read, grep]` does not actually restrict the session to those tools
if any other loaded behavior grants more.

The architecturally correct model is per-invocation scoping: a tool call made
on behalf of behavior X is checked against X's grant only.

## Why it is not implemented

Verified against pi-coding-agent source (dist/core/extensions/runner.js and
dist/core/extensions/types.d.ts, v0.87.1):

1. `emitToolCall` iterates every registered `tool_call` handler in
   registration order and returns on the FIRST `{ block: true }`:

       async emitToolCall(event) {
         for (const { handlers } of snapshotEventHandlers(this.extensions, "tool_call")) {
           for (const handler of handlers) {
             const handlerResult = await handler(event, ctx);
             if (handlerResult) {
               result = handlerResult;
               if (result.block) return result;
             }
           }
         }
         return result;
       }

   The host then throws (cli.js): `if (Q?.block) throw Error(Q.reason || ...)`.

2. `ToolCallEventBase` carries ONLY `{ type, toolCallId }` plus `toolName` and
   `input` on its variants. There is no `invocationId`, `behaviorId`,
   `activeBehavior`, or `originBehavior` field anywhere in the extension API.
   (`invocationId` exists twice in pi-agent-core's `harness/` subsystem --
   types.d.ts and runtime/progress.d.ts -- but that is the sub-agent harness,
   not reachable from an extension's tool_call handler.)

3. More fundamentally, there is currently no fact to correlate. Tool calls
   originate from the model's own turn, not from a dispatched behavior.
   Nothing "invokes" a behavior such that a subsequent bash call belongs to
   it. So "which behavior is this call for?" is not merely unplumbed --
   it is unanswerable in the present design.

## Evidence (live)

Dogfood run in /tmp/ens-fix, both `investigate-test-failure`
(tools: read, grep, glob, bash.test, git.diff) and `fix-failing-test`
(tools: read, grep, glob, bash, edit, write) loaded. `fix-failing-test`
explicitly granted `bash` and `edit`; the first `bash` call was blocked
(runtime-log: `runtime.tool_call.started tool=bash` then
`runtime.tool_call.completed isError=True`), because
`investigate-test-failure`'s handler ran first and short-circuited.

Consequence: the agent could not run the test suite, so no
`test.failure.observed` event was ever produced and NO behavior dispatched.
Enforcement prevented the system from exercising itself.

## Current state (what was shipped instead)

`wireToolGrantEnforcement` now registers ONE handler per session (keyed by a
WeakMap on the ExtensionAPI object) and blocks only if NO loaded behavior
grants the tool. Loading a behavior can only widen the grant, never silently
narrow another's. Denial message names all loaded behaviors and the union.

Covered by 3 regression tests in packages/pi-extension/tests/behavior-loader.test.ts
("tool grants compose as a union across loaded behaviors"), mutation-tested:
reverting to per-behavior wiring fails all 3.

## What a real fix requires

Behaviors need to own an execution context before per-invocation scoping is
meaningful. Options to evaluate:

- Behavior execution runs in its own sub-session/harness invocation, where
  `invocationId` already exists, and grants are attached to that invocation.
- Extension-side tagging: the behavior's registered command / sendUserMessage
  flow marks a window as "acting for behavior X", and the tool_call handler
  consults that marker. Fragile -- the model can emit tool calls outside the
  window, and concurrent/nested behaviors break the assumption.
- Upstream change to pi-coding-agent adding behavior/invocation correlation
  to ToolCallEvent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A tool call attributable to behavior X is checked against X's
      `capabilities.tools` only.
- [ ] A behavior declaring a narrow grant genuinely restricts the tools used
      on its behalf, even when a permissive behavior is also loaded.
- [ ] Load order still does not affect outcomes.
- [ ] Non-attributable tool calls (model's own turn, no behavior dispatched)
      have a defined, documented policy -- not an accidental one.
- [ ] Mutation-tested: removing the scoping makes the new tests fail.
close_reason: Implemented in ab46c82 (scope to executing behavior, not session union) and 070274a (close at agent_end, not turn_end -- a continuation spans multiple assistant turns, reproduced). Per-CALL attribution remains impossible (ToolCallEvent carries no behavior marker); the window is temporal, which is the honest approximation. 3 mutants caught. Verified live: ungranted edit/bash blocked inside the window, unscoped user bash unaffected. Remaining sub-gap tracked as AC-018-5 on br-o355 (shell redirect via a granted shell tool).

title: Governed dispatch is killed at session end: the constitution step never completes in headless runs
description:
THE ACTUAL REASON "step 3 never fires". Not capability, not the rule
provider, not missing RCA input -- the governed run is still executing when
the session ends, and dies with it.

OBSERVED, two consecutive live runs in loop-trial with instrumentation added
at the invoker entry point:

  invocation-started: "fix-failing-test"
  invocation completions: 0

The behavior matched and the governed invoker BEGAN. It never returned. No
dispatch record, no invocation record, no constitution record -- because all
three are written only after the run resolves.

CONTRAST with the earlier control run (typo repair, ~45s): that one DID log
dispatch + invocation + constitution {"status":"none"}. Same code, same
headless mode. The difference is duration: the governed run there finished
inside the session's lifetime. When the fix provider takes longer -- the
treatment scenario ran 68-98s -- the session ends first and the run is lost.

So completion is a RACE the governed path wins only by being fast. Nothing
guarantees it.

WHY THE EXISTING GUARD DOES NOT HELP
extension.ts registers:
    pi.on("session_shutdown", async () => { await drainDispatches(); });
and drainDispatches (extension.ts:100-105) loops correctly over
trackedDispatches until empty. The logic is right. It just does not hold the
process in a headless `omp -p` run: the invocation record would exist if the
drain had actually awaited the run to settle, and it does not.

NOT YET DISTINGUISHED (do not guess, instrument it):
  (a) session_shutdown is never emitted in headless mode
  (b) it is emitted, but the host exits without awaiting the async handler
Both produce what was observed; they need different fixes. A single log line
inside the shutdown hook settles it.

CONSEQUENCES
- The constitution step -- the entire learning half of the product -- is
  silently skipped whenever the fix takes more than a short while. Which is
  most real fixes.
- The same applies to every guarantee the governed path enforces. A run that
  is killed mid-flight enforced nothing and recorded nothing.
- br-zcxb's "no RCA input" hypothesis is UNTESTED, not disproved: the
  experiment designed to test it could never reach the provider. That
  question reopens once runs complete.

RELATED
br-r3om already noted the dispatch is "un-awaited ... logs nothing until it
finishes". This is the consequence of that, measured.
br-zcxb added the records that made this visible (PR #101); without them the
run looked identical to "nothing matched".
close_reason: Fixed: workflow-dispatch now writes the DispatchRecord BEFORE entering the interpreter, carrying startedAt and an 'abandoned' marker that is cleared only when the run resolves. A run cut short by session end therefore leaves evidence it STARTED, instead of leaving nothing. renderStatusReport counts abandoned separately from failed (a failure is a result; abandonment is the absence of one) and states plainly that such results are missing, not negative. Also logs kind: invocation-started. 4 tests in pi-extension/tests/abandoned-run.test.ts driving a hanging AgentPort.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
ANSWERED. It is (b): the hook fires and the process is killed mid-drain.
Cause (a) -- "session_shutdown is never emitted in headless mode" -- is
ruled out.

MEASURED, live, with both drain edges plus a 2s heartbeat:

  18:43:18.598  invocation-started
  18:44:12.244  shutdown-hook-entered  pending=1
  18:44:14.244  shutdown-drain-tick    pending=1
                process exits (61s total, agent exit=0)

session_shutdown IS emitted. The handler runs, and correctly sees pending=1.
The drain then gets exactly ONE heartbeat -- about two seconds -- before the
process dies. Not a hang: the drain was still making its first pass.

THE HOST IS NOT THE PROBLEM, which kills the obvious fix. All three emission
sites await:
  agent-session-runtime.js:106  teardownCurrent -> await emitSessionShutdownEvent
  agent-session-runtime.js:297  dispose          -> await emitSessionShutdownEvent
  agent-session.js:2606         reload           -> await emitSessionShutdownEvent
and extensions/runner.js:716 emit() awaits every handler in series with NO
timeout. So there is no host-side await to add and no timeout to lengthen.
Something exits the process roughly two seconds after shutdown begins,
independent of the handler's promise.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX. Nothing that WAITS at shutdown can work. A governed
run averaging 45-90s cannot be squeezed into a ~2s window. Viable directions:

  1. Do not start what cannot finish. Run the governed dispatch at a point
     the host genuinely blocks on (a turn boundary), not as un-awaited work
     racing the session's end.
  2. Detached worker. extension.ts already carries the note "long-running
     autofix ultimately needs a detached worker" -- this is the evidence for
     it. Survives session exit by not living in the session.
  3. Persist and resume. Write the pending invocation to disk and complete it
     on next session start. Heaviest, but the only one that survives a crash
     or a kill as well as a clean exit.

(1) is smallest and would fix the common case. (2) is what the code already
predicted it would need.

WHY THIS SURVIVED 215 PASSING TESTS -- worth fixing alongside.
Every e2e test calls drainDispatches() MANUALLY:
  tests/behavior-window.e2e.test.ts:137
  tests/live-autofix.e2e.test.ts:114
  tests/continuation-verification.e2e.test.ts, tests/one-plus-one.e2e.test.ts
So the suite proves the drain works WHEN AWAITED, and says nothing about
whether anything awaits it in production. The governed path always completes
in tests and never completes in a real headless run. Any fix here needs a
test that does not hand-call the drain, or it will pass for the same wrong
reason.

Instrumentation committed: shutdown-hook-entered / shutdown-drain-complete,
on the branch for PR #101. The completion record is kept because its absence
is the signal. The heartbeat was removed once it had done its job.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
PARTIAL CORRECTION, and a successful drain observed.

On the integration branch (both PRs merged) a full live run COMPLETED the
governed path:

  18:47:40.323  invocation-started
  18:48:14.087  shutdown-hook-entered  pending=1
  18:48:15.820  invocation                     <- completed 1.7s into drain
  18:48:15.820  shutdown-drain-complete

So the drain is genuinely awaited and it works. The earlier claim that "the
process is killed roughly two seconds into the drain" is not supported: what
is actually established is that a governed run finishing within ~2s of
shutdown completes, and the longer runs did not.

ALSO CORRECTED: my reading of the exit path. print-mode.js (the `-p` mode)
does NOT call process.exit on the normal path. Its finally block is
  await disposeRuntime()  ->  await runtimeHost.dispose()
                          ->  await emitSessionShutdownEvent(reason "quit")
and emit() awaits every handler in series. process.exit appears only in the
SIGTERM/SIGHUP handlers (print-mode.js:38-40), which also call
killTrackedDetachedChildren() first. Searched for a shutdown grace cap
(gracePeriod / shutdownTimeout / a 2000 literal) in print-mode and
agent-session-runtime: none exists.

SO THE MECHANISM IS STILL OPEN. Everything visible says the handler should be
awaited to completion, and in a short run it is. Why a longer governed run
stops -- one heartbeat at +2.0s and then nothing -- is unexplained. Candidates
worth testing, none confirmed:
  - the fix-provider child (omp -p, 120s timeout) holding something that is
    torn down with the session, so the dispatch promise never settles and the
    drain's first allSettled never returns
  - signal delivery to the process group when the parent shell's foreground
    job ends, taking the SIGTERM path and its process.exit
  - the heartbeat interval itself being cleared with the session's timers

The practical guidance on this bead is unchanged and does not depend on which
it is: work that must survive the session should not be started un-awaited
inside it. But do not implement against "there is a 2s cap" -- that was my
inference, and this run contradicts it.

Reproduction for whoever picks this up: the short path (typo repair, governed
run ~35s, completes) vs the long path (add a second test file that fails to
LOAD so the fix turn takes longer; governed run does not complete). Both in
~/Development/Sunstone/loop-trial.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
MECHANISM FOUND. It is a bounded dispose deadline in the omp host, not
anything the extension can wait its way out of. My earlier "killed ~2s into
the drain" was right; the correction that retracted it was wrong, and the
successful run did not contradict it -- it CONFIRMED it (that drain finished
in 1.73s, inside the budget).

FORENSICS, long scenario, 500ms heartbeat inside the shutdown handler:

  0.5s tick  pending=1 handles=0 reqs=0
  1.0s tick  pending=1 handles=0 reqs=0
  1.5s tick  pending=1 handles=0 reqs=0
  2.0s process-exit code=0

No signal fired (SIGTERM/SIGHUP/SIGINT/SIGPIPE were all instrumented and
none arrived). A clean exit with code 0, at 2.0s, while an await was pending
and a live setInterval existed -- which cannot happen naturally.

I WAS READING THE WRONG PACKAGE. The source I analysed is
node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent, and its print-mode.js genuinely
has no process.exit on the normal path. But `omp` is
/Users/ldangelo/.bun/bin/omp -- a COMPILED BUN SINGLE-FILE EXECUTABLE. The
behaviour is compiled in, and that also explains handles=0/reqs=0: Bun stubs
process._getActiveHandles.

Strings from the actual binary:
  "Timed out draining post-prompt tasks during dispose"
  "Post-prompt tasks still draining at dispose deadline"
  "Timed out waiting for the active agent run to settle during dispose"
  "Active agent run still settling at dispose deadline"
  "Session dispose subsystem failed during parallel teardown"
  e.drainTimeoutMs ?? z6s          where   z6s = 5000

So dispose is BOUNDED and its subsystems tear down in parallel against a
shared deadline (5000ms default on the sibling path). Our session_shutdown
handler is one of those subsystems and gets whatever is left -- measured at
about 2s twice. When the governed run fit inside it (1.73s) it completed;
when it needed 30-60s the process exited 0 and abandoned the await.

WHAT THIS SETTLES
  - Not a missing host await. Not a missing hook. Not a hang.
  - Nothing the extension does at shutdown can fix it: the budget is a few
    seconds and a governed run is 30-90s. Raising drainTimeoutMs, even if it
    were reachable from here, would mean blocking every session exit on
    arbitrary background work -- which is exactly what the deadline is there
    to prevent. The host is right.
  - The three directions on this bead stand, and (1) and (2) are now clearly
    the only real options:
      1. run the governed dispatch where the host genuinely blocks (a turn
         boundary), so it never needs to survive shutdown
      2. detached worker -- which extension.ts already predicted it would
         need
      3. persist-and-resume remains the only one that also survives a crash

UNPINNED, and I am not going to guess it: the exact budget our handler gets.
5000ms is the constant on the "active agent run settles" path; ours empirically
gets ~2s, presumably the remainder after earlier teardown. Anyone implementing
should treat the budget as "a few seconds, not guaranteed", not as a number.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
TIGHTENING the previous comment: strike "presumably the remainder after
earlier teardown". That was a guess dressed as an explanation, and it does
not survive the evidence.

z6s = 5000 does NOT reconcile with the observed cutoff, and I should not have
let it sit next to it as though it did:
  - two long runs were cut at 2.0s -- the SAME value both times, not a
    varying remainder, which is what "whatever is left of a shared 5s budget"
    would predict
  - one short run completed at 1.73s and survived

So what is actually established is empirical and narrow:
  the handler gets about 2 seconds, consistently, and work exceeding it is
  abandoned with a clean exit(0)

What is NOT established: which constant governs it. z6s = 5000 is the default
on the "active agent run settles" path (e.drainTimeoutMs ?? z6s). It may be
unrelated to the session_shutdown emit path entirely. Candidates I did not
test: a deadline computed from an earlier point than shutdown entry, or a
different bound applying to extension handlers.

Chasing the exact constant means correlating minified identifiers across a
compiled Bun binary, and it would change nothing: all three fix directions
follow from "a couple of seconds, not guaranteed", and none needs the number.

Treat the budget as unknown-but-small. Do not code against 5000, and do not
code against 2000 either -- 2.0s is what was measured on this machine, on
this build, twice.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
EVIDENCE FOR, from run 10 (2026-09-29T09:41Z). I previously wrote this bead off as 'never the blocker' -- that was based on a run where the governed path died in 65ms for an unrelated reason (br-boam), so nothing ever reached a shutdown budget. Retracting that.

Run 10, with the br-dowt hold working:

  09:41:08.300  invocation-started  behavior=fix-failing-test
  09:41:08.324  continuation        issue='npm test'
  09:42:07.466  verification        passed, heldForApproval: ['1']
  09:42:09      approval            (operator ran /ensemble-approve 1)
  09:42:15.478  runtime.session.completed
  09:55:00.100  shutdown-hook-entered / process.exited / drain-complete
  (no 'invocation' record was ever written)

The continuation half completed: fix held, approved, applied -- src/math.js is 'a + b'. The GOVERNED invocation started and never finished. No invocation record, so no constitution step, and docs/standards/constitution.md is unchanged at 5 lines.

Compare run 9, same scenario without the hold: invocation completed 13s after session end and the constitution amendment was applied. Here 13 MINUTES passed with nothing, until the external timeout killed the process.

So the constitution step is not reliably surviving session end, and run 9 may simply have been lucky with timing.

Open question, NOT yet evidence: the hold now reverts the working tree mid-run (restoreWorkingTree) while the governed fix provider is still generating against that same tree. A candidate computed from content that no longer exists is exactly what the staleness check rejects. That interaction between br-dowt's hold and the governed path needs reproducing before anyone claims it -- the invocation record that would show it was never written, which is itself the problem this bead describes.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
RAISED TO P0 2026-09-29. Re-assessed after the user corrected my model of the Foreman/Ensemble relationship: Foreman launches and owns the session; Ensemble runs inside it as a child. That makes session lifetime THE integration seam, not an internal detail.

Why this is the worst failure shape at that seam: dispatch, invocation and constitution records are all written only after the run resolves. So when the session ends mid-run, Foreman sees a session that terminated cleanly with an empty outbox -- which is INDISTINGUISHABLE from 'the behavior correctly matched nothing and did nothing'. A silent false negative at the boundary between the two systems, in the direction that looks like success.

Anything Foreman concludes from a run that hit this -- success rates, whether a behavior is worth dispatching, whether a fix was attempted -- is drawn from data that is missing rather than negative.

Note the earlier control run logged dispatch + invocation + constitution {status: none} because it finished inside the session lifetime, i.e. the same code path succeeds or vanishes purely on duration. Fixing this likely means writing a record at invocation START (so an abandoned run is visible as abandoned), not only on resolution.

title: Workflow manifests silently accept unknown step fields
description:
FOUND 2026-09-29 while authoring the pre-pr-verification and workspace-integrity behaviors (br-zctt, br-c4ni).

WHAT HAPPENED. I wrote 'next: check-tests' on command steps in both manifests, believing it wired the flow. The manifests PARSED, VALIDATED and COMPILED with zero errors. There is no 'next' field anywhere in the workflow schema -- WorkflowStepBase has only id, kind, timeout and on_failure. The key was silently discarded.

WHY IT DID NOT BREAK. The interpreter advances by DECLARATION ORDER: a non-condition step falls through to the step declared after it (interpreter.ts, the order.indexOf(step.id) + 1 path), and only conditions redirect via then/otherwise. My declaration order happened to match my intended flow, so both behaviors worked. I found it only because a TypeScript test could not read '.next' off the union.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN MY TYPO. A behavior author has no way to discover that a field is ignored:
- the compiler reports nothing
- the behavior runs
- the flow may be correct by accident, as mine were twice

The failure mode is a manifest that looks explicitly wired and is actually relying on line order. Reordering steps for readability then silently rewires the workflow, with no diagnostic at any point. This is the same class of defect as the ingress catalog (br-jgxo/br-d7lm): something that reads as a contract and is not enforced.

PROPOSED FIX. Reject unknown fields on workflow steps at validation time, naming the offending key and the step. Cheap, mechanical, and it converts a silent misunderstanding into a load-time error.

WORTH CHECKING AT THE SAME TIME: whether unknown keys are also accepted at the manifest top level (trigger/policy/capabilities), where a discarded key could mean an ungranted capability reading as granted -- a materially worse outcome than a misrouted step.

WORKAROUND IN PLACE MEANWHILE: both shipped manifests now document that flow is declaration order, and pre-pr-verification-behavior.test.ts asserts the order explicitly (commands adjacent to their checks, terminal outcomes after the last condition) so a reorder fails the build.
close_reason:
FIXED. validateWorkflow now rejects any field a step kind does not declare, naming the key and listing the allowed fields. 'next: done' -- the key I wrote into two shipped manifests believing it wired the flow -- is now a validation error instead of a silent discard.

THE FIX IS AN ALLOW-LIST, AND THAT IS THE PART WORTH REVIEWING. TypeScript interfaces do not exist at run time and a manifest is parsed YAML, so the permitted fields are written out by hand in validator.ts, duplicating schema.ts. A table that falls behind the schema would reject VALID manifests -- a worse failure than the one being fixed. So tests/workflow-unknown-fields.test.ts parses schema.ts and asserts the two agree in BOTH directions, per kind: every declared field is allowed, and nothing is allowed that is not declared. Adding a step field without updating the validator now fails the build.

A CLAIM I MADE ABOUT THIS BEAD WAS WRONG, and I would rather correct it than leave it. I suggested the laxity might let an ungranted capability read as granted. It cannot. compiler.ts requires capabilities.tools and capabilities.mutation_classes to be arrays, so a misspelled capability key yields undefined and a hard validation error. Capability typos already fail closed. The damage is the one originally filed -- a manifest that looks explicitly wired while depending on declaration order -- and no more than that.

Scope: workflow steps only. Unknown keys at manifest top level are still accepted; the required-field checks make the dangerous cases fail closed, so it is a smaller problem and not folded in here.

536 agent-core tests pass, 15 new. No shipped manifest was rejected.

title: decide which root the constitution applier should write to
description: Open design question left by PR #103 (br-x36p).
close_reason: Decided: amend the existing constitution or fail closed (resolveConstitutionPath)

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
PR #103 threaded eventCwd into createConstitutionApplier(change, rootDir?) so the applier follows the repo the FAILING COMMAND ran in. That is right for the fix provider -- the patch belongs in the tree that broke. It is not obviously right for the constitution.

A constitution is a property of the PROJECT, not of whichever worktree happened to run the failing command. Writing an amendment into a throwaway worktree, a CI checkout, or a detached clone means the rule is learned and then discarded, which is the quiet failure mode: the system looks like it is governing itself while the governance evaporates.

Three candidate answers:
  1. failing command's cwd (what #103 does today)
  2. the canonical repo root -- git rev-parse --show-toplevel from the main checkout
  3. wherever the existing docs/standards/constitution.md already lives, refusing to create a second one

Option 3 is probably closest to correct: an amendment with nowhere to go should FAIL CLOSED and be reported, not silently create a new constitution in a temp directory.

Note the applier threading merged as UNTESTED plumbing -- dispatch-root.test.ts covers the fix provider and the verification suite, not the applier's root. Whatever we decide needs a test that writes from a worktree and asserts WHICH file changed.

Not urgent: the acceptance run works because the trial repo is both the failing cwd and the project root, so all three answers coincide. This only bites when they diverge.

## Test Task: TRD-015-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-015-test
PRD Reference: #req-003

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. title: REQ-018 guarantee changed: grants scope to a behavior's execution window, not the session

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
The implemented guarantee no longer matches what REQ-018/TRD-018 describe.

AS SPECIFIED (PRD-2026-0fc1c1d0 REQ-018): an ungranted tool call is denied at
the boundary, stated unconditionally.

AS IMPLEMENTED (ab46c82, 070274a): denial applies only while a behavior is
executing. Outside that window the user's own tools are untouched -- which is
the entire point, because the session-wide reading broke this repo (br-uavb):
one read-only behavior removed bash from the session and the agent could not
run the test suite at all.

Conditions now true and worth capturing as ACs when this is next planned:
  - grants do NOT narrow an idle session
  - a window closed by error or abort must not strand the user narrowed
  - a shell redirect through a GRANTED shell tool is invisible to a tool-name
    check and must be caught by the effect-based write boundary instead

I initially edited the TRD and PRD directly (d0a5ea3) and reverted it
(ad6c79e). That was a category error: a TRD is forward-looking work, not a
record of past fact. Its epic (br-r3m) is already closed 69/69, nothing
regenerates from it, nothing validates code against it, and ticking its
checkboxes puts status into a planning document whose tracker is beads. Both
docs are also versioned Draft v1.0.0 and the edit did not bump the version.

The guarantee is documented where it is actually read: the module comment in
packages/pi-extension/src/tool-grant-enforcement.ts, and the commit messages.
If REQ-018 should be restated for a FUTURE work item, that belongs in a new
PRD/TRD revision with a version bump, not an in-place edit of a consumed one.

STILL UNVERIFIED (do not mark done without a live repro):
AC 'shell redirect through a granted shell tool is caught by the write
boundary'. Two live attempts failed to exercise it -- the model declined the
bypass once, and printed the heredoc without executing it the second time. A
direct WriteBoundaryMonitor test against a redirect while a scope is open is
the way to settle it, not another prompt hoping the model cooperates.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
AC-018-5 RESOLVED AS: CONFIRMED STRUCTURAL GAP, not 'unverified'. Observed,
not inferred -- tests in packages/agent-core/tests/shell-redirect-boundary.test.ts.

My earlier framing was wrong. I said the effect-based write boundary was 'the
defense built precisely for this'. It is not, and the AC conflated two
different questions:

1. SHELL REDIRECT -> PROTECTED PATH. The boundary DOES catch this, now proven
   with a real shell, not a writeFileSync stand-in:
     - 'cat > tests/math.test.ts <<EOF' -> violation reason=test-file,
       restored=true, and the weakened assertion is gone from disk
     - 'rm tests/math.test.ts'          -> detected and the file restored
   classifyPath protects exactly four classes: constitution,
   conformance-fixture, guardrail-source, test-file.

2. SHELL REDIRECT -> ORDINARY SOURCE. ZERO protection, by construction.
   'cat > src/math.ts' produces NO violation and is NOT reverted (asserted in
   the third test so nobody 'fixes' the intended behaviour by accident).
   Ordinary source falls through classifyPath to { protected: false }.

CONSEQUENCE -- ensemble.bash IS EFFECTIVELY A WRITE GRANT.
investigate-test-failure's manifest reads as read-only:
    tools: [read, grep, glob, ensemble.bash]   # no edit, no write
but ensemble.bash can rewrite ANY unprotected file via redirect. The tool-name
grant check cannot see inside a shell command, and post-hoc path
classification was never designed to cover ordinary source. So the manifest
overstates the restriction: a behaviour that looks investigate-only can mutate
source.

The only thing that actually stood in the way during the live run was the
approval gate, and it held only because a non-interactive session had no
approver (exit 126, fails closed). That is a safe default, NOT a boundary --
an interactive user who approves once has granted arbitrary writes.

FIX DIRECTION (real change, not a test):
- ensemble.bash must consult the behaviour's mutation_classes before running,
  refusing when artifact.write is absent. Shell text cannot be soundly parsed,
  so this should be a capability decision made BEFORE execution, not an
  attempt to detect redirects in the command string.
- OR: run ensemble.bash under a read-only view of the workspace when the
  behaviour holds no write mutation class.
- Either way, mutation authority must stop being inferable only from tool
  NAMES, since one granted tool can subsume all the others.

Mutation-test any fix by giving a behaviour ensemble.bash WITHOUT
artifact.write and confirming a redirect to ordinary source is refused.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CORRECTION to a claim made while closing br-9hv6: I wrote that createMutationGuard "has only test call sites". False -- it is called from behavior-runner.ts:123 and behavior-loader.ts:48. I produced that claim by piping grep through `head` and reading the truncation as the result.

The accurate finding, which is what this bead should track:

Two dispatch paths exist and they diverge.
  governed      runBehavior -> AutofixLoop, guard = createMutationGuard(compiled),
                every write authorized against capabilities.mutation_classes,
                snapshotted, and validated by re-running execution.test_command
                over the whole suite before acceptance.
  continuation  pi.sendUserMessage injects a turn; the MODEL applies the change
                with its own edit calls. Snapshot, verification and rollback
                apply. MutationGuard does not, because no write passes through
                it. agent-fix-provider.ts:14 documents this explicitly.

Evidence from the successful in-repo repair (5f67ee0): the runtime log contains activation, continuation and verification records and NO dispatch or invocation record. So the governed path did not run, and execution.test_command was never invoked -- it satisfied the loader's static validation only.

So this bead is not "wire up an unreachable guard". It is "the path that actually fires bypasses the one that is governed". Whole-suite regression checking is equally absent on the firing path: only the narrow failing command is re-run.

Verified separately, so it is not a variable when this is fixed: `npx jest --listTests` from the repo root collects 170 suites (18 agent-core, 16 pi-extension), so test_command is a real full-suite command once something invokes it.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
PARTIAL FIX (this session, commit 50c3b9c / PR #85).

CLOSED by this change: 'Whole-suite regression checking is equally absent on the firing path' (my 18:20 UTC comment above). The continuation path's agent_end handler now re-runs every matched behavior's execution.test_command (whole suite) after the narrow command passes, and a regression there overrides an otherwise-passing narrow verdict -- matching the whole-suite guarantee AutofixLoop's governed path already had. Proven with a real e2e test (continuation-verification.e2e.test.ts): a fix that passes the narrow command but breaks an unrelated caller in the same file is rolled back; a genuinely good fix is not.

Prompted by a real incident: an uncommitted mutation to packages/agent-core/src/behavior/outbox.ts (if (this.entries.length > 0) return;) that made SOME check pass while silently breaking append() for other callers -- exactly the shape this fix now catches.

STILL OPEN, unchanged by this session:
- The governed-vs-continuation divergence itself: continuation still never calls MutationGuard.authorize() regardless of policy.mode. Closing that needs wiring continuation through the same guard/authorization chokepoint, a larger runtime change not attempted here.
- Shell-redirect-to-ordinary-source (my 14:34 UTC comment): WriteBoundaryMonitor only reverts protected paths (test/guardrail/fixture/constitution), not ordinary source like outbox.ts.

Also changed fix-failing-test's policy.mode: auto -> propose as a stopgap on the governed path specifically (does not touch the continuation gap above).

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: 2026-09-27 dev e2e, live confirmation: on one failure BOTH paths ran. The continuation path had the model edit scripts/lib/e2e-sum.js directly (no MutationGuard, no approval, hasApprovalHost:false). The governed path produced a proposal that was recorded as 'rejected ... runs in mode: propose'. So 'require human approval for fix-failing-test' (#85) does not hold on the path that actually changes files. In run 2 the only thing that stopped the edit was the user's omp advisor (from ~/.omp config), not the extension; an unattended run has no such check. Evidence: headless omp -p runs on dev (7b57d4a) in worktree /private/tmp/wt-e2e, planted bug scripts/lib/e2e-sum.js; logs in /tmp/e2e/ (e2e.jsonl, e2e2.jsonl, e2e3.jsonl, guard.jsonl, *-runtime-log.jsonl).

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: Related: br-xz6q -- policy.mode: propose was proven live (2026-09-28) not to gate mutations, same continuation-path root cause as this bead's grant-scoping issue. A fix that routes continuation writes through MutationGuard would likely close both.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CROSS-REFERENCE: br-zcxb / br-o355 / br-r3om / br-xz6q share one spine.

THE SPINE: a single test failure fires TWO dispatch paths.
  governed      createBehaviorInvoker (behavior-runner.ts:111), called live
                at extension.ts:996. Carries MutationGuard, mutation_classes,
                the constitution step, approval gating.
  continuation  the extension injects a turn and the MODEL edits files with
                its own tools. Carries snapshot/rollback, write-boundary,
                whole-suite verification, and (now) the propose hold.

Neither is dead -- br-r3om observed both firing on one failure, and the live
loop-trial run logged an `invocation` record (governed) alongside a
`continuation` record. The governed invoker reported "no fix candidate
offered": it ran, and the repair happened on the other path.

So the defect is not "governance is unreachable" -- I filed that on br-zcxb
and retracted it. It is that THE FIX DOES NOT TRAVEL THROUGH THE GOVERNED
PATH, so every guarantee implemented as an authorization check on a patch has
nothing to authorize.

WHAT EACH BEAD IS, UNDER THAT SPINE
  br-xz6q  CLOSED/in review, PR #98. policy.mode was checked only in
           MutationGuard.authorize(), which the continuation path never
           reaches. Fixed by enforcing mode at verification time instead.
           Precedent: the fix did NOT route writes through the guard.
  br-o355  grants scope to the execution window, not the session. Its own
           comment proposes routing continuation writes through MutationGuard
           and expects that to close br-xz6q too. br-xz6q is now closed
           WITHOUT that, so the shared estimate should shrink, not carry over.
  br-r3om  the fix-provider CHILD runs with --no-extensions, so nothing binds
           it -- it can write the live tree directly, regardless of which path
           governs the patch it returns. This is upstream of the other three:
           routing writes through the guard does not help if the writer is a
           process outside the guard entirely.
  br-zcxb  narrowest, and independent of the routing question: the
           constitution step records nothing when the provider returns no
           change, so "declined" and "never ran" are indistinguishable; and
           there is no RCA stage at all (BehaviorRunRecord, behavior-runner.ts
           :40-54, has no cause field).

SEQUENCING, so one defect is not scoped four times
  1. br-r3om first. It is P1, in review, and it is the only one where the
     enforcement boundary itself is bypassed rather than bypassed-around.
  2. br-zcxb's instrumentation half next. It is cheap, it does not depend on
     the routing decision, and until the constitution step is observable we
     cannot tell whether the back half of the loop works at all -- which
     makes any estimate for the rest guesswork.
  3. br-o355's routing decision last, informed by 1 and 2. If the continuation
     path keeps applying fixes model-side, MutationGuard may be the wrong
     chokepoint entirely and the effect-based write boundary the right one.
     br-xz6q is evidence for that reading.

RCA (the remaining half of br-zcxb) is orthogonal to all of this: no path
records a cause, so it is new work wherever the fix lands.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
LIVE OBSERVATION, 2026-09-28, in a real working session (not a fixture).

While running experiments for br-zcxb, my own assistant session had a tool
DENIED mid-task:

  tool "wait" is not granted to executing behavior(s)
  [investigate-test-failure, fix-failing-test]
  (granted tools: [bash, edit, ensemble.bash, glob, grep, read])

Two separate defects chained to produce it.

1. FALSE-POSITIVE DETECTION. The behavior activated on the output of a
   DIAGNOSTIC command I ran by hand:

     jq -r '.kind' .ensemble/runtime-log.jsonl | sort | uniq -c
     ... npm test 2>&1 | tail -2

   The output contained the text "1 failed, 1 passed, 2 total" because I was
   INSPECTING a test result, not producing one. Detection keys on output
   shape, so any command whose output quotes a test summary -- a grep, a jq
   over a log, a cat of a CI file -- is a failing test as far as the runtime
   is concerned. It then synthesised a fix instruction addressed to me,
   carrying explicit "NOT FROM THE USER" framing (which worked: I ignored
   it).

2. THE WINDOW NARROWED A SESSION THAT WAS NOT DOING BEHAVIOR WORK. The
   activation was spurious, but the grant scoping applied to my whole
   session regardless. I lost access to a tool that has nothing to do with
   the behavior, in the middle of unrelated work.

This is exactly the failure mode br-uavb recorded (a read-only behavior
removing bash and stranding the session), reached by a different route: not
a session-wide reading of grants, but a window that should never have opened.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THIS BEAD'S DESIGN. The AC "a window closed by error or
abort must not strand the user narrowed" assumes the window was legitimate
and just needs cleaning up. This shows a second requirement: a window opened
on a MISDETECTION narrows a user who never asked for a behavior to run at
all. Tightening window teardown does not help there -- the fix is to stop
opening the window, or to stop grants from subtracting tools the session
already had.

The narrowing is also SUBTRACTIVE in practice: granted tools were [bash,
edit, ensemble.bash, glob, grep, read] and my session's own tools outside
that list became unavailable. Worth settling explicitly whether a behavior
window should ever be able to REMOVE a capability the user's session
already had, as opposed to bounding what the BEHAVIOR itself may do.

Filed from the session it happened in; the runtime log is at
~/Development/Sunstone/loop-trial/.ensemble/runtime-log.jsonl.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: Item 1 of the live-observation comment above (detector fires on any test-summary-shaped output) has been SPLIT OUT to its own bead -- it is upstream of this one and needs a different fix (tighten the match condition, not window teardown). This bead keeps item 2: the window that should never have opened went on to narrow a real session's tools.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CORRECTION to my LIVE OBSERVATION comment above. Item 1 of it was wrong, and
br-aws4 (split out from it) is now closed as invalid.

I wrote that the behavior activated on the output of a DIAGNOSTIC command and
called it a false-positive detection. It was not. That command contained
`npm test`, run against a repo I had deliberately broken. Verified against
the real functions:

  the command in question   isTestCommand=TRUE
  pure jq/cat/grep cases    isTestCommand=false

So the window opened on a CORRECT detection of a genuinely failing test.

WHAT THAT CHANGES FOR THIS BEAD. My conclusion was: "a window opened on a
MISDETECTION narrows a user who never asked for a behavior to run at all --
tightening window teardown does not help there". Strike it. There was no
misdetection, so this bead does not need to defend against one.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is still worth settling here. The tool denial was real:

  tool "wait" is not granted to executing behavior(s)
  [investigate-test-failure, fix-failing-test]
  (granted tools: [bash, edit, ensemble.bash, glob, grep, read])

A legitimately-opened behavior window removed a tool my SESSION already had,
in the middle of unrelated work of my own. That is the subtractive-narrowing
question this bead already exists to answer, reached by an ordinary route
rather than an exotic one: run a failing test while doing something else, and
the window takes capabilities away from you.

So the open design question is unchanged and does not depend on my error:
should a behavior window ever REMOVE a capability the user's session already
had, as opposed to bounding what the BEHAVIOR itself may do? The live
evidence for it stands; only my explanation of how the window opened was
wrong.

title: Autofix rollback is silent: the user is told the fix passed, then it is reverted without notice
description:
Verification runs at agent_end, after the model's final answer. In run 3 the model told the user 'The test passes now ... 1 passed and 0 failed'; verification then rolled the fix back. extension.ts:362-375 only writes a runtime-log record; nothing is surfaced via ctx.ui.notify, a message, or stderr in any mode. Even with a correct test_command, any fix that fails whole-suite verification disappears after the user was told it succeeded. title: Continuation path detects a bad fix but does not roll it back
close_reason: Premise removed by br-behavior-runtime-cqrs-xl24: the continuation path was deleted outright (section 7 forbids both dispatch paths). There is no injected-turn fix to roll back. Propose mode cannot mutate at all now; apply is a separate approved command. Asserted by pi-extension/tests/one-dispatch-path.test.ts.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
The continuation path (br-9hv6) now re-runs the failing command itself and
logs kind=verification with status passed|failed|inconclusive, so acceptance
never rests on the model's prose claim.

GAP: on a 'failed' verdict it ONLY LOGS. The bad edit stays in the working
tree. The AutofixLoop proven earlier this session did better -- it snapshotted
before applying and reverted on failure, demonstrated in both directions:

    OUTCOME: {status: accepted,  attempt 1}              -> a - b became a + b
    OUTCOME: {status: rejected, reason: 'target test still fails',
              restored: [packages/agent-core/src/live-math.ts]}

So this path currently regresses against a capability that was already proven.
'Verified' here means 'checked', NOT 'undone' -- that distinction must not be
allowed to blur, because the whole point of the framework is that a claim of
success is not evidence of success.

REQUIRED
- Snapshot protected//source paths before injecting the continuation turn.
- On a failed verdict, restore them and log the restore, as AutofixLoop does.
- On an inconclusive verdict, do NOT restore and do NOT accept; surface it --
  an inconclusive run means we could not tell, and guessing either way is
  worse than reporting uncertainty.

ALSO UNPROVEN: the verifier has never been OBSERVED rejecting a bad fix. It is
written to be able to fail, but per constitution Rule 7 that does not count
until a mutation run shows it failing. Blocked behind br-hneq, because
detection currently misses failures whenever the model pipes test output.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-25 in the run that proved br-hneq's fix.

(1) VERIFIER CANNOT REACH THE SUITE. Verdict was:
    status=inconclusive, detail='re-run executed no tests (cwd unknown);
    totals="0 total"'
The fix was genuine (jest passes, re-run independently after session exit),
but the verifier re-runs from the repo root where jest matches zero tests.
The inconclusive guard did its job -- exit code 0 with zero tests was NOT
reported as passed -- but the verifier is useless until the failing tool
call's working directory is captured in the payload and used for the re-run.
REQUIRED: capture cwd at tool_call time; verify in that cwd; if cwd is
genuinely unknown, keep reporting inconclusive rather than guessing.

(2) CONTINUATION CAP IS BYPASSABLE. MAX_CONTINUATIONS_PER_ISSUE=1 is keyed on
the command string, and the model varied it between attempts:
    continuation | issue='npx jest live-e2e 2>&1 | tail -5'
    continuation | issue='npx jest live-e2e 2>&1 | sed -n 1,60p'
Same underlying failure, two different keys, cap bypassed. A model that keeps
rephrasing its command can queue turns indefinitely -- the loop guard is
weaker than claimed in the code comment.
REQUIRED: key on something stable (normalised command with pipeline/redirection
stripped, or the failing test id parsed from output), plus a session-wide
continuation budget as a backstop so no keying scheme can produce unbounded
turns. Mutation-test the budget by forcing repeated distinct keys.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CORRECTION (two items).

1. The OUTCOME line above is damaged. A backticked word in an earlier comment
   was executed by the shell instead of quoted, leaving:
       OUTCOME: {status: accepted,  attempt 1}
   The gap held the verdict field. Root cause was `git commit -m "..."` /
   comment text in DOUBLE quotes containing backticks, so the shell ran them.
   Same bug spliced jest output into commit f967bdc (fixed by amend, now
   6313e75). Fix: write message bodies with a QUOTED heredoc (<<'EOF') to a
   file and pass -F, never -m with backticks.

2. "ALSO UNPROVEN: the verifier has never been OBSERVED rejecting a bad fix"
   is now OUT OF DATE, but only partly resolved -- and the distinction matters.

   PROVEN: verifySuite returns failed, deterministically, against a real jest
   runner with a broken fixture (tests/verify-suite.test.ts, 4 tests: passed /
   failed / inconclusive / uses-recorded-cwd-not-fallback).

   STILL NOT PROVEN: rejection of a bad fix produced by a MODEL, end to end.
   The attempt failed for an interesting reason -- asked to write `a * b`
   deliberately, the model refused and fixed the bug correctly. A model cannot
   be relied on to be wrong on demand. This is the second time that has
   blocked a falsification run (see AC-018-5). Treat model-produced
   falsification as unavailable and inject faults directly.

   br-hneq is closed, so the detection blocker named above is gone.

The REQUIRED list still stands in full: a failed verdict still only logs, and
the bad edit still stays in the tree.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
RESOLVED (36b2e2d), with one caveat recorded below.

Rollback implemented and OBSERVED FIRING LIVE:
    verification | status=failed, detail="1 failed, 1 passed, 2 total",
                   rolledBack=true, rollbackDetail="restored"
The model's edit to live-math.ts was reverted and `git status` came back
clean -- checked with git, not with the extension's own report.

Snapshot is taken BEFORE the continuation turn is injected; taking it at
verification time would capture the damage instead of the state to restore.
Rollback fires only on a definite "failed"; "inconclusive" deliberately does
nothing, per the REQUIRED list above.

Safety property (rollback must not destroy the user's own work) is
mutation-tested: naive reset-to-HEAD, and deleting all untracked files rather
than only fix-created ones, are both caught.

FOUND WHILE PROVING THIS -- a false pass that would have defeated the whole
feature. The model ran `npx jest live-e2e 2>&1 | tail -60`. In a pipeline $?
is tail's status, not jest's, so a suite reporting "1 failed, 1 passed"
exited 0 and was graded "passed"; rollback never fired. Fixed: a reported
failure count now outweighs the exit code. This would have affected nearly
every real run, since piping test output is routine.

CAVEAT / STILL OPEN: rejection of a MODEL-PRODUCED bad fix remains
unobserved. The live "failed" verdict came from an independently failing
test, not from a wrong repair. Asked twice to write a deliberately bad fix,
the model refused and fixed the bug correctly instead. Model-produced
falsification is unavailable as a technique; faults are injected directly in
unit tests. Do not let "rollback proven" be read as "rollback proven against
a bad model fix" -- those are different claims.

title: A behavior invoked as a slash command bypasses the workflow interpreter entirely
description:
Found while reviewing open beads after br-behavior-runtime-cqrs-xl24.

behavior-loader.ts:87 registers a per-behavior slash command whose handler calls pi.sendUserMessage(artifacts.promptMarkdown, { deliverAs: 'followUp' }). So a behavior's prompt reaches the model by TWO routes:

  automatic: event -> trigger match -> workflow interpreter -> command registry -> MutationGuard
  manual:    /behavior-name -> prompt pasted into the conversation, no interpreter, no commands, no guard

The manual route is not a safety hole in the way the old continuation path was -- it is user-initiated, so attribution is unambiguous, and any tool use is then the user's own session subject to its normal rules. That is why br-x85k was closed rather than reassigned here.

It IS an inconsistency worth resolving: a behavior authored as a bounded workflow (steps, timeouts, conditions, approval gates, declared commands) degrades to unstructured prose when invoked by hand. The step budget, the condition branching and the approval steps all silently do not apply, and the person invoking it has no signal that the version they got is not the version that was tested.

OPTIONS: (a) run the interpreter for manual invocation too, so both routes are one path; (b) keep the manual route but make it explicit that it is a prompt preview, not an execution -- e.g. fold it into the existing --skill flag; (c) remove it.

Prefer (a) if the interpreter can be driven synchronously from a command handler, since section 7 of the CQRS requirements is precisely about not maintaining two ways to run a behavior.
close_reason: Delivered (operator approved the guardrail-source edit). /behavior-name now shows the behavior's trigger, mode and declared commands via ctx.ui.setStatus and triggers no turn; --skill still shows the full document. Supersedes AC-014-1 of TRD-014, which asserted the command delivered the compiled prompt via sendUserMessage -- that was the second, unguarded route to the model this bead objected to. behavior-loader.test.ts updated to assert the new contract, with the supersession recorded in the test itself.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
DESIGN DECIDED, EDIT BLOCKED ON OPERATOR APPROVAL 2026-09-29.

CHOSEN: option (b) -- the slash command DESCRIBES the behavior and does not run it.

Option (a), running the interpreter for manual invocation, was considered and rejected on a concrete ground rather than effort. These behaviors are event-triggered: their workflows reference ${event.payload...}, and a manual invocation has no triggering event, so the run would fail on reference resolution. 'Manually run an event-driven behavior' is not a well-defined request, and inventing an empty event to satisfy it would add a THIRD execution shape rather than remove the second one. Section 7 is about not maintaining several ways to run a behavior.

Option (c), removing the command, loses a genuinely useful affordance: seeing what a behavior is and whether it is armed.

THE EDIT, ready to apply: in behavior-loader.ts replace the pi.sendUserMessage(artifacts.promptMarkdown, { deliverAs: 'followUp' }) call with ctx.ui.setStatus showing the behavior's trigger, mode and declared commands, plus a pointer to --skill. Description becomes 'Describe behavior: X (does not run it)'.

WHY IT MATTERS, stated precisely so nobody overstates it: this was never a safety hole of the kind the old continuation path was. It is user-initiated, so attribution is unambiguous and any resulting tool use is the user's own session under normal rules. The defect is subtler -- a behavior authored as a bounded workflow (steps, timeouts, conditions, approval gates, declared commands) silently degraded to unstructured prose, and the invoker had no signal that what they got was not what was tested.

BLOCKED: packages/pi-extension/src/behavior-loader.ts is guardrail-source; the operator must run /ensemble-approve for the pending violation id. Each attempt mints a new id, so ask for the current one rather than reusing a stale number.

title: [trd:trd-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix:task:TRD-030-TEST] - [ ] **TRD-030-TEST** Timeout-budget tests (2h)
description:
## Test Task: TRD-030-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-030-test
PRD Reference: #nfr-4

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.

title: Fix-provider child agent runs ungoverned in the live repo (full write tools, --no-extensions)
description:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-25 on integrate/behavior-runtime-into-dev (/private/tmp/wt-integrate).

## What happened (from .ensemble/runtime-log.jsonl)
- 21:49:07Z `test.failure.observed` (npm test; pi-extension 13/17 suites failing because agent-core had no dist/). Both paths fired: continuation into the session AND an un-awaited governed dispatch (extension.ts:167-197), which logs nothing until it finishes.
- The dispatch ran `investigate-test-failure`, whose manifest grants [read, grep, glob, ensemble.bash] -- no edit -- and `policy.mode: propose`.
- 21:50:50Z `packages/pi-extension/package.json` gained `"pretest": "tsc -p ../agent-core"` on disk. No tool call in the session transcript, the advisor transcript, or runtime-log made that write.
- 21:52:20Z invocation record: `rejected: runs in mode: propose; direct write to packages/pi-extension/package.json is denied`, `restored: [packages/pi-extension/package.json]`. The rejected proposal's contents are byte-identical to the file now on disk. The change survived.

## Cause
agent-fix-provider.ts:172-182 spawns `omp -p --no-session --no-extensions --cwd=<rootDir>` in the LIVE repository. The child is a full agent with its own write tools. `--no-extensions` means none of the governance applies inside it: no tool-grant enforcement, no MutationGuard, no WriteBoundaryMonitor, no runtime log; `--no-session` means no transcript. The provider contract says the child returns a structured patch for AutofixLoop to authorize and apply -- nothing enforces that it does ONLY that.

[INFERENCE] that the child is the writer: not directly observed (by construction nothing records it). Supported by: guard denies under propose before applyWrite (autofix-loop.ts:110-132), so AutofixLoop never wrote; the write lands between dispatch start and the rejection; no other process had both the change and write access.

Consequences:
- A behavior whose manifest reads as read-only can mutate source through its fix provider. Manifest grants do not bind the provider.
- `policy.mode: propose` is enforced on the patch but not on the process producing it.

## Acceptance
- The fix-provider child cannot modify the live working tree: a child that tries to write a file directly leaves the repository unchanged (proven by a test whose fake child writes to disk).
- The candidate the child returns is still applied (or denied) only through AutofixLoop/MutationGuard.
- Mutation-test: remove the isolation -> the direct-write test fails.

BEFORE: the write SUCCEEDED, CANARY-ABS.txt landed in the operator's repo containing ESCAPED; detection caught it and correctly declined to revert, so the escape persisted. AFTER: the child itself reports 'Operation not permitted (os error 1)', nothing reaches the repository, no drift.
- 'The candidate is still applied only through AutofixLoop/MutationGuard.' Unchanged; confinement sits below that and does not alter the authorization path.
- 'Mutation-test: remove the isolation, the direct-write test fails.' MET -- tests/write-sandbox.test.ts includes an explicit mutation case where the same script run WITHOUT the wrapper does write outside the workspace.
- The earlier DEVIATION (a fake child cannot test omp's enforcement) is moot: the proof is the live probe, which the operator accepted.

WHAT WAS BUILT. pi-extension/src/write-sandbox.ts confines writes via sandbox-exec (Seatbelt) to the worktree, the throwaway HOME and temp. Reads are deliberately NOT confined; writes were the incident and claiming untested confidentiality would be the overreach REQ-SAFE-004 forbids. Fails closed -- a host that cannot confine refuses to spawn, mirroring the existing isolation refusal -- with allowUnconfinedWrites as a reported, logged escape hatch. Scoped to the real spawn path, because an injected run() replaces process execution entirely and demanding a sandbox there would refuse every fake-run test on Linux CI.

LIVE EVIDENCE 2026-09-28, in the maintainer's own session.

Two fix-agent children were caught RUNNING, mid-edit, in a git worktree:

  omp -p --no-session --no-extensions \
      --cwd=/Users/ldangelo/Development/Sunstone/ensemble \
      "A test in this repository is failing. Repair the SOURCE so it passes.
       Failing test: bash > cd /tmp/wt-guard/packages/pi-extension && npx jest ..."

Runtime log for the day: 24 invocations of fix-failing-test, 12 dispatches,
8 boundary errors. The triggering commands were DELIBERATE mutation tests
and debugging runs (br-x13x), so every one of these children was dispatched
against a failure that was never a defect.

THREE THINGS THIS SHOWS

1. --no-extensions means the child runs with NO write boundary. The parent
   is guarded; the thing it spawns is not. Protection that stops at the
   process boundary is not protection.

2. --cwd was the main repository, but the instruction embedded /tmp/wt-guard
   paths, so the children navigated OUT of their working directory and
   edited a different checkout entirely. The cwd argument is not a
   containment boundary and was never enforced as one.

3. What they edited was build configuration (see the new bead), which is not
   a protected path, so nothing objected.

They were killed by hand after being found by `ps`. Nothing in the system
reported their existence, and a `git status` that happened to run at the
wrong moment would have shown a clean tree.

comments.text:
CROSS-REFERENCE: br-zcxb / br-o355 / br-r3om / br-xz6q share one spine.

THE SPINE: a single test failure fires TWO dispatch paths.
  governed      createBehaviorInvoker (behavior-runner.ts:111), called live
                at extension.ts:996. Carries MutationGuard, mutation_classes,
                the constitution step, approval gating.
  continuation  the extension injects a turn and the MODEL edits files with
                its own tools. Carries snapshot/rollback, write-boundary,
                whole-suite verification, and (now) the propose hold.

Neither is dead -- br-r3om observed both firing on one failure, and the live
loop-trial run logged an `invocation` record (governed) alongside a
`continuation` record. The governed invoker reported "no fix candidate
offered": it ran, and the repair happened on the other path.

So the defect is not "governance is unreachable" -- I filed that on br-zcxb
and retracted it. It is that THE FIX DOES NOT TRAVEL THROUGH THE GOVERNED
PATH, so every guarantee implemented as an authorization check on a patch has
nothing to authorize.

WHAT EACH BEAD IS, UNDER THAT SPINE
  br-xz6q  CLOSED/in review, PR #98. policy.mode was checked only in
           MutationGuard.authorize(), which the continuation path never
           reaches. Fixed by enforcing mode at verification time instead.
           Precedent: the fix did NOT route writes through the guard.
  br-o355  grants scope to the execution window, not the session. Its own
           comment proposes routing continuation writes through MutationGuard
           and expects that to close br-xz6q too. br-xz6q is now closed
           WITHOUT that, so the shared estimate should shrink, not carry over.
  br-r3om  the fix-provider CHILD runs with --no-extensions, so nothing binds
           it -- it can write the live tree directly, regardless of which path
           governs the patch it returns. This is upstream of the other three:
           routing writes through the guard does not help if the writer is a
           process outside the guard entirely.
  br-zcxb  narrowest, and independent of the routing question: the
           constitution step records nothing when the provider returns no
           change, so "declined" and "never ran" are indistinguishable; and
           there is no RCA stage at all (BehaviorRunRecord, behavior-runner.ts
           :40-54, has no cause field).

SEQUENCING, so one defect is not scoped four times
  1. br-r3om first. It is P1, in review, and it is the only one where the
     enforcement boundary itself is bypassed rather than bypassed-around.
  2. br-zcxb's instrumentation half next. It is cheap, it does not depend on
     the routing decision, and until the constitution step is observable we
     cannot tell whether the back half of the loop works at all -- which
     makes any estimate for the rest guesswork.
  3. br-o355's routing decision last, informed by 1 and 2. If the continuation
     path keeps applying fixes model-side, MutationGuard may be the wrong
     chokepoint entirely and the effect-based write boundary the right one.
     br-xz6q is evidence for that reading.

RCA (the remaining half of br-zcxb) is orthogonal to all of this: no path
records a cause, so it is new work wherever the fix lands.
