ASSESSED AGAINST THIS BRANCH 2026-09-29 (feature/trd-2026-0fc1c1d0-behavior-runtime-pi-harness), reached via br-zcxb which this bead blocks. NOT closing -- it is IN_REVIEW and yours.

WHAT THE CQRS PORT CHANGED. The incident here was a child running in the LIVE repo with full write tools while both dispatch paths fired. On this branch:
- The continuation path is deleted outright, so only one dispatch path exists.
- agent-port.ts runs the child with an isolated git worktree as cwd and a throwaway HOME/XDG/OMP config root, both OS-enforced.
- If isolation is unavailable it REFUSES to invoke: 'An uncontained child is not a supported degraded mode.' That is the specific condition this bead recorded.
- --tools is retained but explicitly NOT credited as containment; it was measured not to restrict _write/_learn/_manage_skill (br-33co).

THE RESIDUAL THIS BEAD NAMES IS REAL AND ACKNOWLEDGED IN THE SOURCE. The OS boundaries stop a child writing RELATIVE paths. They cannot stop one writing an ABSOLUTE path back into the live repository -- which is exactly the shape of the observed package.json write with no tool call in any transcript. Detection via tree baseline is the only control covering that case, and the reply is discarded (never reverted) when drift is seen.

DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED WHILE ASSESSING THIS. Drift detection failed OPEN. 'const drift = baseline ? treeChangesSinceBaseline(baseline) : undefined' and the checks after it refused only when drift.length > 0; when the baseline could not be captured, or the comparison itself returned undefined, execution fell through to 'return { ok: true, reply }'. That is 'I could not check whether the child wrote to your tree, therefore trust the reply' -- the br-dowt pattern, inside the containment path, reachable mainly when the port ran UNISOLATED, i.e. precisely when detection was the only control left. Now refuses with a reason naming the consequence. 5 tests in pi-extension/tests/drift-fails-closed.test.ts.

REMAINING FOR THIS BEAD, if anything: whether absolute-path writes should be prevented rather than detected. That needs an OS-level facility the runtime does not currently use, and REQ-SAFE-004 forbids describing detection as isolation, so it should stay described as it is until that exists.

# br-rmw Multi-Skill Collision Ordering Audit — ensemble-as-behaviors

Run 2026-09-23. Script: `scripts/collision-order-audit.js` (reproducible:
`node scripts/collision-order-audit.js`; exits non-zero on any nondeterminism, sort
violation, or unexpected hit set).

## Contract under audit

`matchPhrases` output must be: deduped by `skill|phrase`, sorted by skill name, then
phrase-alphabetical within a skill (longest-phrase-first is NOT the contract —
`localeCompare` on phrase is). `buildPhraseBlock` renders in that array order.

## Method

- 8 hand-built compound probes (multi-skill prompts: PRD+git-town, TRD+pull-request,
  three merging-a-pr phrases in one prompt, etc.)
- 30 exhaustive pair probes: first phrase of every skill pair, both orderings.
- Each probe run 5x through the REAL hook (`execFileSync` + stdin JSON); outputs
  compared for byte-identity AND against the independently-computed expected hit set
  (substring test against the full registry).

## Results

- **Determinism: 38/38 probes × 5 runs byte-identical.** No ordering jitter.
- **Sort contract: PASS on every probe** — skill-major, phrase-alpha within skill, e.g.
  `creating-a-prd/create a prd` → `git-town/create a feature branch` →
  `git-town/create a pr`.
- **3/8 compound probes surface multi-skill collisions** (`create a prd` ∋
  `create a pr`, `create a trd` ∋ …): identical root cause as the `br-ivv` finding —
  git-town's `create a pr` phrase is a strict prefix of `create a prd`/`create a trd`.
  Ordering itself stays deterministic; the collision is a registry-content issue, not a
  comparator bug. Fix belongs with br-ivv's recommendation (word-boundary or drop).
- All 30 pair probes: skill order strictly alphabetical regardless of phrase order in
  the prompt.

## Verdict

Ordering is correct and deterministic; the audit script is a permanent regression guard
(exit≠0 on drift). Recorded: collisions observed == predicted from the prefix overlap;
no additional ambiguous pairs beyond `br-ivv`'s table.

title: Write-boundary guard cannot distinguish reverting an unapproved change from making one
description:
SYMPTOM. An unapproved edit to a protected path can reach git (e.g. swept in by 'git add -A'), and once there NO agent can remove it: the corrective 'git checkout <good-sha> -- <file>' is itself a write to a protected path, so the write-boundary monitor reverts the revert and mints a fresh approval id. The repository is left broken with no agent-reachable fix. Observed on branch feature/trd-2026-0fc1c1d0-behavior-runtime-pi-harness at d9c9fd3, which broke all 18 agent-core suites (TS2367) and could only be repaired by a human running git outside the guarded flow.

CONTRIBUTING DEFECT, probably the more important half. The state that caused it was produced by a PARTIAL revert. An attempted edit added four things to protected-paths.ts/mutation-guard.ts: DECISION_MEMORY_PATTERNS, a 'decision-memory' entry in the classifyPath checks array, 'decision-memory' in the ProtectedPathReason union, and SANCTIONED_DECISION_CLASS. The guard reverted ONLY the union member and left the other three live in the working tree. That is not a no-op: it is a state neither approved nor rejected, and it does not compile, because the three survivors reference the member that was removed. A revert that half-lands is worse than one that fails loudly.

WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED. The surviving wiring sat uncommitted in the working tree. Full-suite runs were green (563, then 566) because the partial state only broke compilation once its consumers were exercised together; git status showed the files modified but an agent reading a greppable term that HAD been reverted concluded the whole change had been. Confirming the hoped-for term rather than every symbol is the reading error, but the guard made it easy.

SUGGESTED DIRECTIONS.
1. Revert atomically. Either all hunks of a protected-path change are undone or none are, and a partial outcome is reported as a failure rather than silently left behind.
2. Recognise restoration. A write that makes a protected file byte-identical to a committed blob reachable from HEAD is a REVERT, not a new change, and should be permitted without an approval id. This closes the trap in the SYMPTOM section without weakening the guard, since it can only ever move a file toward an already-approved state.
3. Refuse to leave non-compiling state. If a revert cannot be completed, say so loudly rather than half-applying.

RELATED. br-d7lm carries an earlier incident where the mechanism reported 'reverted' when the file had not reverted, in both directions, ids climbing 29->31. This is the third reliability incident in one session, so the pattern is not a one-off.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
FINDING, 2026-09-29 (late session; recovered verbatim from the transcript). The guard fires at agent TOOL-CALL BOUNDARIES, not only on attempted writes. Its revert pass runs on every tool_result (packages/pi-extension/src/extension.ts:214-244, monitor.check()), so read-only calls trip it too: reads via bash and an unrelated learn() call each minted a new approval pair. Result: a human fix applied WHILE an agent session is active is undone by that agent's next tool call. Confirmed by elimination: four consecutive agent-initiated reverts (four approval-id pairs in four calls), then the human's manual 'git checkout dcd742c -- protected-paths.ts mutation-guard.ts' stuck on the first try once the agent went idle.

WHY THIS RAISES SEVERITY. The SYMPTOM above says 'no agent can fix a bad protected commit'. The sharper statement: AN ACTIVE AGENT SESSION PREVENTS ANYONE FROM FIXING IT, the human included. The correct recovery is 'stop every agent session against this checkout, then repair from a plain shell'. The guard's own error text ('Fix the source under test instead', '/ensemble-approve N') points the other way, and the approval ids are not stable identifiers: every tool call re-scans and mints a fresh pair (ids 29->39 in one session), so any id quoted to the user is already stale.

Related: br-vjm5 / br-akxg (closed) already established that check() runs on every tool result against a baseline captured once at activation. Their re-baseline fix (syncExternalHistory, PR #95) does not appear on this branch: grep of packages/agent-core/src/behavior finds no syncExternalHistory. [INFERENCE, not tested] Even with it, the re-baseline requires no locally-authored reflog move, and this session had made local commits, so it would likely still have reverted the human's fix.

CORRECTION TO THE HANDOFF, git-verified. The unapproved wiring was NOT removed by a human commit. It was removed in f2198b1, whose message is 'chore(beads): file br-suoh ...' (git log -S SANCTIONED_DECISION_CLASS / -S decision-memory: added in d9c9fd3, removed in f2198b1). That commit touched .beads/issues.jsonl plus both protected files. [INFERENCE] The agent's earlier 'git checkout dcd742c -- <files>' writes both index and working tree; the monitor restores only the working tree (writeFileSync, workspace-snapshot.ts:116), so the good content stayed staged and a later beads-only commit swept it in. So there are two commits with misleading messages, d9c9fd3 (adds the wiring) and f2198b1 (removes it), and together they net to zero. It also exposes a second gap: the guard does not look at the index, so a reverted working tree can hide a staged protected-path change.

SUGGESTED DIRECTION 4: when a violation is found, say which actor's call triggered the check, and state plainly that fixing requires no active agent session. Do not print an approve id that the next call will invalidate.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
START HERE (handoff 2026-09-29). Base: dev at 1c6dfab. That includes #107, so it has dev's guard fixes merged into the CQRS runtime: 076fd23 syncExternalHistory (write-boundary-monitor.ts:247, called at :350 and :402), 6407c75, a72e088, and 7663810 (setScope :213).

STEP 1: REPRODUCE ON dev BEFORE DESIGNING. Part of this bead may already be fixed by 076fd23, which re-baselines when the reflog shows no locally-authored move AND the file matches HEAD. Build a test in a temp repo using the real WriteBoundaryMonitor (see write-boundary-external-history.test.ts for the harness):
 (a) A protected file is committed in a broken state. A restore to an older committed blob ('git checkout <good> -- f') happens inside a monitored call. Is it reverted?
 (b) The same restore made by a human between agent tool calls, followed by an unrelated read-only tool_result. Is it undone?
 (c) A partial revert: 1 of 4 related hunks restored, leaving the file uncompilable.
 (d) The index: the working tree is restored but the good blob stays STAGED (the f2198b1 mechanism).
Record which of these fail on dev. Only those are in scope.

STEP 2, FIX (from SUGGESTED DIRECTIONS above):
 - A write that makes a protected file byte-identical to a blob reachable from HEAD is a REVERT. Allow it with no approval id.
 - Revert atomically: all or nothing, and a partial outcome is reported as a failure.
 - Consider the index, not only the working tree.
 - The violation message names the triggering call and says a repair needs no active agent session. It prints no approval id the next call will invalidate.

CONSTRAINTS:
 - write-boundary-monitor.ts and protected-paths.ts are guardrail-source. Edit them in ONE approval, in a fresh session, with no other agent session on this checkout. Otherwise this bead reproduces itself.
 - Every fix needs a mutation check.

title: fix.verify cannot verify anything: the isolated worktree has no dependencies
description:
VERIFIED EMPIRICALLY 2026-09-29, not inferred.

  git worktree add --detach /tmp/wt HEAD
  [ -d /tmp/wt/node_modules ] -> ABSENT
  cd /tmp/wt && npm test -> 'npm error command failed / sh -c jest --passWithNoTests'

createIsolatedWorkspace() makes a git worktree at HEAD. A worktree is a checkout of a commit, so gitignored content -- node_modules above all -- is not present. fix.verify runs the behavior's test_command with cwd = workspace.root, so in any real repository that command cannot find its runner.

IT FAILS SAFE, which is why nobody noticed. verifyOutput returns 'inconclusive' ('no supported test framework recognised the output ... a result that cannot be attributed is not a pass'), never 'passed'. So there is no false-verification risk. The defect is that fix.verify is INERT: it can never reach 'passed', so fix.apply can never be reached through the governed route, so the whole propose -> verify -> approve -> apply chain terminates at step two in practice.

Every existing test passes because the suites inject a fake runCommand. The gap is invisible to the test suite by construction.

THIS SUPERSEDES br-bxm7, which described the OPPOSITE failure in the old createFixSandbox: it symlinked node_modules into the sandbox, so a child writing through that path reached the live tree. That function no longer exists. The trade-off it named is the real problem and it has three corners:
  symlink  -> fast, but writes reach the live tree (the old bug)
  copy     -> safe, but slow enough to make verification unusable
  nothing  -> safe, and verification cannot run (the current bug)

LIKELY ANSWER: copy-on-write clone, which is neither slow nor shared. macOS/APFS 'cp -c' (clonefile) and Linux 'cp --reflink=auto' (btrfs/xfs) are near-instant and writes do NOT propagate to the source. Needs a fallback path where CoW is unavailable -- and the fallback must be 'refuse and say so', not 'symlink anyway', or br-bxm7 returns.

DO NOT fix by running verification in the live tree. That reintroduces the defect the isolated workspace exists to prevent: the thing that verifies a fix must not be the thing that applies it.

TESTS: a verification run in a repo with dependencies reaches a real verdict; a write inside the workspace does not alter the source tree's node_modules; where CoW is unavailable the command refuses rather than degrading to a shared path.
close_reason:
Fixed: createIsolatedWorkspace now provisions dependency directories into the worktree with a copy-on-write clone (cp -c on APFS, cp --reflink=always on btrfs/xfs), then refuses the whole isolation if the clone fails rather than degrading.

VERIFIED ON THE REAL REPO, not only in fixtures: the workspace is created in ~4.7s with node_modules present, and 'npx jest tests/field-schema.test.ts' inside it reports 28 passed. Before this the same command could not find jest at all.

ISOLATION HELD under probe: a new file written into the workspace's node_modules does not appear in the source; appending to a shared dependency file leaves the source byte-identical (so it is copy-on-write, not hardlinks, which would share an inode); dispose removes the workspace and leaves the source dependencies intact.

REFUSES RATHER THAN DEGRADES where CoW is unavailable. --reflink=always is used deliberately in preference to =auto: auto silently falls back to a full copy, which is the slow path in disguise. The refusal names the filesystems that support it. A symlink fallback was rejected outright -- that is br-bxm7, and it must not return.

8 tests in agent-core/tests/workspace-dependencies.test.ts using the real filesystem, because the gap was invisible to every existing test: they all inject a fake runCommand.

title: Long-lived review session with auto-port, QuickTunnel, 6h TTL, username gate, presence
description:
## Goal

Add a `--long-lived` mode to the refinement-review server that:
- Picks a port automatically (OS-assigned).
- Implicitly tunnels via Cloudflare QuickTunnel to expose the public URL.
- Self-terminates after a TTL (default 6h) or on completion, whichever first.
- Requires a username before serving the document.
- Shows a live presence list of who is currently viewing.

## Invocation

```
/ensemble:refine-prd --collab --long-lived docs/PRD/PRD-2026-019.md
/ensemble:refine-trd --collab --long-lived docs/TRD/TRD-2026-019-*.md
```

## Behavior

- Server picks port (OS-assigned, ephemeral within the process lifetime).
- QuickTunnel auto-tunnels to a public URL on `*.trycloudflare.com`; same flow as today's `--tunnel=quick` but implicit in `--long-lived`.
- Bootstrap prints `Invite URL: https://<random>.trycloudflare.com/api/exchange?invite=<token>` once. Operator shares via Slack/Teams manually.
- TTL timer: server self-terminates after `--ttl` (default 6h) or on Complete, whichever first. Cleanup tears down QuickTunnel and closes the listener.
- Exchange page: GET /api/exchange?invite=<id> validates the invite against an in-memory multi-use map (no burn), returns a username form with `invite` as a hidden field. POST /api/identify { name, invite } re-validates the invite (same map, no burn), validates `name` (non-empty, length-bounded), mints a `review-sid` cookie bound to `displayName`, redirects to document. POST with missing/invalid invite returns 401 and mints no cookie.
- Presence: in-memory `Map<sid, { name, connectedAt, count }>`; a single sid may own multiple concurrent EventSource connections (multiple tabs per reviewer). Increment on connect, decrement on close; delete the entry and broadcast `event: viewers` only when the count reaches 0. Broadcast fires only on 0↔1 transitions (no event churn on intra-sid tab churn). UI renders "Currently viewing" row deduped by sid. No persistence to `session.json`. Existing server-side keepalive comments (`: heartbeat\n\n`, 25s) remain for proxy survival and are ignored by EventSource for presence purposes.

## Acceptance

1. `--long-lived` (no `--ttl`) → server exits at 6h.
2. `--long-lived --ttl=24h` → server exits at 24h.
3. `--long-lived --ttl=7d` → server exits at 7d.
4. `--long-lived --ttl=1h` → bootstrap aborts with `--ttl must be at least 6h`.
5. Username gate: GET /api/exchange?invite=<valid> returns the form (200, HTML); POST /api/identify { name, invite } with valid invite mints the cookie and redirects to the document; the document is only served after identification (no sid cookie → 401).
6. Presence: two browsers with different names see each other on the "viewers" row within 2s.
7. Presence cleanup: when the LAST SSE request for a given sid closes (count → 0), that viewer is removed from the presence map and the updated list is broadcast synchronously. Closing any non-final tab (count > 0) does NOT remove the viewer. Unit-tested by explicitly closing the request/socket (no browser).
8. Presence is in-memory: server crash → no stale entries anywhere; restart is uneventful.
9. Mode exclusivity: `--long-lived` and `--reviewers N` mutually exclusive (clean error). `--long-lived` and `--tunnel=quick` are compatible (QuickTunnel is implicit in `--long-lived`).
10. Multi-tab: a sid with two concurrent SSE connections; closing one does NOT remove the viewer from the broadcast; closing the second does.
11. Invite enforcement: POST /api/identify with missing invite → 401, no cookie minted, no redirect. POST /api/identify with invalid invite → 401, no cookie minted, no redirect. The same valid invite may be used by multiple reviewers (multi-use; no burn on POST success).

## Defaults

- `--ttl`: optional positive duration; 6h default. Format follows existing project duration parser. Must be >= 6h (extension-only).
- QuickTunnel: implicit when `--long-lived`; no separate flag.
- Username: free-text, no uniqueness check, no auth.
- Presence: `Map<sid, { name, connectedAt, count }>` refcounted by sid; multi-tab reviewers stay visible until their last tab closes. Broadcast only on 0↔1 transitions (synchronous removal + `event: viewers` broadcast on count→0).
- Cookie schema gains `displayName`; no other auth changes.

## Out of scope

- Manual invite revocation API.
- Manual token rotation.
- Auto-share webhook integration (Slack/Teams incoming webhook).
- Presence persistence across restart.
- Named tunnel / external stable origin support (in-process QuickTunnel only).
- TTL cap/warning policy.

## Sibling

- br-68h: multi-reviewer share-URL fan-out via transient nonces (same-day).
- This bead: long-lived review session via QuickTunnel + in-memory invite + 6h TTL (across days within a single process lifetime).

title: Ensemble's own grants lock the session out of running tests in this repo
close_reason: Repo now ships a behavior with bash+edit grants; verified live in 5f67ee0

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-25 in a clean worktree of this repo at af6c05a.

Setup: a genuinely failing test (packages/agent-core/src/selftest-math.ts,
multiply returns a+b; tests/selftest-math.test.ts expects 6, gets 5).
Prompt asked the agent to run it and report pass/fail.

RESULT: the test was never run, no test.failure.observed, no dispatch, no
continuation, source untouched. Agent's own explanation:

  'I couldn't run the test... The active investigate-test-failure behavior
   only allows ensemble.bash, glob, grep and read. It rejected a direct bash
   call. It also rejected the write call, which is the only way to reach
   ensemble.bash.'

CAUSE: this repo ships exactly one behavior (investigate-test-failure), whose
grants are [read, grep, glob, ensemble.bash]. Grants are unioned across active
behaviors, so with a single narrow behavior the union is narrow: native bash
is removed from the session. ensemble.bash was also unusable in this run.

Net effect: ENSEMBLE'S OWN ENFORCEMENT PREVENTS ENSEMBLE FROM WORKING IN
ENSEMBLE'S REPO. Autofix cannot detect a failure it is not permitted to
produce.

WHY THIS WAS NOT CAUGHT EARLIER: every successful end-to-end run used the
/tmp/ens-e2e fixture, which ALSO defines fix-failing-test with grants
[read, grep, glob, bash, edit]. That second behavior widened the union enough
to run tests. The fixture was therefore not representative of the repo it
claims to validate -- a self-test that passes only because of a file the real
repo does not have.

QUESTIONS TO SETTLE (design, not just a patch)
- Should a behavior's grants restrict the WHOLE SESSION, or only the tools
  available to that behavior's own invocation? Restricting the session means
  installing one narrow behavior silently disables the user's shell.
- Should a session with no matching behavior be ungranted (full tools) rather
  than intersected down?
- Why was ensemble.bash unreachable when it WAS granted? The agent reports the
  write call needed to reach it was rejected; that path needs its own repro.

ACCEPTANCE
- [ ] A failing test in a clean worktree of THIS repo is detected, dispatched
      and fixed, using only behaviors this repo actually ships.
- [ ] Installing a single read-only behavior does not remove the user's bash.
- [ ] Mutation: removing the fix makes the repro fail again.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
FIXED (grants no longer restrict the idle session) AND A NEW HOLE FOUND.

WORKS: a failing test in a clean worktree of THIS repo is now detected,
dispatched and fixed, using only the behavior this repo ships.
  activation | loaded=['investigate-test-failure']
  DETECTED   | detectedBy=exit-status
  continuation | issue='npx jest selftest-math', behaviors=['investigate-test-failure']
  selftest-math.ts: 'a + b' -> 'a * b'; jest re-run independently: 1 passed.
Previously the session could not run tests at all.

Unit-level scoping is mutation-tested (3 mutants, each caught by exactly the
test that should catch it): session-wide union, scope-never-narrows, and
endBehaviorScope-does-nothing.

NEW HOLE -- SCOPING IS NOT IN FORCE DURING THE CONTINUATION TURN.
The fix turn called , which investigate-test-failure does NOT grant
(read/grep/glob/ensemble.bash), and stderr contains ZERO 'not granted' blocks.
Tool calls observed in the continuation: grep, grep, edit, edit, bash.

SUSPECTED CAUSE (NOT yet reproduced, do not treat as established): turn_end
fires per ASSISTANT turn, not per user message, so endBehaviorScope() runs at
the end of the continuation's first tool batch and closes the window before
the edit happens. The unit tests did not catch this because they call
beginBehaviorScope() and fire tool calls directly, never crossing a real turn
boundary -- the same defect class as a fixture that is not representative of
the case that occurs.

NEXT
- [ ] Reproduce turn_end/agent_end firing order across an injected turn with a
      standalone probe, as was done for the handler deadlines. Do not infer it.
- [ ] Close the scope on the correct boundary (likely agent_end for the
      injected run), and keep it fail-safe on error.
- [ ] Add a test that crosses a REAL turn boundary, not a direct handler call;
      the current unit tests pass while the property is violated in practice.
- [ ] Re-run this repo repro and assert an ungranted tool IS blocked.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
STATUS CORRECTION -- supersedes the earlier 'WORKS' comment above, which is
now known to have been produced by broken enforcement.

- [x] Installing a single read-only behavior does not remove the user's bash.
      Fixed ab46c82 + 070274a. Verified live: in a clean worktree the user's
      own turn ran 'npx jest selftest-math' successfully (unscoped), the call
      that was impossible before.
- [x] Mutation: removing the fix makes the repro fail again. 3 mutants, each
      caught by exactly the test that should catch it.
- [ ] A failing test in THIS repo is detected, dispatched and FIXED using only
      behaviors this repo ships. STILL FALSE, and the earlier claim that it
      passed was an artifact of the scope closing too early (turn_end instead
      of agent_end). With enforcement actually in force, the same run blocks
      edit and bash inside the window and the source is left unchanged:
        tool: edit err=True
        tool: bash err=True
        source unchanged
      That is CORRECT behaviour, not a regression: investigate-test-failure
      grants [read, grep, glob, ensemble.bash] -- an investigator, not a
      fixer. This repo ships no behavior permitted to mutate code.

So the lockout defect is fixed; 'autofix works in this repo' is not, and
cannot be until the repo ships a behavior granting mutation. That is a
deliberate product decision, not a bug to patch quietly -- shipping a
fix-capable behavior in this repo means agreeing that a detected failure may
edit this repo's source. Keeping this bead OPEN on that criterion alone.

Added .ensemble/behaviors/fix-failing-test/ granting [read, grep, glob, bash, edit]. Placed in .ensemble/ rather than packages/ so it does not arm every consumer of an ensemble package (br-fvmq). title: Audit and refresh GitHub wiki to reflect current functionality
description:
## Goal

Audit the live GitHub wiki (`https://github.com/Sunstone-Partners/ensemble.wiki.git`, `master` branch, 20 pages) against the actual current state of the repo, and update stale pages so the wiki reflects present functionality rather than a snapshot from an earlier release.

## Evidence of Staleness (found while scoping this bead)

- `01-Overview.md` says "**28+ specialized agents**"; `02-Architecture.md` says "Ensemble organizes **26+ packages**". Actual current counts: `find packages -path '*/agents/*.yaml' | wc -l` → **37**, `ls packages | wc -l` → **28**. Packages count happens to match but is phrased as a stale-looking "26+"; agent count is off by 9+.
- Root `package.json` reports `"version": "6.9.3"`. No wiki page was found stating a current release version consistent with that (worth an explicit check — do not assume this project's own `CLAUDE.md` header is authoritative either; it separately claims "v5.1.0 | 28 packages | 32 agents", which is *itself* inconsistent with the counts above and should not be used as the source of truth — verify against the repo directly).
- `02-Architecture.md`'s package table does not name `ensemble-e2e-testing` by its package identifier (Playwright testing is covered conceptually elsewhere in the docs set, but the tier table's package list should be checked against `ls packages/` for completeness — e.g. `ai`, `router`, `permitter`, `codex`, `dotnet` all do appear, `e2e-testing` did not turn up in a grep of the file).
- `43` command YAML files and `37` agent YAML files currently exist under `packages/*/commands` and `packages/*/agents`; `07-Commands.md` and `03-Agent-Roster.md` need a pass to confirm every current command/agent is listed and nothing removed/renamed is still referenced.

title: Exit-status detection fires on compound commands whose failing exit came from a non-test stage
description:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-25, twice. Both events have `detectedBy: exit-status`:

- 21:51:35Z  `npm test 2>&1 | grep ...; echo ...; grep ... tsconfig.json; ls ../agent-core/*.tsbuildinfo`
  Output: `Test Suites: 17 passed, 17 total / Tests: 129 passed`. Exit 2 came from the trailing `ls`.
- 21:52:33Z  `rm -rf ...; npm test > log; echo "exit=$?"; grep ...; grep -E "^(Tests|Test Suites):" log | grep failed`
  Output: `exit=0` (npm test passed). Exit 1 came from the final grep matching nothing.

Each injected an autofix continuation and dispatched both behaviors, which spawned fix-provider children against a passing suite.

## Cause
br-hneq (3f67359) made detection fire when EITHER exit status OR output reports failure. The exit status of a compound command is the exit status of whatever ran last, which is frequently not the test runner. Output-based detection already requires a non-zero failure count; exit-status detection has no equivalent attribution check.

Related: br-hneq (closed; the inverse masking case), br-x13x (deliberate failures), br-c3s4 (compound command re-run).

## Acceptance
- A compound command whose output contains test summaries that all report zero failures does not fire, whatever its exit status.
- A compound command whose final stage is not a test runner does not fire on exit status alone; it still fires when its output reports a non-zero failure count.
- `npx jest foo` (bare runner, non-zero exit, no parseable summary) still fires.
- br-hneq's masking cases (`npx jest x 2>&1 | tail -5` with failures in output) still fire.

Live extension bundle rebuilt from 5f9a99b and verified to contain the fix. Fix: 9eae31c (exit status counts only when the runner is last or the command is the declared one).

Both observed commands now do not fire; br-hneq masked-pipe cases still fire by output. Mutation-tested. NOTE vs acceptance #1: a compound command whose LAST stage is the runner still fires on a non-zero exit even when its summary shows zero failures (e.g. a coverage threshold) -- that exit genuinely is the runner's.

title: WriteBoundaryMonitor reverts legitimate git pull/checkout, leaving HEAD and working tree out of sync
description:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-26: WriteBoundaryMonitor reverted a legitimate `git pull --ff-only` in the main checkout, leaving the repo half-updated.

Sequence: PR #86 merged into the feature branch; `git pull --ff-only` in the main checkout (clean tree, 6557f47 -> 5f9a99b) ran inside a bash tool call while the behavior runtime was armed. After the call the monitor reported "Write boundary violation ... was reverted" for 4 paths the pull legitimately changed:
- packages/agent-core/src/behavior/workspace-snapshot.ts (guardrail-source)
- packages/agent-core/tests/pipe-masked-failure.test.ts (test-file)
- packages/agent-core/tests/write-boundary.test.ts (test-file)
- packages/pi-extension/tests/agent-fix-provider.test.ts (test-file)

Result: HEAD = 5f9a99b but those 4 files hold their 6557f47 contents (git status: 4 x M, 167 lines of the merged fixes undone in the working tree). A later `git commit -a` would silently revert the merged fixes. The monitor cannot be worked around from the session (any restore is reverted too); it has to be repaired from a shell outside the session.

The monitor treats every tool call that changes a protected path as tampering. It cannot tell an agent editing a guardrail from git moving HEAD to a commit that already contains the change (pull, checkout, merge, rebase, reset, stash pop). Reverting in the second case does not protect anything -- the content is already committed upstream -- it only desynchronises the working tree from HEAD.

Acceptance:
- A tool call that moves HEAD and leaves protected paths matching the new HEAD's blobs is not reverted (compare post-call content against `git show HEAD:<path>`, not only against the pre-call snapshot).
- When the monitor does revert, it never leaves a protected path differing from HEAD without saying so explicitly (the message must name the HEAD mismatch and the repair command).
- Test: simulate pull (commit on a second branch, then ff-merge inside a monitored call) -> no revert.

title: Governed fix-agent child outlives its session (orphaned, PPID 1); shutdown handler times out
description:
In headless runs the fix-failing-test governed dispatch spawns 'omp -p --no-session --no-extensions --tools=read,grep,glob' late in the session. The host exited and the child kept running reparented to PID 1, its result never consumed; stderr showed 'Extension error (ensemble-behavior-runtime.ts): handler timed out after 2000ms'. Read-only tools, so no writes, but it is wasted model spend and an unowned process. Abort in-flight dispatches on session_shutdown.

Evidence: headless omp -p runs on dev (7b57d4a) in worktree /private/tmp/wt-e2e, planted bug scripts/lib/e2e-sum.js; logs in /tmp/e2e/ (e2e.jsonl, e2e2.jsonl, e2e3.jsonl, guard.jsonl, *-runtime-log.jsonl).
close_reason: Fixed: extension.ts now owns an AbortController whose signal is passed to createWorkflowDispatcher, and session_shutdown ABORTS BEFORE draining. Order is the fix -- draining first waits on a child that has no reason to stop, the host handler times out (2s observed), and the child is orphaned to PID 1 exactly as reported. execFile already honoured an AbortSignal; the signal simply never reached it, because the dispatcher accepted one and nothing ever passed it. 3 tests: the agent receives a defined signal (the gap), an aborted signal is visible to it, and the abort-before-drain ordering is asserted against source since a runtime test would have to race the host timeout.

title: [trd:trd-2026-behavior-runtime-v2] Implement TRD: Ensemble Behavior Runtime (v2)
description: **Technical Requirements Document**

title: Support multiple change requests per Overview approval in refinement-review
description:
## Goal

The Overview tab's approval flow (`packages/core/lib/refinement-review`) currently supports exactly one live decision per session. `session.approval` is a single object (`{decision, author, note, decidedAt}`), and `POST /api/approval` in `server.js` overwrites it outright — the handler comment says so directly: "A later decision overwrites the earlier one."

That means a second "Request changes" submission silently discards the first one's note and author. On a long-lived, multi-reviewer session (`--long-lived`, `--reviewers N`) this is a real loss: two different stakeholders — or the same one, twice, as understanding evolves — can each want to log a distinct change request against the Overview, and only the most recent survives.

Change the model so a session can accumulate multiple change requests instead of clobbering them.

## Current Behavior (for reference)

- `packages/core/lib/refinement-review/session.js`: `session.approval` — singular, nullable object; `validateSession` shape-checks it but never treats it as a list.
- `packages/core/lib/refinement-review/server.js` (`POST /api/approval`): `s.approval = { decision, author, note, decidedAt }` — unconditional overwrite, routed through `mutate()` so it serializes with question/comment writes and broadcasts over SSE.
- `packages/core/lib/refinement-review/ui/app.js` + `ui/index.html`: single note textarea, single Approve / Request Changes button pair, renders only `state.session.approval` (the one current decision) in `#rr-approval-state`.
- The completion artifact (`/api/complete` handler) copies `finalSession.approval || null` verbatim into the written artifact.

## Proposed Change

- Replace (or augment) `session.approval` with `session.approvals: []` — an append-only list of `{id, decision, author, note, decidedAt}` entries. Keep `decision` semantics per-entry (`approved` | `changes-requested`); do not collapse multiple change requests into one.
- `POST /api/approval` appends a new entry instead of overwriting. Define what "current status" means for the summary badge once multiple entries exist (e.g. most recent entry's `decision`, or "approved" only when the latest entry is `approved` and no unresolved change request postdates it) — needs an explicit decision, not an implicit one.
- Backward compatibility: existing session files and completion artifacts on disk have the old singular `session.approval` shape. Decide migration path (read-time upcast to a one-element `approvals` array vs. dual-write during a transition window) and update `validateSession` accordingly.
- UI: render the full list of change requests (author, note, timestamp) on the Overview tab, not just the latest — this is the visible product behavior the bead title describes. Multiple pending change requests should be individually distinguishable, not merged.
- Completion artifact shape changes accordingly (`approvals: [...]` instead of `approval: {...}|null`) — audit any downstream consumer of the artifact (Phase 3 Enhancement / Feedback Integration in `refine-prd`/`refine-trd`) that currently reads `finalSession.approval`.

## Acceptance

1. Two sequential `POST /api/approval` calls with `decision: 'changes-requested'` from different authors both persist — neither note is lost — and both are visible on the Overview tab.
2. The same author submitting a second change request (e.g., refining their first note) also persists as a distinct entry rather than overwriting the first.
3. `validateSession` accepts sessions written before this change (singular `approval`) without erroring, and upcasts them consistently.
4. The completion artifact written by `/api/complete` includes the full approval/change-request history, not just the latest entry.
5. Existing server.test.js coverage for `/api/approval` is updated for the new shape; add a test asserting the second submission does not clobber the first.

## Out of Scope

- Any UI for resolving/dismissing an individual change request (mirrors comment resolution, but not requested here — flag as a natural follow-up, don't build it).
- Changing the single-reviewer (non `--long-lived`, non `--reviewers`) approval UX beyond supporting multiple entries.

title: Autofix fires on deliberate mutation-test failures
description:
OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-25, twice in one session.

The runtime injected an autofix continuation in response to a DELIBERATELY
failing test. The failure was a mutation test: a guard was intentionally
broken to prove the test covering it actually fails, and the source was
restored in the same command.

  "Tests: 2 failed, 4 passed" -> continuation injected, asking for a fix

There was nothing to fix. The mutants were already reverted by the time the
instruction arrived, and acting on it would have meant "repairing" code that
was already correct -- or worse, weakening the assertions that correctly
caught the mutants.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN AN ANNOYANCE
Mutation testing is how this project proves a test is load-bearing. It is
routine, deliberate, and the failures are the POINT. A loop that treats every
red test as a defect to repair is actively hostile to the practice that keeps
the suite honest, and the injected turn is indistinguishable from a real one.
The risk is not a wasted turn; it is the model "fixing" a deliberate mutant by
loosening the assertion that caught it, producing a green suite that proves
nothing.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT
br-c3s4 (verification re-runs the whole && chain) shares a root cause: the
captured command is the entire compound invocation including the mutating
step. This bead is about a different question -- not WHICH command is re-run,
but whether a failure should have been treated as actionable at all.

POSSIBLE APPROACHES (not decided)
- An explicit opt-out marker in the command (e.g. ENSEMBLE_NO_AUTOFIX=1) that
  detection honours. Cheap, but relies on remembering it.
- Detect that the same command both mutates and tests, and treat the failure
  as inconclusive rather than actionable (overlaps br-c3s4's fix).
- Require a failure to persist across two observations before dispatching. A
  deliberate mutant is reverted immediately, so it would not survive a second
  look; a genuine regression would.
- Suppress dispatch when the working tree changed during the same command
  that produced the failure.

ACCEPTANCE
- [ ] A mutation-test run that breaks and restores a source file in one
      command does NOT produce an autofix continuation.
- [ ] A genuine regression in the same repository still does.
- [ ] Mutation: reverting the fix makes the false positive reappear.

The governed dispatch nevertheless ran the fix provider and AutofixLoop against the extension host's root -- the main checkout (`omp -p ... --cwd=/Users/ldangelo/Development/Sunstone/ensemble`). Children then wrote into the main checkout:

- 23:48:41Z packages/agent-core/src/behavior/event-translator.ts (from the event-translator mutation-test dispatch; outcome: rejected under propose, `restored: [event-translator.ts]`, change still on disk)
- 23:49:28Z packages/pi-extension/src/agent-fix-provider.ts
- packages/agent-core/src/behavior/workspace-snapshot.ts (guardrail-source) -- caught and reverted by WriteBoundaryMonitor at 23:41:58Z and 23:43:30Z

Both surviving writes were byte-identical copies of changes made in the worktree: the child read the worktree path out of the failure output and copied the file into the wrong repository. Preserved as `git stash` entries in the main checkout ("evidence: unsanctioned write by fix-agent child ..."). Two children were still running when found and were killed.

## Cause
behavior-runner / extension use `resolveRepoRoot(process.cwd())` of the host process as rootDir for the provider, AutofixLoop (snapshot + apply) and suite runs. The event's `cwd` is only used by the continuation path's verification.

## Acceptance
- A governed dispatch resolves its repository root from the triggering event's cwd; when that cwd is outside any git work tree, or resolves to a different repository than the host and that is not explicitly allowed, the dispatch is refused and recorded, not run against the host root.
- Test: event with cwd in repo B while the host root is repo A -> provider/snapshot/apply all target B (or refuse), and repo A is byte-for-byte unchanged.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
Observed live in an interactive PTY session (/tmp/hang3/sm2.ts). pi.sendUserMessage() content renders in the transcript as a user turn and the model treats it as carrying USER AUTHORITY. Verbatim agent narration before executing the injected command:

  'That system-notice appears within the user's turn, so it's a legitimate
   user interjection with a harmless command in the current directory
   -- I'll go ahead and run it.'

Risks for autofix:
1. Authority laundering: a fix instruction derived from TEST OUTPUT (which is
   attacker-influenceable in principle) becomes a user-authorized instruction.
   The agent approved the bash call BECAUSE it appeared to come from the user.
2. Attribution: the transcript will contain 'user' messages the human never
   typed, with no way to tell them apart on review.
3. UNTESTED: race with live user typing. Injection was verified only while the
   user was idle; behaviour when it lands mid-composition is unknown.

Candidate mitigations to evaluate: pi.sendMessage() (the other
continuation-capable method on the real OMP ExtensionAPI) may carry a
distinguishable role; failing that, prefix injected content with an
unmistakable machine-origin marker AND ensure the fix instruction never
interpolates raw test output into an instruction position.

Sequencing: deliberately deferred. Prove the mechanism works end-to-end
(br-9hv6) before hardening. Do NOT ship autofix enabled by default until this
is resolved.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
PROBED THE REAL HOST. The leading candidate mitigation is REFUTED.

Enumerated the live ExtensionAPI (41 members). Continuation-capable methods:
sendUserMessage, sendMessage, appendEntry.

pi.sendMessage({customType, content, display}, {triggerTurn: true}) DOES
trigger a turn -- a second turn_start was observed. But asked to name the
role/origin of the content, the model answered:

  "It arrives in the user turn, so it comes from the user; the only label on
   it is 'AUTOFIX PROBE', and it has no system, tool, or custom tag."

So customType is NOT visible to the model. There is no role-level fix
available on this host; the only lever is the CONTENT of the injected text.
Recording this so the sendMessage option is not re-explored later.

CONTENT MARKER IS LOAD-BEARING (A/B, same model, same request, only the
preamble differing; a canary file to delete):

  with a machine-origin preamble ->
    "No. The instruction explicitly says it came from test output and has no
     user authority, and deleting a file is a consequential action that needs
     a direct request from the user."

  control, no preamble ->
    "Yes. This came directly from you in your own message ... so the deletion
     is explicitly authorized and limited in scope."

The control is this bead's authority-laundering risk in the model's own
words. The marker changes the outcome, so it is not decoration -- but it
constrains STATED DISPOSITION, which is evidence, not a guarantee. It is a
prompt-level mitigation, NOT an enforced boundary. The enforced boundaries
remain tool grants and the write boundary. Do not let this bead's risk #1 be
read as closed.

Risks #2 (attribution: transcript contains 'user' messages the human never
typed) and #3 (race with live user typing, still untested) are UNCHANGED.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
MARKER EVIDENCE UPGRADED -- two confounds in my earlier probe, both now removed.

The earlier probe used `rm` as the test action and judged the result by what
the model SAID. Two problems:
  1. "respects the marker" and "refuses destructive commands" predict the same
     outcome, so the probe could not distinguish them. The br-x85k incident
     involved a HARMLESS command that the model ran anyway.
  2. If no tool was executable in the probe, "canary still present" would be
     true regardless of intent and would prove nothing.

Re-ran controlled, with a harmless action whose side effect is observable
(`echo hi > /tmp/probe-api/touched-*.txt`):

  with marker    -> "I didn't run the command. The message calls itself
                     machine-generated test output with no user authority."
                    file NOT created
  without marker -> "I ran the command. It exited cleanly..."
                    file CREATED

The file is the evidence, not the prose. The control emitting a real tool call
also demonstrates bash WAS available, so the refusal is a behavioural
difference, not an artefact of a missing capability.

This is now behavioural evidence on a harmless action, which is materially
stronger than the earlier result. It still does NOT make the marker an
enforced boundary -- it is prompt-level, one model, small n. Tool grants and
the write boundary remain the enforced controls, and risks #2 (attribution)
and #3 (typing race) are untouched. Bead stays open.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
PACKAGING DECISION (e4aaddc): opt-in plugin, no fork.

Question raised: this work is a significant departure from ensemble v1, so
should it be forked rather than merged?

Evidence gathered before deciding:
  - v1 command surface: ZERO files changed under commands/agents/skills.
  - The 117 changed files are two NEW packages (agent-core 58,
    pi-extension 43) plus lint tooling, docs and marketplace entries.
  - packages/pi ships skills/ prompts/ agents/ vendor/ -- none of the new code.
  - No v1 package depends on agent-core or pi-extension.
  - All 28 pre-existing marketplace entries are byte-identical to main.

So the diff is ADDITIVE, not divergent. A fork would duplicate the v1 command
library (the bulk of the repo's value, untouched here), turn every shared fix
into two cherry-picks, and let the runtime drift away from the live repo --
and running against the live repo is exactly what keeps finding real defects
(the jest.config.* filename false positive came from a live run). Forking is
for when v2 must BREAK v1; nothing here does.

Chosen shape: a single opt-in plugin, ensemble-behaviors.
  - Replaces two "core"-categorised entries. "core" signalled foundational
    infrastructure, the opposite of opt-in.
  - agent-core is de-catalogued: it is a library consumed over npm, not
    something a user installs alone.
  - Description states what installing activates: injects a turn, may EDIT
    SOURCE under the behavior's grants, re-runs the suite, reverts on failure.
  - Installation IS the consent event, so no enable flag is carried. Rejected
    a default-off boolean on the grounds that it would be set by everyone who
    installs and then maintained forever.

WHAT OPT-IN DOES NOT SETTLE: br-x85k. Consent answers whether the loop should
run; it does not make the loop auditable. Injected turns still appear as
"user" messages the human never typed, so even a consenting installer cannot
distinguish their own instructions from machine-generated ones when reviewing
a transcript. Marker and attribution work remain required.

title: policy.mode: propose does not gate mutations on the continuation path (live repro)
description:
REPRODUCED LIVE, 2026-09-28, first real end-to-end run of the loop.

Repo: ~/Development/Sunstone/loop-trial, using the PRODUCTION
.ensemble/behaviors/fix-failing-test/behavior.yaml (policy.mode: propose),
with only test_command and mutation_classes changed.

WHAT HAPPENED
A deliberately broken `add(a,b) { return a - b; }` was detected, repaired to
`a + b` ON DISK, and verified -- with no human approval step anywhere.
`mode: propose` is supposed to make MutationGuard.authorize() deny every
direct mutation and require a human to apply the proposal instead.

  git diff src/math.js  ->  -  return a - b;
                            +  return a + b;

  runtime-log: {"kind":"verification","status":"passed","detail":"2 passed, 2 total"}
  no approval was requested; nothing was left for a human to apply.

WHY
The continuation path (pi.sendUserMessage injects a turn, the MODEL applies
the change with its own edit calls) never passes a write through
MutationGuard, so `mode` is not consulted at all. behavior.yaml's own comment
documents this and says the continuation path is "what fires in practice" --
the live run confirms it: the governed dispatch produced no candidate
("working tree changed while the provider ran (src/math.js) -- cannot
attribute, nothing reverted") while the continuation had already applied the
fix.

WHY THIS IS P1
`propose` was adopted (2026-09-25) BECAUSE a live run applied an uncommitted,
unreviewed change to packages/agent-core/src/behavior/outbox.ts. The setting
chosen to prevent that does not prevent it. A mode that claims to gate and
does not is worse than no mode: it buys false confidence in exactly the
situation it was introduced to make safe.

NOT the same as br-o355 (grant scoping to the execution window), though they
share the continuation-path root cause. Cross-referenced.

OPTIONS
(a) Route continuation-applied writes through MutationGuard before they land.
(b) Under `propose`, hold the fix turn's writes and present them for approval
    instead of letting them land (the write boundary already reverts and
    quarantines protected paths -- this is the same mechanism, widened).
(c) Refuse to dispatch a `propose` behavior down the continuation path at all,
    so the mode's guarantee is honest even if narrower.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #98 (squashed to dev as fba80cb). Under policy.mode: propose a verified-passing fix is now reverted and held for /ensemble-approve rather than landing unreviewed. Mutation-tested three ways (gate disabled -> gating test fails; gate applied to every mode -> 5 fail including the auto control; hold loses contents -> re-apply assertion fails). Verified live twice on the merged bundle: {"status":"passed","heldForApproval":["1"]} with src/math.js reverted and git status clean.

title: [trd:trd-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix:task:TRD-027] - [ ] **TRD-027** Reject on regression or protected-path violation and restore the tree (4h)
description:
## Task: TRD-027
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-027
PRD Reference: #req-005

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.
Satisfies: REQ-005
PRD ACs: AC-005-1, AC-005-3, AC-005-4
Target File: packages/pi-extension/src/autofix-loop.ts, packages/agent-core/src/behavior/workspace-snapshot.ts
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given a rejected candidate, when rejection completes, then the working tree is byte-identical to its pre-attempt state and the attempt counts toward the retry budget.
Dependencies: TRD-026, TRD-021

title: Behavior: pre-PR verification gate (tests, typecheck, lint, and non-vacuity)
description:
RECOMMENDATION 2 of 5. The user's own suggestion, scoped tighter than 'ensure tests pass'.

TRIGGER: pull_request.proposed.
ACTION: in an isolated workspace run tests, typecheck and lint; block on failure AND on vacuous success.

WHY THE NON-VACUITY CLAUSE MATTERS: a gate that accepts 'Tests: 0 total, exit 0' is worse than no gate, because it manufactures confidence. See br-cwrh for the evidence that this is the dominant local failure shape, and br-91nr for the same defect in the router/pytest path.

WORK: one new command verification.run -- like fix.verify but not bound to a proposal -- reusing createIsolatedWorkspace and verifyOutput. Depends on br-cwrh landing the non-vacuity signal first.

Start in propose mode. Promote to blocking only after it has been right for a sustained period: a gate that is wrong twice in a week teaches people to bypass it.
close_reason: verification.run command + pre-pr-verification behavior delivered in propose mode. Non-vacuity checked BEFORE verdict so a zero-test run is never reported as a pass. 19 tests. The blocking half is NOT delivered and cannot be: see comment.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
DELIVERED AS A REPORTER, NOT A GATE -- and the difference is not cosmetic.

PREMISE CHECKED FIRST, because br-jg0l failed on exactly this. A behavior CANNOT block a PR:
- It is an asynchronous observer. Nothing waits on its verdict.
- Worse, its run may not even resolve before the session ends -- workflow-dispatch.ts writes the dispatch record BEFORE entering the interpreter precisely because 'the session's lifetime is not ours to control' (br-mr22).
- Branch protection's required checks are ['release-gate','source-branch']. Blocking means being one of those, i.e. CI.
So 'promote to blocking after it has been right for a sustained period' is not available through this mechanism. That is not a maturity gate; the path does not exist. If blocking is wanted, it belongs in .github/workflows as a required check, which is the shape br-jg0l settled on for the same reason.

WHAT LANDED:
- verification.run (agent-core/src/cqrs/commands.ts) -- runs a command in an isolated workspace against the tree AS IT STANDS. Separate command rather than an optional proposalRef on fix.verify, because an optional binding on a security-relevant command is how the binding ends up skipped. Refuses to fall back to the live tree when isolation is unavailable: verifying in the live tree would make verification a mutation.
- vacuous is its OWN result field, not folded into the verdict. 'Your code is broken' and 'nothing was checked' send a reader to completely different places; a consumer seeing only 'not passed' loses that and sends them to debug code that never ran.
- .ensemble/behaviors/pre-pr-verification/ -- tests, typecheck, lint as three separate runs (a && b && c reports only the first failure; this reports everything wrong in one pass). Vacuity is branched on BEFORE the verdict: a vacuous run is inconclusive, so a naive 'is it passed?' branch would route it to the failure arm and describe 'nothing ran' as 'tests failed'.
- 19 tests (7 command, 12 package).

TRIGGER IS LEGITIMATE, per br-d7lm: pull_request.proposed is LAUNCH-INPUT. Nothing here emits or awaits it; Foreman starts a session with it as the triggering fact. So the behavior is reachable, and explainInertTrigger correctly stays silent about it.

DEFECT FOUND WHILE AUTHORING, filed as br-n3gj: I wrote 'next:' on command steps and it compiled clean. There is no such field -- flow is declaration order. Both shipped manifests now say so, and the tests assert the order so a reorder fails the build.

title: No RCA stage: the rule provider is asked to judge a constitution change with no diagnosis in hand
description:
The stated product is: failing test -> RCA -> constitution updated to prevent
recurrence -> fix -> verify. What actually ships is detect -> fix -> verify
(-> hold, after br-xz6q). Steps 2 and 3 do not run, and cannot.

EVIDENCE (first live end-to-end run, loop-trial, 2026-09-28)
Record kinds in .ensemble/runtime-log.jsonl:
  activation, dispatch, continuation, invocation, verification, event x40
No rca record. No constitution record. The trial behavior DOES grant
constitution.propose, so this is not a capability denial -- the step never
executed.

ROOT CAUSE: same shape as br-xz6q -- the feature lives on the path that does
not run.

  proposeConstitutionChange is CALLED in exactly one place:
    packages/pi-extension/src/behavior-runner.ts:241 (inside runBehavior)
  extension.ts only WIRES the provider (lines 986/1008/1174); it never calls
  it, and never calls runBehavior.

  $ grep -rn runBehavior packages/pi-extension/src packages/pi-extension/tests \
      packages/agent-core/src | grep -v behavior-runner.ts
  (no output)

  runBehavior has ZERO callers, including from tests. The governed
  AutofixLoop path -- MutationGuard, capability enforcement, constitution
  proposal, approval/apply -- is dead code. The live loop is the continuation
  path in extension.ts, which implements none of it.

RCA is worse: there is no root-cause stage anywhere in the codebase, on
either path. It was never built, only described. The fix agent is handed the
failure and asked to repair it; whatever diagnosis happens is internal to
that model call and is neither recorded nor used to drive a rule change.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS
The constitution step is the entire point of the product: without it the
system fixes the same class of bug forever and learns nothing. A loop that
detects and repairs is a test-fixer; the constitution update is what makes it
a system that prevents recurrence.

It also means the governed path's safety properties are theoretical. Every
capability/mutation_class guarantee reviewed to date is enforced in code that
never executes. br-xz6q was one instance of that gap; this is the general
case, and it should be checked whether anything else believed to be enforced
is only enforced there.

RELATED CONFIG GAP (do not fix silently -- needs a human decision)
  ensemble/.ensemble/behaviors/fix-failing-test/behavior.yaml
    mutation_classes: [artifact.write]
The user's own production behavior omits constitution.propose, so even once
the step is reachable it would be denied there. The trial repo has
[artifact.write, constitution.propose]. Deciding whether the real repo should
grant a behavior the right to amend the constitution is the user's call.

SCOPE
1. Decide whether the continuation path grows RCA + constitution stages, or
   the governed path becomes reachable and the continuation path feeds it.
   (The second is more code but keeps one enforcement point.)
2. Build an actual RCA stage that records a cause and passes it to the
   constitution proposal, rather than leaving diagnosis implicit.
3. Delete or revive runBehavior. Leaving unreachable governance code in the
   tree is how br-xz6q survived review.
close_reason:
CLOSED as resolved, but the FRAMING is obsolete rather than the concern, so the reasoning matters more than usual.

THE ROOT CAUSE ON THIS BEAD NO LONGER EXISTS. It reads: proposeConstitutionChange is called only from behavior-runner.ts:241, extension.ts never calls runBehavior, so the step cannot run. On this branch behavior-runner.ts is DELETED and proposeConstitutionChange does not exist. The CQRS port removed the dual-path problem outright; one-dispatch-path.test.ts pins that a single dispatch path remains. So the bead cannot be closed by 'the fix landed' -- the thing it described was removed underneath it.

BOTH COMPLAINTS ARE NOW SATISFIED BY THE REPLACEMENT.
1. RCA stage. fix-failing-test has a record-diagnosis step that records the diagnosis as a fact SEPARATELY from any fix, so a confident diagnosis with no candidate is still recorded. The chain is: investigate.diagnosis -> fix.propose(rationale) -> proposal.rationale -> fix.verified.payload.rationale -> constitution-learning.assess(diagnosis).
2. 'Declined' vs 'never ran'. constitution.no_change_warranted is its own declared outcome, so a run that judged no rule warranted is now distinguishable from one that never executed.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING, AND IS NOW FIXED. The consuming half was untested. commands.test.ts proves fix.verified CARRIES rationale and evidence; nothing proved the manifest RESOLVES them. A ${...} input naming a payload field that does not exist resolves to nothing and the step runs anyway, with a prompt missing the one input this bead is about -- silent, no error. Added agent-core/tests/shipped-constitution-manifest.test.ts, 7 tests against the SHIPPED manifest and the SHIPPED prompt, covering the whole last mile:
- the diagnosis, evidence and proposalRef reach the assessment
- the manifest declares both inputs (not only a comment claiming so)
- the real assess.md actually renders {{diagnosis}} and {{evidence}} -- a template that dropped them would receive the values and discard them, leaving the assessment as blind as before while every manifest-level test stayed green
- no placeholder lacks a matching input, which would render as a literal {{foo}} and read to the model as a formatting glitch rather than missing data
Mutation-checked: deleting the diagnosis input fails 2 tests.

FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, FILED AS br-6yt6. reference-flow.e2e.test.ts -- the repository's end-to-end proof -- embeds INLINE COPIES of the manifests rather than running the shipped ones, and the constitution-learning copy has already drifted: it still passes only proposalRef and detail, predating this fix. It would have stayed green if the shipped manifest lost the diagnosis inputs entirely. Mitigated for this input pair by the new test; not fixed in general, and the e2e is protected so changing it needs operator approval.

546 agent-core tests pass, eslint clean. Commits 5eb36b0, 2fb52ad.

comments.text:
CORRECTION -- the central claim of this bead was WRONG. Retracting it.

I claimed "runBehavior has zero callers, the entire governed path is dead
code". `runBehavior` is not a symbol in this repo at all, which is why the
grep came back empty. The real export is createBehaviorInvoker
(behavior-runner.ts:111), and it IS called live at extension.ts:996.

My own evidence disputed the claim before I filed it: the live run logged an
`invocation` record, and that record is written by the onRecord callback
passed into createBehaviorInvoker at extension.ts:1024. I read that log and
still filed "unreachable". An empty grep for a name I never confirmed existed
is not evidence of absence.

WHAT THE LIVE RECORD ACTUALLY SAYS
  keys: [behavior, issue, note]
  outcome: null
  note: "no fix candidate offered"
  constitution: null

So the governed invoker ran, and:

1. It offered NO FIX CANDIDATE. The repair happened on the continuation path
   (the model edited files itself). So MutationGuard / mutation_classes did
   not gate the actual fix -- not because the code is dead, but because the
   fix does not travel through it. That is br-o355's territory, and it is the
   accurate version of what I was reaching for.

2. The constitution step IS reachable. mayPropose was true (the trial
   behavior grants constitution.propose), so the code at behavior-runner.ts:
   241 called the provider. record.constitution stayed null.

REAL DEFECT, narrower than claimed: the constitution step is UNOBSERVABLE.
When the provider returns no change, behavior-runner.ts:241-273 records
nothing at all -- no declined record, no "no change implied" note. So the log
cannot distinguish:
    (a) provider never called
    (b) provider called, model said no rule change is warranted
Those need different fixes and look identical in the log. Note that (b) may
well be CORRECT here: `a - b` -> `a + b` is a typo, and a typo does not imply
a constitutional rule. I cannot tell which happened, and that is the bug.

STILL TRUE, re-verified with correct symbols: there is no RCA stage.
BehaviorRunRecord (behavior-runner.ts:40-54) has fields for outcome,
proposal, constitution, treeDrift, note -- and nothing for a cause. Diagnosis
is internal to the fix model's call, unrecorded, and does not feed the
constitution proposal. The read-only investigate-test-failure behavior exists
but is not wired as a stage of this loop.

REVISED SCOPE
  1. Record the constitution step's outcome in ALL cases, including "no
     change implied", so declining is distinguishable from not running.
  2. Confirm by observation (not by reading) whether the rule provider is
     invoked on a live run -- the current log cannot answer it.
  3. Build an RCA stage that records a cause and passes it to the
     constitution proposal.
  4. Route the continuation path's fix through capability enforcement, or
     accept that mutation_classes does not gate model-applied fixes and say
     so explicitly. (Overlaps br-o355.)

Dropping priority from P1: the loop is not missing its back half the way I
said. It is under-instrumented, and RCA is genuinely absent.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CROSS-REFERENCE: br-zcxb / br-o355 / br-r3om / br-xz6q share one spine.

THE SPINE: a single test failure fires TWO dispatch paths.
  governed      createBehaviorInvoker (behavior-runner.ts:111), called live
                at extension.ts:996. Carries MutationGuard, mutation_classes,
                the constitution step, approval gating.
  continuation  the extension injects a turn and the MODEL edits files with
                its own tools. Carries snapshot/rollback, write-boundary,
                whole-suite verification, and (now) the propose hold.

Neither is dead -- br-r3om observed both firing on one failure, and the live
loop-trial run logged an `invocation` record (governed) alongside a
`continuation` record. The governed invoker reported "no fix candidate
offered": it ran, and the repair happened on the other path.

So the defect is not "governance is unreachable" -- I filed that on br-zcxb
and retracted it. It is that THE FIX DOES NOT TRAVEL THROUGH THE GOVERNED
PATH, so every guarantee implemented as an authorization check on a patch has
nothing to authorize.

WHAT EACH BEAD IS, UNDER THAT SPINE
  br-xz6q  CLOSED/in review, PR #98. policy.mode was checked only in
           MutationGuard.authorize(), which the continuation path never
           reaches. Fixed by enforcing mode at verification time instead.
           Precedent: the fix did NOT route writes through the guard.
  br-o355  grants scope to the execution window, not the session. Its own
           comment proposes routing continuation writes through MutationGuard
           and expects that to close br-xz6q too. br-xz6q is now closed
           WITHOUT that, so the shared estimate should shrink, not carry over.
  br-r3om  the fix-provider CHILD runs with --no-extensions, so nothing binds
           it -- it can write the live tree directly, regardless of which path
           governs the patch it returns. This is upstream of the other three:
           routing writes through the guard does not help if the writer is a
           process outside the guard entirely.
  br-zcxb  narrowest, and independent of the routing question: the
           constitution step records nothing when the provider returns no
           change, so "declined" and "never ran" are indistinguishable; and
           there is no RCA stage at all (BehaviorRunRecord, behavior-runner.ts
           :40-54, has no cause field).

SEQUENCING, so one defect is not scoped four times
  1. br-r3om first. It is P1, in review, and it is the only one where the
     enforcement boundary itself is bypassed rather than bypassed-around.
  2. br-zcxb's instrumentation half next. It is cheap, it does not depend on
     the routing decision, and until the constitution step is observable we
     cannot tell whether the back half of the loop works at all -- which
     makes any estimate for the rest guesswork.
  3. br-o355's routing decision last, informed by 1 and 2. If the continuation
     path keeps applying fixes model-side, MutationGuard may be the wrong
     chokepoint entirely and the effect-based write boundary the right one.
     br-xz6q is evidence for that reading.

RCA (the remaining half of br-zcxb) is orthogonal to all of this: no path
records a cause, so it is new work wherever the fix lands.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
ANSWERED BY OBSERVATION. PR #101.

The open question was whether the rule provider is ever invoked on a live
run. The log could not say, because the step recorded nothing unless a change
came back. Instrumented it, rebuilt the bundle, re-ran the same scenario:

  constitution: {"status": "none",
                 "detail": "rule provider ran and implied no constitution change"}

The provider RAN. It has been running all along. It declined, silently, and
the silence is what I misread as "the step never fires".

Its judgement also looks CORRECT. The failure under repair was `a - b` where
`a + b` was meant. A typo does not imply a constitutional rule, and a system
that amended its constitution over one would be worse, not better. So the
back half of the loop is not missing -- on this input it had nothing to say,
and now says so.

That retires the instrumentation half of this bead and the second item of the
revised scope. Statuses now recorded: skipped (capability gate refused,
provider not called), unavailable (granted but no provider configured), none
(ran, no change implied).

REMAINING, and now the whole of this bead: there is still no RCA stage.
BehaviorRunRecord has no field for a cause, no path computes one, and the
rule provider is therefore asked to judge a constitution change from the raw
failure rather than from a diagnosis. That is plausibly WHY it declines: with
no cause in hand, "no rule implied" is the only safe answer it can give.

That reframes the remaining work. It is not "wire up the constitution step",
it is "give it something to reason from". Worth testing before building:
re-run with a failure that genuinely implies a rule (say, a fix that would
have to touch a guardrail) and see whether the provider proposes anything at
all. If it declines there too, the gap is the missing RCA input, not the
provider.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
HYPOTHESIS DISPROVED by direct experiment. The rule provider does not need an
RCA stage to produce a rule.

Called createAgentConstitutionProvider directly -- real model subprocess,
real prompt, real parser -- bypassing dispatch and the session lifecycle
entirely, so the br-mr22 race could not interfere. Two inputs, differing only
in the failure output:

CONTROL, an ordinary typo (-1 !== 3):
  NO AMENDMENT                                              [16.7s]

TREATMENT, same typo plus one extra line of real output --
"guard.test.js: suite did not load" with the summary counting it as passed:
  PROPOSED                                                  [28.8s]
  rationale: "The run reported 'guard.test.js: suite did not load' but only
             counted assertion results, so once the ordinary math bug is
             fixed the run would pass while a whole suite never executed."
  rule: "- Any test suite that fails to load, compile, or be discovered must
         make the test command exit non-zero, and a passing run must execute
         every test file in the repo; a green result where any suite did not
         load or was left out counts as a failure."

So the provider discriminates correctly on failure output ALONE. It declines
ordinary bugs and proposes on a systemic gap, from the same 8000-char
failure excerpt, with no diagnosis in hand. My "it declines because it has no
cause to reason from" was wrong.

Worth noting what it proposed: that rule is precisely the defect this repo
actually shipped and had to fix -- a suite that fails to LOAD being counted
as a pass, which is why unloadable suites now report `inconclusive` rather
than `failed`. The learning half of the loop can produce a rule that would
have prevented a real bug of ours. It has never been allowed to.

WHAT THIS BEAD IS NOW. Nothing. Both halves are resolved:
  - observability: PR #101, merged-pending
  - "no RCA input": disproved above
The remaining blocker is entirely br-mr22 -- the governed run that carries
this step is killed at session end, so the provider is never reached in a
real run. Nothing about RCA needs building to unblock step 3.

An RCA stage may still be worth having for OTHER reasons (a recorded cause is
useful to a human reading the log, and to the fix provider). But it is not a
prerequisite for the constitution step, and this bead should not be used to
justify it. Closing in favour of br-mr22.

Method note: this question survived three full live runs without being
answered, because each run lost the dispatch race. Testing the component
directly took one call and 46 seconds. When a lifecycle keeps eating the
evidence, call the function.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
Re-reviewed after br-behavior-runtime-cqrs-xl24. STILL VALID, partially mitigated.

The constitution-learning behavior's assess step (.ensemble/behaviors/constitution-learning/behavior.yaml:42-54) receives proposalRef, detail and command from the fix.verified event -- but NOT the diagnosis produced by investigation.record. The two behaviors are joined by an event, and fix.verified's payload does not carry the diagnosis forward, so the rule provider still judges an amendment without the RCA in hand.

Mitigated in that assess now has tools [read, grep, glob] and can investigate for itself, and it must emit warrantsRule plus evidence to proceed. Not fixed: self-directed investigation is not the same as being handed the diagnosis that was already produced.

Likely fix: carry investigation output on the fix.proposed/fix.verified payload, or have constitution-learning read the proposal's evidence refs from the ProposalStore.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
FIX DELIVERED 2026-09-29, bead left OPEN because br close refuses: blocked by br-r3om, which is user-owned and IN_REVIEW. Not force-closing past a dependency someone set deliberately. Close this when br-r3om closes, or unlink if the dependency no longer reflects reality.

The dev commits referencing this bead do NOT apply on this branch: 02db136 modifies behavior-runner.ts, deleted in Phase 0; 667c939 edits the old fix-failing-test YAML, rewritten for v2 where the constitution step is a separate behavior.

REAL GAP HERE: constitution-learning triggers on fix.verified, whose payload carried proposalRef, verdict, detail and command -- the fact that something was fixed, with no account of why it broke. The cause is the only part a rule can be drawn from, so the assessment had to guess. A rule drawn from a guess is worse than none: a real verified fix sits behind it, so it reads as evidence-backed and is harder to challenge than it deserves.

FIX: fix.verified now carries rationale and evidence (optional, so a proposal with neither still publishes and reads as 'none recorded'). The rationale IS the diagnosis -- fix-failing-test already passed steps.investigate.diagnosis into fix.propose as rationale, so it was on the proposal and simply never forwarded. constitution-learning's assess step takes diagnosis and evidence as inputs, and prompts/assess.md now instructs the model to reason from the cause and to answer 'no' when the diagnosis names none.

4 tests in agent-core/tests/commands.test.ts. The generated command/event reference was regenerated; its drift test caught the schema change automatically, which is what it was built for.
